q: An atom’s valence electrons are found in which shell?
e: Valence electrons are the outermost shell’s electrons — the ones involved in bonding.

q: Carbon (atomic number 6) has how many valence electrons?
e: Carbon sits in group 14, and for the p-block you subtract ten: 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons. Those four are the only electrons that bond, which is why carbon forms four bonds and why the whole subject is built on it.

q: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. In a neutral molecule, how many bonds and lone pairs does it carry?
e: Every shared pair counts toward the octet of both partners, so for a second-row atom bonds + lone pairs = 4. Nitrogen brings 5 electrons of its own: three of them go into bonds (each picking up a partner's electron to make 3 shared pairs) and the remaining two stay behind as one lone pair.

q: A structure shows an oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair. What has to be written on that oxygen?
e: Neutral oxygen takes 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Here it has swapped a lone pair for a third bond, so it owns only half of that pair instead of all of it: one electron fewer than a free oxygen atom, which is a +1.

q: Two isotopes of the same element always have the same number of:
e: Isotopes share the same number of protons (same element) but differ in neutron count, which changes the mass number.

q: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
e: Neutral atoms have no net charge, so the negative electrons exactly balance the positive protons.

q: An atom's mass number is the sum of its:
e: Electrons contribute negligible mass, so mass number counts only protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

q: A neutral atom that gains an extra electron becomes:
e: Adding an electron gives the atom one more negative charge than positive, making it a negatively charged anion.

q: Electrons travel around the nucleus in fixed, planet-like circular orbits.
e: Modern quantum theory describes electrons as occupying probability clouds (orbitals), not fixed circular paths — the old planetary picture is an oversimplification.

q: Nitrogen has atomic number 7. A neutral nitrogen atom contains how many protons?
e: Atomic number is defined as the number of protons, so atomic number 7 means 7 protons (and, when neutral, 7 electrons).

q: An oxygen atom (8 protons) that has gained 2 extra electrons (10 electrons total) carries an overall charge of:
e: Charge equals protons minus electrons: 8 − 10 = −2, consistent with the oxide ion O²⁻ that oxygen commonly forms.

q: All atoms of a given element must contain the same number of neutrons.
e: Atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts — these variants are isotopes, and they still behave identically in chemical reactions.

q: Which pair of atoms bonds by transferring an electron outright rather than sharing one?
e: Transfer is only cheap when one atom gives an electron up easily and the other takes it eagerly. Sodium has a single loose valence electron and chlorine is one short of a full shell, so the electron moves across and the resulting Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract electrostatically.

q: A carbon is drawn with a double bond to oxygen and single bonds to two hydrogens. How many electrons surround that carbon?
e: Count shared pairs, not neighbors. The double bond is two shared pairs and each C–H is one more, so four pairs — eight electrons, a full octet. The slip this question is built on is counting three neighboring atoms and concluding the carbon is two electrons short.

q: A group leaves a carbon and takes the shared pair with it. How many valence electrons does that carbon have left?
e: The carbon started with four bonds, so eight electrons surrounded it. Losing a whole bonding pair removes two of them, leaving three bonds and six electrons — an incomplete octet with an empty orbital.

q: The second electron shell (n = 2) can hold a maximum of how many electrons?
e: The second shell contains one 2s and three 2p orbitals (4 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 8.

q: Valence electrons are mainly responsible for an atom's:
e: Valence (outermost) electrons are the ones available to be shared or transferred in bonds, so they govern how an atom reacts chemically.

q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon that differ in their number of:
e: Both have 6 protons (defining them as carbon), but carbon-14 has 2 extra neutrons, giving it a higher mass number.

q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 react at exactly the same rate.
e: Almost, but not quite. Identical electron counts mean identical bonds, so for nearly every purpose the two are interchangeable — but a heavier nucleus sits in a slightly deeper vibrational well, so a bond to it breaks a little more slowly.

q: How many valence electrons does a neutral nitrogen atom (group 15) have?
e: Nitrogen is in group 15, and for main-group elements the group number minus ten gives 5 valence electrons.

q: How many valence electrons does a neutral oxygen atom (group 16) have?
e: Oxygen sits in group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons — which is why it typically forms 2 bonds to complete an octet.

q: Chlorine is in period 3, group 17. How many valence electrons does it have?
e: For main-group elements, the group number minus ten (17 − 10, or 7A) gives 7 valence electrons, explaining why chlorine needs just one more electron for a full octet.

q: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons. In a neutral organic molecule, what does a chlorine atom carry?
e: Bonds + lone pairs = 4 for an atom reaching an octet. Chlorine already owns 7 of the 8 electrons it needs, so a single shared pair finishes the octet and the other 6 electrons stay put as 3 lone pairs.

q: In an ionic bond the electrons are shared between the two atoms, just far less evenly than in a covalent bond.
e: That describes a polar covalent bond, which is what most organic bonds are: shared, but pulled toward one end. In a true ionic bond the electron is handed over completely — sodium keeps no share in it at all — and what holds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together is plain electrostatic attraction between opposite charges.

q: Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table share similar chemical properties mainly because they have:
e: Chemical behavior is driven by valence electrons, and elements in a group share the same valence electron count, giving them similar reactivity.

q: A nitrogen in a structure has four bonds and no lone pair. What is true of it?
e: Neutral nitrogen takes 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. A fourth bond has replaced that lone pair, so nitrogen now shares a pair it used to own outright and comes out one electron short: +1.

q: Magnesium is in group 2 and chlorine in group 17. What kind of bonding forms between them?
e: Magnesium has two loose valence electrons and each chlorine is one electron short of a full shell, so each chlorine takes one outright. Nothing is shared: the result is Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻ held together electrostatically.

q: Fluorine (7 valence electrons) strongly tends to:
e: Being one electron short of an octet, fluorine strongly favors gaining an electron to form the stable F⁻ ion rather than losing one.

q: A carbon drawn with three bonds and one lone pair carries a negative charge.
e: Neutral carbon comes with four valence electrons and takes four bonds. Three bonds plus a lone pair means it owns 3 (one from each shared pair) + 2 = 5 electrons against the 4 it started with, so it is −1.

q: Sodium (Na) readily loses one electron to form Na⁺. This is best explained by sodium having:
e: Sodium (group 1) has just 1 valence electron; losing it leaves sodium with the same stable electron configuration as neon, a noble gas.

q: Which orbital shape is dumbbell-shaped with two lobes?
e: p orbitals have two lobes on either side of the nucleus along one axis; s orbitals are spherical.

q: How many electrons can a single orbital hold at most?
e: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

q: Which orbital fills first: 4s or 3d?
e: Energy, not shell number, sets the filling order. An s electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than a d electron does, so it is screened less by the inner electrons and feels a stronger pull — enough that 4s drops below 3d.

q: Which orbital shape is spherical?
e: The s orbital is the only orbital type with a simple spherical shape centered on the nucleus.

q: How many individual orbitals make up a p subshell?
e: A p subshell consists of three orbitals (px, py, pz), oriented along the three perpendicular axes.

q: How many individual orbitals make up an s subshell?
e: An s subshell has just one spherical orbital, regardless of which energy level it belongs to.

q: An orbital is a region of space, not a path, so an electron in a p orbital passes through the node at its center.
e: A node is a surface where the probability of finding the electron is exactly zero, so it is never found there — which is impossible to picture if you imagine the electron as a ball tracing a route between the two lobes. That is the point of dropping the orbit picture: the orbital is a probability distribution, and the two lobes are two regions where the electron is likely to be.

q: What is the maximum number of electrons a full p subshell (3 orbitals) can hold?
e: Each of the 3 p orbitals holds up to 2 electrons, so 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6 electrons maximum.

q: What is the maximum number of electrons the entire 2p subshell can hold?
e: Like any p subshell, 2p has three orbitals that each hold 2 electrons, giving a maximum of 6 electrons.

q: Why can a single orbital hold at most 2 electrons?
e: Two electrons fit in one orbital only if their spins are opposed, one up and one down. A third electron would have to match one of them exactly, and the Pauli exclusion principle forbids that — so two is the ceiling for every orbital, of every shape, in every shell.

q: Orbitals represent fixed, definite paths that electrons travel along.
e: Orbitals are regions of space describing the probability of finding an electron, not fixed trajectories — this is a key distinction from the outdated Bohr model.

q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of nitrogen (7 electrons)?
e: Fill from the bottom: 1s takes 2, 2s takes 2, and the remaining 3 go into the 2p set. Because the three 2p orbitals are equal in energy, those 3 electrons go one to each rather than pairing up — so nitrogen has three unpaired electrons and makes three bonds, and the 2s pair that has nowhere else to go is ammonia's lone pair.

q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state oxygen atom have?
e: Oxygen is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. The 1s and 2s are full, and four electrons go into three equal-energy 2p orbitals: one each first, then the fourth has to double up in one of them.

q: The Pauli exclusion principle is what limits an orbital to two electrons. What does it require of those two?
e: An orbital can hold two electrons only if they differ in spin, one up and one down. A third has no way to be different from both, so it cannot join them — which is why every subshell's capacity is exactly twice its number of orbitals: 2 for s, 6 for p, 10 for d.

q: Hund's rule says that when filling a set of degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals, electrons will:
e: Hund's rule minimizes electron-electron repulsion by spreading electrons into separate same-energy orbitals before any pairing happens.

q: How many total orbitals exist in the entire n = 2 shell (2s + 2p)?
e: The n=2 shell has one 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals, totaling 4 orbitals (which can hold up to 8 electrons).

q: Why does the 4s orbital fill with electrons before the 3d orbital, even though n=3 is lower than n=4?
e: Electron-electron shielding changes the relative energies of orbitals in multi-electron atoms, making 4s slightly lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first according to the Aufbau principle.

q: p orbitals have two lobes with a node (zero probability) at the nucleus.
e: Unlike the spherical s orbital, a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two lobes separated by a node right at the nucleus.

q: A node in an orbital represents a region where:
e: A node is a location where the probability of finding the electron drops to zero, separating regions (lobes) of the orbital.

q: Fluorine is 1s² 2s² 2p⁵. How many bonds and lone pairs does that predict?
e: Five electrons spread over the three 2p orbitals fill two of them and leave one with a single electron; the 2s pair is already full. So one unpaired electron is available to bond, and the three filled pairs (one 2s, two 2p) stay put as lone pairs.

q: The three p orbitals (px, py, pz) are oriented:
e: Three mutually perpendicular axes is the arrangement that puts the three orbitals as far from each other as possible, which keeps the electrons in them apart and the repulsion between them at a minimum. It is also why the three of them are identical in energy: no axis is special.

q: Two of carbon's 2p orbitals hold one electron each and the third is empty. What does this predict about carbon's bonding?
e: Counting unpaired electrons, the prediction is two — and it is wrong, since carbon plainly forms four. That mismatch is the paradox the next section resolves: carbon promotes one 2s electron into the empty 2p, giving four unpaired electrons in four orbitals, and then mixes them.

q: Which of these box diagrams for the 2p subshell of carbon violates Hund's rule?
e: Hund's rule says electrons spread singly across orbitals of equal energy before any of them pairs. Forcing both 2p electrons into one orbital puts them in the same small region where they repel each other, when two empty orbitals of identical energy are sitting there unused.

q: Which box diagram breaks the Pauli exclusion principle rather than Hund's rule?
e: Pauli forbids two electrons in one orbital from having the same spin — an orbital can hold two only if they are opposed, ↑↓. Two arrows pointing the same way in one box is therefore impossible, not merely unfavorable.

q: Orbitals are best described as:
e: Quantum mechanics describes orbitals as three-dimensional probability distributions for where an electron is likely to be found, not fixed paths.

q: What is the electron configuration of the sodium ion, Na⁺?
e: Neutral sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The electron it loses is the outermost, highest-energy one — the lone 3s — leaving a filled n = 2 shell. That is the whole reason sodium gives up exactly one electron and stops: the ion has the configuration of neon, and prising a second electron out of a full shell is enormously expensive.

q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the entire n = 3 shell (3s + 3p + 3d)?
e: The n=3 shell has 1 s-orbital, 3 p-orbitals, and 5 d-orbitals (9 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 18.

q: Two electrons occupying the same orbital must have opposite spins.
e: The Pauli exclusion principle requires that the two electrons sharing an orbital differ in their spin quantum number, since all their other quantum numbers are identical.

q: Why can carbon never hold more than eight valence electrons?
e: Count them: one 2s and three 2p is four orbitals, and an orbital holds at most two electrons, so the shell tops out at eight. A ninth electron on carbon, nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine would have nowhere to sit.

q: Which subshell is lower in energy, 2s or 2p, and why?
e: An s orbital's shape lets its electron spend more of its time very close to the nucleus, inside the screening cloud of the inner electrons. Feeling less shielding means feeling a stronger nuclear pull, and that means lower energy.

q: A carbon with one double bond and two single bonds (3 total attachments, trigonal planar) is hybridized as:
e: Three regions of electron density (trigonal planar) come from mixing one s and two p orbitals — sp².

q: An sp carbon (like in a triple bond) has a bond angle of about:
e: sp hybridization gives 2 regions of electron density arranged linearly, 180° apart.

q: A carbon with 2 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds (a triple bond partner) is hybridized as:
e: 2 regions of electron density (linear) come from mixing one s and one p orbital — sp, leaving 2 unhybridized p orbitals for the 2 pi bonds.

q: A tetrahedral sp3 carbon (4 single bonds, no pi bonds) has a bond angle of about:
e: sp3 hybrid orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving the characteristic 109.5° bond angle.

q: An sp3 hybridized carbon has no unhybridized p orbitals left, meaning it cannot form any pi bonds.
e: sp3 hybridization uses all of the atom's s and p orbitals (one s and all three p's), leaving none available for pi bonding.

q: Ethene's carbons are trigonal planar, so VSEPR predicts 120°. The measured H–C–H angle is about 117°. Why?
e: The ideal angles assume the three groups are identical, and here they are not: two C–H bonds and one C=C holding four electrons. The double bond takes up more angular room than a single bond, so it squeezes the two hydrogens a few degrees closer together.

q: A carbon atom with four single bonds and no multiple bonds is hybridized as:
e: With 4 sigma bonds and 0 lone pairs (steric number 4), the carbon mixes one s and three p orbitals into four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

q: In ammonia (NH3), nitrogen has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. What is nitrogen's hybridization?
e: Counting 3 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 4, corresponding to sp3 hybridization, even though one 'position' is a lone pair rather than a bond.

q: In water (H2O), oxygen has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. What is oxygen's hybridization?
e: Adding 2 sigma bonds and 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 4, so oxygen is sp3 hybridized despite forming only 2 visible bonds.

q: An atom's hybridization can be determined by counting its number of sigma bonds plus lone pairs (its steric number).
e: Steric number 2 gives sp, 3 gives sp2, and 4 gives sp3 — this simple count is the standard shortcut for assigning hybridization.

q: A carbonyl carbon (C=O, plus two other single bonds) is hybridized as:
e: The carbonyl carbon has 3 sigma bonds total (the double bond counts once for sigma purposes) and 0 lone pairs, giving a steric number of 3 and sp2 hybridization.

q: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on an sp hybridized carbon?
e: sp hybridization mixes only one s and one p orbital, leaving 2 p orbitals unhybridized and available to form two pi bonds.

q: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on an sp2 hybridized carbon?
e: sp2 hybridization mixes one s orbital with two p orbitals, leaving exactly 1 p orbital unhybridized for pi bonding.

q: Why does an sp2 hybridized carbon have exactly one unhybridized p orbital left over?
e: Hybridization never changes the number of orbitals: one s plus two p goes in, three sp2 orbitals come out, and the third p orbital simply was not invited. It survives untouched, standing perpendicular to the plane of the three hybrids, and it is what makes the pi bond of a C=C.

q: A terminal alkyne's C–H bond (attached to an sp carbon) is more acidic than a C–H bond on an sp3 carbon mainly because:
e: Taking H⁺ off leaves the bonding pair behind on carbon, so the question is which carbon holds that pair most comfortably. An sp orbital is 50% s against sp3's 25%, and s character means density close to the nucleus — so an sp carbon holds the leftover pair tightly and gives the proton up far more readily.

q: As the s-character of a carbon's hybrid orbitals increases (sp3 → sp2 → sp), the ideal bond angle around that carbon:
e: More s-character spreads the hybrid orbitals further apart in angle — from 109.5° (sp3) to 120° (sp2) to 180° (sp).

q: Which C–H bond is generally the shortest?
e: Greater s-character pulls the bonding electron pair closer to the carbon nucleus, making sp C–H bonds shorter (and stronger) than sp2 or sp3 C–H bonds.

q: Any atom with exactly 4 sigma bonds, 0 pi bonds, and 0 lone pairs is sp3 hybridized.
e: A steric number of 4 with no lone pairs always corresponds to sp3 hybridization and a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds.

q: An imine is a C=N group (the nitrogen analogue of a C=O). Its nitrogen has one double bond, one single bond and one lone pair. What is its hybridization?
e: Counting 2 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 3, so the imine nitrogen is sp2 hybridized, just like the carbon it's double-bonded to.

q: Boron in BF3 (3 bonds, no lone pair, electron-deficient) is hybridized as:
e: With 3 sigma bonds and no lone pairs, boron has a steric number of 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape, even though boron lacks a full octet.

q: In allene (H2C=C=CH2), the central carbon is bonded via two separate double bonds. What is its hybridization?
e: The central carbon has only 2 sigma bonds (one to each neighboring carbon, with each double bond contributing one sigma and one pi bond), giving a steric number of 2 and sp hybridization.

q: Among sp3, sp2, and sp hybrid orbitals, which has the greatest percentage of s-character?
e: sp hybrids are formed from one s and one p orbital (50% s-character), more than sp2 (about 33%) or sp3 (25%), making sp orbitals hold electrons closest to the nucleus.

q: sp2 hybridized atoms arrange their three hybrid orbitals in a single plane, 120° apart from each other.
e: Trigonal planar geometry is the direct geometric consequence of mixing one s and two p orbitals into three equivalent sp2 hybrids.

q: A carbocation carbon (3 bonds, no lone pair, empty p orbital) is hybridized as:
e: With only 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair, the carbocation's steric number is 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape with an empty, unhybridized p orbital.

q: In a carbonyl group (C=O), the oxygen has 1 sigma bond to carbon, a pi bond, and 2 lone pairs. What is oxygen's hybridization?
e: Counting 1 sigma bond plus 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 3, so the carbonyl oxygen is sp2 hybridized, matching its planar carbon partner.

q: In propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, how many of the three carbons are sp³?
e: Assign each carbon separately. The CH₃ carbon has four groups — three hydrogens and the neighboring carbon — so it is sp³. Each of the two alkene carbons has three groups, counting the double bond once, so both are sp².

q: In acetic acid, CH₃COOH, what are the hybridizations of the carbonyl carbon and of the OH oxygen?
e: The carbonyl carbon has three groups — the methyl, the OH oxygen, and the C=O counted once — so it is sp², and it plus its three neighbors are flat. The OH oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, four groups, so nominally sp³ and bent.

q: A carbon atom's hybridization can change during a reaction — for example from sp3 to sp2 when a bonded group leaves, taking the shared pair with it and leaving
e: Hybridization reflects the current bonding situation, not a fixed property, so it shifts as bonds break and form — here losing a sigma bond drops the steric number from 4 to 3.

q: An amide nitrogen (R–CO–NH₂) has three bonds and one lone pair, yet it is flat rather than pyramidal. What does that tell you?
e: This is the one case where counting groups gives the wrong answer. The lone pair is next door to the C=O pi bond, and it does better sitting in a p orbital where it can overlap sideways with that pi system than in a hybrid orbital of its own.

q: Why do the two hybrid orbitals on an sp carbon point exactly 180° apart?
e: Two orbitals, each built from the same s and the same p, can only be equivalent if they point in exactly opposite directions — and that also puts the two electron groups as far apart as they can get. The linear geometry is a consequence of the mixing, not an extra rule laid on top of it.

q: Why can’t you freely rotate around a C=C double bond?
e: Twisting misaligns the parallel p orbitals that form the pi bond, breaking that overlap — sigma bonds alone allow free rotation.

q: Which bond is shorter: C=C or C–C?
e: More bonds between the same two atoms pulls the nuclei closer together, so C=C (~134 pm) is shorter than C–C (~154 pm).

q: A double bond consists of how many sigma and pi bonds?
e: A double bond is always composed of exactly one sigma bond plus one pi bond, never two sigma bonds.

q: The 'Strength' column of a bond table is the bond dissociation energy, measured for homolytic cleavage. What does homolytic mean?
e: Homolytic cleavage splits the shared pair down the middle and leaves two neutral radicals. The alternative, heterolytic cleavage, sends the whole pair off with one fragment and gives a cation and an anion — which is what almost every polar mechanism you will draw does.

q: Which type of bond forms from direct, head-on orbital overlap along the axis connecting two nuclei?
e: Sigma bonds are defined by overlap directly along the internuclear axis, concentrating electron density right between the two nuclei.

q: Which type of bond forms from side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the bond axis?
e: Pi bonds arise specifically from parallel p orbitals overlapping off to the sides of the bond axis, not along it.

q: Why is a C≡C triple bond shorter than a C=C double bond between the same two carbons?
e: Each additional bond (sigma or pi) increases the electron density held between the two nuclei, which pulls them closer together and shortens the bond.

q: Ionic bonds typically form between two nonmetal atoms with similar electronegativity.
e: Ionic bonds form when there's a large electronegativity difference, typically between a metal (low electronegativity) and a nonmetal (high electronegativity), not between two similar nonmetals.

q: A covalent bond is best described as:
e: Covalent bonding involves two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, as opposed to ionic bonding's complete electron transfer.

q: An ionic bond is best described as:
e: Ionic bonding occurs when electrons are essentially transferred rather than shared, producing a cation and an anion held together by electrostatic attraction.

q: The O–H bonds within a single water molecule are an example of what type of bond?
e: Bonds within a molecule connecting atoms like O and H, where electrons are shared, are covalent bonds (here, polar covalent).

q: Given equally good orbital overlap, which is generally the stronger bond: a sigma bond or a pi bond?
e: Head-on sigma overlap is more efficient than the side-by-side overlap of a pi bond, so sigma bonds are typically stronger per bond.

q: Why does rotating around a C=C double bond require breaking the pi bond?
e: The pi bond depends on two p orbitals staying parallel to overlap; rotating one end of the double bond twists the orbitals out of alignment, breaking the pi bond's overlap.

q: Which bond type allows free rotation around the bond axis?
e: Because a sigma bond's overlap is symmetric around the bond axis, rotating the atoms at either end doesn't disrupt the bonding — unlike a pi bond.

q: Carbon typically forms a total of 4 bonds in stable, neutral organic molecules.
e: With 4 valence electrons and a strong drive to complete an octet, neutral carbon almost always forms exactly 4 total bonds (counting each bond in a double or triple bond separately).

q: How many sigma and how many pi bonds are there in propenal, CH₂=CH–CHO?
e: Count connections first, then the extra lines. Four C–H bonds, two C–C connections and one C–O connection is seven links, and every link contributes exactly one sigma: 7 σ. Then the extra line of the C=C and the extra line of the C=O are one pi each: 2 π.

q: As bond order increases from single to double to triple between the same two atoms, bond length generally:
e: More shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer together, so higher bond order consistently means shorter bond length.

q: As bond order increases from single to double to triple, bond dissociation energy (strength) generally:
e: More shared electron pairs create a stronger overall attraction holding the atoms together, so higher bond order means more energy is needed to break the bond.

q: Bond strength increases but bond length also increases when going from a single to a triple bond between the same two atoms.
e: The opposite is true: as bond order increases, bond length decreases while bond strength increases — both trends move together, not apart.

q: Which best describes a polar covalent bond?
e: Polar covalent bonds occur when the bonded atoms differ enough in electronegativity that the shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom.

q: A nonpolar covalent bond is most likely to form between two atoms with:
e: When two bonded atoms have essentially the same electronegativity, the shared electrons are distributed evenly, producing a nonpolar bond.

q: Which of these bonds is purely (or nearly) nonpolar?
e: A bond between two identical carbon atoms has zero electronegativity difference, making it essentially nonpolar, unlike bonds to more electronegative heteroatoms.

q: In CH₃–CH=CH₂, which bond can the two halves of the molecule freely rotate about?
e: Rotation twists the two ends relative to each other. A sigma bond's overlap lies along the axis you are twisting about, so it survives the twist and the bond spins freely.

q: A triple bond between two carbons consists of 2 pi bonds and 1 sigma bond.
e: A carbon-carbon triple bond is made of one sigma bond plus two perpendicular pi bonds, totaling three bonds overall.

q: In a typical C=C double bond, which bond (sigma or pi) is generally easier to break, making it more reactive toward addition reactions?
e: The pi bond's electrons are held less tightly (weaker, more exposed overlap above and below the bond axis), making it the part of the double bond that typically reacts first in addition reactions.

q: Which orbitals overlap to make a C–H bond in methane?
e: Carbon has four groups, so it mixes its 2s and three 2p into four sp³ hybrids, and hydrogen brings the only orbital it has, a 1s. The two meet head-on along the bond axis, which makes it a sigma bond.

q: A double bond between two atoms is made up of two identical sigma bonds.
e: A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond — these are fundamentally different types of overlap, not two sigma bonds.

q: Across a period (left to right), electronegativity generally:
e: Nuclear charge increases across a period while shielding stays roughly constant, pulling electrons in more tightly.

q: Down a group (top to bottom), electronegativity generally:
e: Atomic radius increases down a group, so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held — electronegativity decreases.

q: Electronegativity measures an atom's ability to:
e: Electronegativity is specifically about how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it is sharing in a covalent bond.

q: In chloromethane, CH₃Cl, which atom carries the δ+?
e: Chlorine (3.16) outpulls carbon (2.55), so the shared pair in the C–Cl bond sits closer to chlorine: chlorine is δ− and the carbon it is attached to is δ+. That δ+ carbon is the point of the whole section — it is short of electron density, so it is where anything electron-rich will come and attack.

q: Electronegativity describes an atom on its own, unbonded to anything.
e: It describes an atom in a bond. Pauling's scale, the one this course uses, is derived from bond energies, so the number only means anything once the atom is bonded to something. Ionization energy and electron affinity are the quantities measured on isolated atoms.

q: In CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–Cl, which carbon is the most electron-poor?
e: The pull is strongest in the bond the chlorine is actually part of, so the carbon it sits on is the most depleted. The middle carbon feels a weaker, second-hand version of the same pull through the sigma framework, and the far methyl feels almost nothing.

q: Rank F, Cl, and Br from highest to lowest electronegativity.
e: Electronegativity decreases going down a group, and fluorine, chlorine, and bromine appear in that order from top to bottom, so F is most electronegative and Br is least.

q: A bond between two identical atoms (like H–H) is essentially:
e: With zero electronegativity difference between identical atoms, the shared electrons are distributed perfectly evenly, making the bond nonpolar.

q: Why is fluorine the most electronegative element on the periodic table?
e: Fluorine's small size means its nucleus is close to the bonding electrons, and its high effective nuclear charge gives it an especially strong pull on those shared electrons.

q: Metals generally have lower electronegativity values than nonmetals.
e: Metals tend to lose electrons easily (low electronegativity), while nonmetals tend to attract electrons strongly (high electronegativity) — this split underlies much of ionic bonding.

q: C–F is the most polar bond in organic chemistry. Does that make it the easiest to break?
e: This is the commonest misreading of the section. Opposite partial charges attract each other, so polarity generally helps hold a bond together; C–F is both the most polar and among the strongest single bonds carbon makes.

q: Carbon is 2.55 on the Pauling scale and hydrogen 2.20. What does that make a C–H bond?
e: ΔEN is 0.35, below the 0.5 line this course draws for polar covalent, so C–H is treated as essentially nonpolar throughout. Not exactly zero — the difference is real and shows up in spectroscopy — but small enough that the carbon skeleton of a molecule is a spectator and the chemistry lives on the C–O, C–N and C–halogen bonds instead.

q: Which bond is more polar: C–F or C–Cl?
e: Fluorine (≈4.0) is more electronegative than chlorine (≈3.0), giving the C–F bond a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity.

q: In acetic acid, CH₃COOH, which atoms carry the largest δ−?
e: Oxygen at 3.44 is the most electronegative atom present, so both oxygens pull density toward themselves and both carry δ−. The carbonyl carbon, pulled on from two sides, is correspondingly the most δ+ atom in the molecule — which is exactly why carbonyl carbons are attacked by electron-rich reagents over and over in the second half of the course.

q: Electronegativity values generally increase toward the upper right corner of the periodic table (excluding noble gases).
e: Electronegativity increases across a period (left to right) and decreases down a group (top to bottom), so the highest values cluster in the upper right, with fluorine as the extreme.

q: Why does electronegativity decrease going down a group, despite the increasing number of protons in the nucleus?
e: Even though nuclear charge increases down a group, the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so the net attraction on bonding electrons actually weakens.

q: Lithium is 0.98 on the Pauling scale and carbon is 2.55. In a C–Li bond, which atom is δ−?
e: The pull runs the other way here. Carbon outpulls lithium by a wide margin, so the shared pair sits on the carbon and the carbon is the negative end — the reverse of almost every bond in the course.

q: Which of these bonds is essentially nonpolar?
e: A bond between two atoms of the same element has a ΔEN of exactly zero, so neither end pulls harder and there is no δ+ or δ−. C–H, at 0.35, is treated the same way in practice.

q: Rank the polarity of the C–N, C–O and C–F bonds.
e: Subtract from carbon's 2.55: nitrogen 3.04 gives 0.49, oxygen 3.44 gives 0.89, fluorine 3.98 gives 1.43. All three sit in period 2, and electronegativity rises steadily left to right across a period, so the order follows the row.

q: The electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms determines whether a covalent bond is polar or nonpolar.
e: A small or zero electronegativity difference gives a nonpolar bond, while a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond — this difference is the key diagnostic.

q: Two bonded atoms with an electronegativity difference of roughly 1.7-2.0 or greater tend to form a bond that is best described as:
e: Very large electronegativity differences pull shared electrons so strongly toward one atom that the bond behaves more like a full electron transfer — approaching ionic character.

q: Why is the carbon of a C=O bond a good place for an electron-rich reagent to attack?
e: Electronegativity decides where density is missing, and a reagent looking to donate a pair goes where density is missing. Oxygen pulls the electrons of the double bond toward itself, so the carbon is left short — and a large fraction of the reactions in the second half of this course are something electron-rich arriving at exactly that carbon.

q: Moving left to right across a period, atomic radius generally decreases while electronegativity generally:
e: A smaller atomic radius means the nucleus is closer to the bonding electrons, strengthening its pull on them and increasing electronegativity across the period.

q: Why does a smaller atomic radius within the same period generally correlate with higher electronegativity?
e: Within the same period, a shorter distance between the nucleus and the outer (bonding) electrons lets the nucleus attract those electrons more strongly, raising electronegativity.

q: Among C–N, C–O, and C–F bonds, which is the most polar?
e: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of the three, giving the C–F bond the largest electronegativity difference and therefore the greatest polarity.

q: Which statement about the C–H bonds in a long hydrocarbon chain is correct?
e: With a ΔEN of 0.35 there is no meaningful partial charge on either end, so nothing is drawn to them and they attack nothing. This is why organic chemistry is organized around functional groups: the skeleton is inert, and all the chemistry happens at the handful of polar bonds and lone pairs stuck onto it.

q: Among the halogens F, Cl, Br, and I, which is the least electronegative?
e: Electronegativity decreases down a group, and iodine is the lowest (largest, furthest down) of these four common halogens.

q: Sulfur and oxygen are in the same group and both have 6 valence electrons. Why is oxygen more electronegative?
e: Being higher up the group, oxygen is smaller than sulfur, so its bonding electrons sit closer to the nucleus and experience a stronger pull, despite both elements sharing the same valence electron count.

q: A C–H bond (ΔEN 0.35) is treated as essentially nonpolar throughout this course, even though the difference is not exactly zero.
e: 0.35 sits below the 0.5 boundary for polar covalent, so C–H counts as nonpolar in practice. That is a working simplification, not a measurement: the small real polarity is why a hydrogen next to an electronegative atom shifts in an NMR spectrum.

q: Formal charge = (valence electrons) − (nonbonding electrons) − ?
e: Formal charge = valence e⁻ − nonbonding e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻), since each atom "owns" half of each shared bond.

q: A nitrogen with 4 bonds and no lone pairs has a formal charge of:
e: N normally has 5 valence e⁻; with 4 bonds (8 shared e⁻, 4 "owned") and 0 lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

q: An oxygen with 1 bond and 3 lone pairs has a formal charge of:
e: O normally has 6 valence e⁻; with 1 bond (1 "owned" electron) and 3 lone pairs (6 nonbonding e⁻): 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

q: What is the complete formula for formal charge?
e: Formal charge subtracts an atom's nonbonding electrons and half of its bonding (shared) electrons from its normal number of valence electrons.

q: A carbon atom with 4 bonds and no lone pairs has a formal charge of:
e: 4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, matching carbon's normal, neutral bonding pattern.

q: The sum of all formal charges in a neutral molecule must equal zero.
e: Formal charges are a bookkeeping device, and for consistency they must sum to the molecule's actual overall charge — zero for any neutral molecule.

q: A carbon atom with only 3 bonds and no lone pairs (as in a carbocation) has a formal charge of:
e: 4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 3 = +1, consistent with the positive charge of a carbocation.

q: A carbon atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair has a formal charge of:
e: 4 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 2 − 3 = -1, consistent with a carbanion.

q: An oxygen atom with 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs (as in water) has a formal charge of:
e: 6 valence electrons − 4 nonbonding − 1/2(4 bonding) = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, matching oxygen's usual neutral bonding pattern.

q: An oxygen atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair has a formal charge of:
e: 6 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, which is why an oxygen with 3 bonds (like a protonated ether oxygen) carries a positive formal charge.

q: A nitrogen atom with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair (a typical neutral amine nitrogen) has a formal charge of:
e: 5 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 5 − 2 − 3 = 0, confirming that a nitrogen with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair is neutral, as expected.

q: An oxygen is drawn with one bond and a −1 written on it, but no lone pairs are shown. How many lone pairs must it have?
e: Run the formula backwards: lone-pair electrons = valence − bonds − formal charge = 6 − 1 − (−1) = 6, which is 3 lone pairs. Structures are often drawn with charges shown and lone pairs left off, and supplying the missing pairs is a standard exam task — the arithmetic is the same, just solved for a different unknown.

q: Formal charge is a bookkeeping tool used mainly to compare competing Lewis structures, rather than a measure of the literal true charge on an atom.
e: Formal charge assumes perfectly even sharing of bonding electrons, which isn't physically exact, but it's extremely useful for judging which of several Lewis structures is more reasonable.

q: In the ammonium ion NH4+, nitrogen has 4 bonds and no lone pairs. Its formal charge is:
e: 5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1, matching the overall +1 charge carried by the ammonium ion.

q: When two Lewis structures are both chemically valid for the same molecule, which is generally preferred?
e: Structures with smaller (closer to zero) formal charges, and with any unavoidable negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, are considered more stable and realistic.

q: When a negative formal charge cannot be avoided in a structure, it is generally best placed on:
e: More electronegative atoms are better able to stabilize extra electron density, so placing a negative formal charge there produces a more reasonable, lower-energy structure.

q: A Lewis structure with a negative formal charge on oxygen is generally more stable than one with the same negative charge placed on carbon.
e: Oxygen's high electronegativity makes it far better suited to hold extra negative charge than carbon, so structures matching charge to electronegativity are favored.

q: In methoxide, CH₃O⁻, which atom carries the −1 and why?
e: Neutral oxygen takes 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Here it has only one bond, so the pair it would have shared stays entirely on it as a third lone pair: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. The carbon is at its usual four bonds, 4 − 0 − 4 = 0.

q: Which of these is an impossible structure?
e: Five bonds means ten electrons around a period-2 atom, and n = 2 has only four orbitals to hold them. No formal charge can rescue it — the other three are all ordinary, correctly charged species, but a five-bonded carbon cannot be written at all.

q: A carbonyl oxygen has two lone pairs and a double bond to carbon. What is its formal charge?
e: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. The trap is the bond term: it counts shared pairs, so a double bond is 2, not 1. Count it as 1 and you get +1 on an oxygen that is plainly neutral, and every carbonyl in the course comes out wrongly charged.

q: A fluorine atom with 0 bonds and 4 lone pairs (as in the fluoride ion F−) has a formal charge of:
e: 7 valence electrons − 8 nonbonding − 1/2(0 bonding) = 7 − 8 − 0 = -1, matching the known -1 charge of the fluoride ion.

q: Nitrate, NO₃⁻, is drawn with nitrogen double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to the other two. What are the formal charges?
e: Run the arithmetic atom by atom. Nitrogen has 4 bonds and no lone pair: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. The double-bonded oxygen has 2 lone pairs and a double bond: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Each single-bonded oxygen has 3 lone pairs and 1 bond: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Sum: +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1, which is the ion's charge.

q: It is acceptable for individual atoms within a polyatomic ion to carry nonzero formal charges, as long as all the formal charges sum to the ion's overall charge
e: Unlike neutral molecules (which must sum to zero), ions are expected to have formal charges summing to their actual net charge, whether +1, -1, or otherwise.

q: In methylammonium, CH₃NH₃⁺, which atom carries the +1?
e: Nitrogen started neutral with 3 bonds and a lone pair. Protonating it turns that lone pair into a fourth bond, so it now shares a pair it used to own outright: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Carbon is unchanged at 0.

q: If a lone pair on one atom becomes a new pi bond to a neighboring atom (to relieve that neighbor's negative formal charge), how does the first atom's own formal
e: Converting 2 nonbonding electrons into 2 bonding electrons removes 2 from the nonbonding count (+2 to formal charge) but only adds 1 to the half-bonding count (-1 to formal charge), for a net change of +1.

q: In acetate, CH₃COO⁻, drawn with one C=O and one C–O single bond, where does the −1 sit?
e: Take the oxygens one at a time. The double-bonded one has 2 lone pairs and 2 shared pairs: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. The singly bonded one has 3 lone pairs and 1 bond: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

q: In the bicarbonate ion HCO3− (overall charge -1), the -1 formal charge is most likely located on:
e: Oxygen's high electronegativity and its role as a terminal atom with extra lone pairs make it the atom that typically carries the ion's formal negative charge.

q: A carbon atom can never have a nonzero formal charge in any valid Lewis structure.
e: Carbocations (+1) and carbanions (-1) are valid, commonly drawn species in organic chemistry, showing that carbon's formal charge is not always zero.

q: A structure is drawn with a nitrogen carrying four bonds and no charge written beside it. What is wrong?
e: Four bonds and no lone pair gives 5 − 0 − 4 = +1, so the charge has to be written. Four-bonded nitrogen is perfectly legal — ammonium, protonated amines, the nitrogen of a nitro group — it is just never neutral.

q: Nitromethane, CH₃NO₂, is neutral overall. Its nitrogen has one bond to carbon, a double bond to one oxygen and a single bond to the other. What is the nitrogen'
e: The bond term counts shared pairs, so the double bond contributes 2: one plus two plus one is 4 bonds, with no lone pair. 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. The singly bonded oxygen comes out at −1 and everything else at 0, so the charges sum to zero — a neutral molecule that nonetheless must be drawn with charges inside it.

q: What is the first step in drawing a Lewis structure?
e: You need the total valence electron count before you can distribute bonds and lone pairs correctly.

q: Which atom is 'central' in methanol, CH₃OH?
e: The central-atom recipe is for small molecules genuinely built around one atom, like CO₂ or BF₃. Organic molecules are chains: methanol is C–O with hydrogens hung off both, and asking which is central has no answer.

q: If, after distributing bonds and lone pairs, an atom is short of an octet, what should you try next?
e: Converting a lone pair on a neighboring atom into a pi bond (multiple bond) often completes the octet without changing the molecular formula.

q: How many valence electrons must a Lewis structure of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, account for?
e: Add them up by atom: two carbons at 4 is 8, six hydrogens at 1 is 6, one oxygen at 6. Total 20. Check it against the finished drawing: 8 bonds (16 electrons) plus 2 lone pairs on the oxygen (4 electrons) is 20.

q: How many lone pairs does the nitrogen of methylamine, CH₃NH₂, carry?
e: Nitrogen's quota is 3 bonds and 1 lone pair, and here it has exactly its three bonds — one to carbon, two to hydrogen — so one lone pair completes the octet. That single pair is the whole chemistry of amines: it is what makes them basic, what makes them attack electron-poor carbons, and what makes the molecule pyramidal instead of flat.

q: Hydrogen can never be the central atom in a Lewis structure.
e: Hydrogen can form only one bond (it has just one valence electron and no available orbitals to expand), so it must always be a terminal (outer) atom, never central.

q: For methane, CH4, how many total valence electrons must be distributed in the Lewis structure?
e: Carbon contributes 4 valence electrons and each of the 4 hydrogens contributes 1, giving 4 + 4(1) = 8 total valence electrons.

q: For carbon dioxide, CO2, how many total valence electrons are there to distribute?
e: Carbon contributes 4 and each oxygen contributes 6, giving 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 total valence electrons.

q: For the carbonate ion, CO3²−, how many total valence electrons should be used, accounting for the charge?
e: Carbon (4) plus three oxygens (6 each = 18) gives 22, plus 2 extra electrons for the 2− charge, totaling 24.

q: When drawing a Lewis structure for a polyatomic ion with a negative charge, you should add that many extra electrons to the total electron count.
e: A negative charge means the species has gained that many extra electrons beyond the neutral sum of its atoms' valence electrons, so they must be added to the total before distributing them.

q: After connecting all atoms to the central atom with single bonds, what is the typical next step in drawing a Lewis structure?
e: Once the basic skeleton is bonded, remaining electrons are placed as lone pairs, typically satisfying the outer (terminal) atoms' octets before addressing the central atom.

q: When drawing SO2, sulfur initially ends up short of a full octet after single bonds and lone pairs are placed. The standard fix is to:
e: Moving a lone pair from an outer atom into a new pi bond gives the electron-deficient central atom the electrons it needs without changing the total electron count.

q: Which of these drawn structures is impossible?
e: Hydrogen's only shell holds two electrons, which is one shared pair, so it bonds to exactly one thing. An H drawn between two atoms is a slip of the pen. The other three are all ordinary species with their charges correctly written: an alkoxide, an ammonium, a carbocation.

q: In a correctly drawn Lewis structure, the total number of electrons shown (in bonds and lone pairs) must equal:
e: Every valence electron counted up front must appear somewhere in the final structure — none can be added or left out along the way.

q: Which type of atom is typically a terminal (outer) atom rather than a candidate for the central position?
e: Hydrogen and the halogens generally form only one bond each, making them well suited as terminal atoms rather than as a central, multiply-bonded atom.

q: Period 3 and beyond elements, such as sulfur or phosphorus, can sometimes exceed a simple octet in a valid Lewis structure.
e: They genuinely do — SF₆, H₂SO₄ and PCl₅ are all real. What allows it is that a period-3 atom is physically larger, so more neighbors fit around it, and that the extra bonds carry substantial ionic character.

q: Which of these atoms is NOT generally allowed to exceed an octet in a standard Lewis structure?
e: Carbon sits in period 2, whose shell holds one 2s and three 2p orbitals — four in all, so eight electrons and no more. Sulfur and phosphorus are in period 3 and can exceed an octet; carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine never can, which is why a five-bonded carbon is always an error rather than an exotic case.

q: In a neutral molecule, what do bonds + lone pairs add up to for C, N, O and the halogens?
e: Each bond brings in one shared pair and each lone pair is one pair kept, and an octet is four pairs — so the two always total 4. That single line generates the whole table: carbon 4 bonds and 0 lone pairs, nitrogen 3 and 1, oxygen 2 and 2, a halogen 1 and 3.

q: When more than one atom could plausibly be the central atom, which is generally chosen?
e: Less electronegative atoms are usually less 'greedy' for electrons and can form more bonds, making them well suited to sit at the center, surrounded by more electronegative terminal atoms.

q: How many lone pairs are there in a full Lewis structure of acetic acid, CH₃COOH?
e: Only the oxygens carry any. The C=O oxygen has two bonds' worth of sharing (the double bond) plus 2 lone pairs; the O–H oxygen has two single bonds plus 2 lone pairs. Carbons at their quota of four bonds have none, and hydrogens have none.

q: Carbon almost always forms exactly 4 total bonds in a valid, neutral Lewis structure.
e: With 4 valence electrons, neutral carbon needs 4 more (shared) to complete its octet, so it reliably forms 4 total bonds (single, double, and triple bonds all counted toward that total).

q: In a neutral, uncharged Lewis structure, oxygen typically forms how many total bonds?
e: With 6 valence electrons, oxygen needs 2 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 2 total bonds (plus 2 lone pairs) when neutral.

q: In a neutral, uncharged Lewis structure, nitrogen typically forms how many total bonds?
e: With 5 valence electrons, nitrogen needs 3 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 3 total bonds (plus 1 lone pair) when neutral.

q: If a period-2 central atom like carbon or nitrogen ends up surrounded by 10 electrons in a drawn structure, this most likely indicates:
e: A period-2 shell contains four orbitals, one 2s and three 2p, which hold eight electrons and no more. Ten electrons on carbon or nitrogen is therefore not an exotic structure but an arithmetic mistake — most often a fifth bond, or a lone pair left on an atom that already has four bonds.

q: Which molecule requires an expanded octet on its central atom to be drawn correctly: SF6 or CH4?
e: SF₆ needs six bonds on sulfur, which is twelve electrons — only possible because sulfur is in period 3. Methane's carbon has four bonds and exactly eight electrons, the ordinary octet.

q: Drawing the skeletal structure (atom connectivity) before placing electrons matters because it:
e: Electrons can only be placed once you know which atoms are actually connected — getting the skeleton right first is essential to arriving at a sensible final structure.

q: A correct Lewis structure must account for every single valence electron counted at the start — none can be left out or added extra.
e: The entire process is essentially careful electron bookkeeping: the total electrons placed in bonds and lone pairs must exactly match the total counted up front.

q: In formaldehyde, H2CO, which best describes the central carbon's bonding?
e: Carbon forms a C=O double bond plus two C–H single bonds (4 bonds total, 0 lone pairs), giving it a complete octet with no formal charge.

q: Why is fluorine essentially never chosen as a central atom when other options are available?
e: Since fluorine needs only 1 bond to complete its octet, it naturally sits at the edge of a structure rather than at the center, where more bonds are usually needed.

q: Why can a carbon never carry five bonds, while sulfur can carry six?
e: One 2s and three 2p is four orbitals, and four orbitals hold eight electrons, so a ninth has nowhere to sit on any period-2 atom. Sulfur is in period 3, which has more room around a physically larger atom, and its extra bonds carry substantial ionic character.

q: A central atom with 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what geometry?
e: 4 electron domains with no lone pairs arrange tetrahedrally (VSEPR) — 109.5° angles.

q: Why does water (2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs) have a bent shape instead of linear?
e: VSEPR counts lone pairs as occupying space — with 4 total domains around O, the electron geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular shape (just the atoms) comes out bent.

q: A central atom with 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair has what molecular shape?
e: 4 total electron domains give a tetrahedral electron geometry, but with one domain as a lone pair, the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramidal shape (like NH₃).

q: A central atom with 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
e: With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs to push them around, they spread as far apart as possible: 180° apart, giving a linear shape.

q: A central atom with 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
e: Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread out evenly in a single plane, 120° apart, giving a trigonal planar shape.

q: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on minimizing repulsion between electron groups around a central atom.
e: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory's core idea is that electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion.

q: What is the key difference between 'electron-pair geometry' and 'molecular geometry'?
e: Electron-pair geometry considers every region of electron density (including invisible lone pairs), while molecular geometry describes the shape traced out by the actual atoms, which can look different when lone pairs are present.

q: Ammonia (NH3) has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around nitrogen. What is its molecular (atoms-only) shape?
e: Although the electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total electron groups), one position is a lone pair, so only 3 atoms are visible, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.

q: Water's H–O–H bond angle (104.5°) is smaller than ammonia's H–N–H angle (107°), which is smaller than methane's H–C–H angle (109.5°). Why does water compress th
e: Each extra lone pair adds more repulsion pushing the bonding pairs closer together; with 2 lone pairs instead of ammonia's 1, water's H–O–H angle gets squeezed down the most.

q: Lone pairs occupy more space around a central atom than bonding pairs, causing greater repulsion on neighboring electron groups.
e: Because lone pairs aren't held between two nuclei, they spread out more and exert stronger repulsive forces, compressing bond angles involving bonding pairs nearby.

q: What is the ideal bond angle for tetrahedral molecular geometry (4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs)?
e: Four identical electron groups with no lone pairs spread out symmetrically to 109.5° apart, the ideal tetrahedral angle.

q: What is the ideal bond angle for trigonal planar geometry?
e: Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread evenly in a plane at 120° apart to minimize repulsion.

q: What is the ideal bond angle for linear geometry?
e: With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs, the maximum possible separation is a straight 180° angle.

q: A central atom with 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs has what molecular shape?
e: The underlying electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total groups), but with 2 lone pairs removed from view, only the 2 bonded atoms remain visible, producing a bent shape.

q: In acetic acid, CH₃COOH, what is the geometry at the carbonyl carbon?
e: It has three electron groups — the methyl carbon, the OH oxygen, and the C=O counted once — and no lone pairs, so trigonal planar at about 120°. That carbon and its three neighbors are flat, which is why a reagent arriving at a carbonyl can approach from either face equally.

q: A central atom with 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs (an expanded octet, as in PCl5) has what geometry?
e: Five electron groups with no lone pairs arrange themselves into a trigonal bipyramidal shape, with three equatorial and two axial positions.

q: A central atom with 6 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs (an expanded octet, as in SF6) has what geometry?
e: Six electron groups with no lone pairs spread into an octahedral arrangement, the most symmetric way to separate 6 groups evenly.

q: Molecular geometry describes only the positions of bonded atoms, even though lone pairs still influence the overall observed shape.
e: Lone pairs aren't drawn into the final molecular shape, but their repulsive effect on the bonding pairs still shapes the angles and arrangement that we actually observe.

q: In ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, what is the geometry at each of the two carbons and at the oxygen?
e: Every heavy atom here has four electron groups. Each carbon has four bonds, so both are tetrahedral at about 109.5°. The oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs — still four groups, so still built on a tetrahedron, but with only two corners holding atoms it is described as bent, at about 104.5°.

q: Why does ammonia's trigonal pyramidal shape differ from a full tetrahedron, even though both arise from a tetrahedral electron-pair geometry?
e: The electron-pair geometry (4 total groups) is tetrahedral, but since one of those groups is an unseen lone pair, only 3 hydrogen atoms plus the nitrogen are visible, producing the trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.

q: In formaldehyde, the carbon has 3 bonding groups (one of which is a double bond to oxygen) and 0 lone pairs. What is its molecular geometry?
e: A double bond still counts as just one electron group for VSEPR purposes, so with 3 total groups and no lone pairs, the carbon is trigonal planar.

q: In VSEPR theory, a double or triple bond between the central atom and another atom counts as how many electron groups for determining geometry?
e: VSEPR treats an entire multiple bond (single, double, or triple) as one region of electron density occupying one position around the central atom, since the pi bonds don't point in separate directions.

q: The ideal angles in the VSEPR table are exact measurements of real molecules.
e: They are what the model predicts when all the groups are identical, and real molecules land a degree or two off whenever they are not. Ethene's carbons are trigonal planar, but the measured H–C–H angle is about 117° rather than 120°, because the double bond is a fatter electron group than a C–H and squeezes the hydrogens together.

q: A carbocation carbon with 3 bonds and no lone pair (and an empty p orbital) adopts what molecular geometry?
e: With only 3 electron groups (the 3 bonds) and no lone pair present, the 3 substituents spread out in a plane at 120°, giving trigonal planar geometry.

q: Why do carbocations adopt a trigonal planar geometry rather than a tetrahedral one?
e: An empty orbital holds no electrons and therefore exerts no repulsion, so with only 3 true electron groups present, the molecule minimizes repulsion by going flat (120° apart) rather than puckering into a tetrahedron.

q: Which atoms of propenal, CH₂=CH–CHO, lie in one plane?
e: Count groups on each heavy atom: both alkene carbons have three, the aldehyde carbon has three, and the oxygen has one bond plus two lone pairs, also three. Three groups means trigonal planar at every one of them, and a chain of trigonal planar atoms joined end to end is flat.

q: How many total electron groups (bonding pairs plus lone pairs) surround the central oxygen in a water molecule?
e: Water's oxygen has 2 bonding pairs (to the 2 hydrogens) plus 2 lone pairs, for a total steric number of 4, even though the visible molecular shape only shows 2 atoms.

q: A tetrahedral electron-pair geometry always results in a tetrahedral molecular geometry.
e: A tetrahedral electron-pair geometry only produces a tetrahedral molecular shape when there are no lone pairs; if lone pairs are present, the molecular shape becomes trigonal pyramidal or bent instead.

q: What is the molecular geometry of the central carbon in CO2, which has 2 double bonds and 0 lone pairs?
e: Each double bond counts as just one electron group, so carbon has 2 total groups with no lone pairs, giving a linear molecule with 180° bond angles.

q: A student draws a tetrahedral carbon with the wedge and the dash on opposite sides of the atom. What is wrong?
e: On a real tetrahedron the bond coming toward you and the bond going away are next to each other, so drawing them opposite depicts a shape that does not exist. Swapping which of the two is the wedge is the other error, and it fails differently: that drawing is perfectly legal, it is just the mirror image of the molecule you meant.

q: A bond is considered polar covalent when the electronegativity difference is roughly:
e: Below about 0.5 the pull is too even to matter and the bond is treated as nonpolar; above about 1.7 the electron is effectively transferred and the bonding is ionic. In between is polar covalent, which is where nearly every bond in organic chemistry sits.

q: In a C–O bond, which atom carries the partial negative charge?
e: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the shared electron density toward itself, becoming δ⁻.

q: A molecule can have polar bonds but still be a nonpolar molecule overall if:
e: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of all bond dipoles — symmetric arrangements (like CO₂ or CCl₄) can cancel polar bonds into a net nonpolar molecule.

q: In CH₃–CH₂–OH, which atoms carry a δ+?
e: Mark the polar bonds and ignore the rest. C–H at ΔEN 0.35 is treated as nonpolar, so the methyl end carries nothing. The C–O bond makes that carbon δ+ and the oxygen δ−; the O–H bond makes the hydrogen δ+ and, again, the oxygen δ−.

q: In an O–H bond, which atom carries the partial positive charge?
e: Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling the shared electrons toward itself and leaving hydrogen with a partial positive charge.

q: A bond between two identical atoms (such as C–C) is always nonpolar.
e: Identical atoms have exactly equal electronegativity, so there is zero tendency for the shared electrons to shift toward one side, making the bond perfectly nonpolar.

q: Which bond is more polar: C–Cl or C–Br?
e: Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, so the C–Cl bond has a larger electronegativity difference and is therefore more polar than C–Br.

q: Which of these bonds has the greatest electronegativity difference and the most ionic character: C–F, C–N, or C–O?
e: Fluorine is the most electronegative of the three atoms, giving C–F the largest electronegativity gap and the greatest degree of ionic character among typical organic bonds.

q: In a polar bond, the dipole arrow (pointing from partial positive to partial negative) points toward:
e: The dipole arrow represents the net pull on the shared electrons, which always points toward the more electronegative (more electron-hungry) atom in the bond.

q: Which of these can donate a hydrogen bond?
e: Donating needs a hydrogen sitting directly on N, O or F, stripped of most of its density. Ethanol's O–H qualifies. Dimethyl ether has the same formula as ethanol and an oxygen with lone pairs, so it can accept a hydrogen bond, but with no O–H it cannot donate one — which is why ethanol boils at 78°C and the ether at −24°C.

q: The symbol δ− placed near an atom indicates:
e: Like δ+, the δ− symbol represents a partial charge from unequal electron sharing, showing which end of a polar bond carries extra (but not whole) negative character.

q: Carbon dioxide (CO2) has two polar C=O bonds but is overall a nonpolar molecule. Why?
e: Because CO2 is linear and symmetric, the two equal-but-opposite C=O dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero, leaving no net molecular dipole.

q: Butane, acetone and propan-1-ol all weigh about the same. Rank their boiling points, lowest first.
e: With weight held constant, the only thing left is the strongest attraction each one can make. Butane has dispersion forces alone (−1°C), acetone has a strong C=O dipole and so dipole–dipole (56°C), propan-1-ol has an O–H and so hydrogen bonding (97°C).

q: Why is carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) a nonpolar molecule despite having 4 individually polar C–Cl bonds?
e: Because CCl4's tetrahedral geometry places the 4 equal C–Cl dipoles in perfectly symmetric directions, their vector sum is zero, making the overall molecule nonpolar even though each bond is polar.

q: Is the C–C bond in ethane (CH3–CH3) considered polar or nonpolar?
e: Since both atoms in the bond are carbon, there is zero electronegativity difference, making the C–C bond essentially nonpolar.

q: Which of these dissolves readily in water?
e: Dissolving means water has to break its own hydrogen-bond network and get something back. Ethanol's O–H both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds, so it pays water back and mixes in any proportion.

q: An electronegativity difference greater than roughly 1.7-2.0 between two bonded atoms typically signals:
e: Once the electronegativity gap is large enough, the bonding electrons are held so strongly by one atom that the bond is better described as mostly ionic rather than simply polar covalent.

q: If a molecule has individual polar bonds, the overall molecule must always be polar as well.
e: Bond polarity and molecular polarity don't always match — if a molecule's shape is symmetric enough, individual bond dipoles can cancel out, leaving a nonpolar molecule despite polar bonds.

q: Which bond is more polar: N–H or C–H?
e: Nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the N–H bond has a larger electronegativity difference from hydrogen than C–H does, making N–H more polar.

q: In the carbonyl group C=O, the oxygen end of the dipole is best described as:
e: Oxygen's much higher electronegativity pulls the shared pi and sigma electrons toward itself, giving it the partial negative (δ−) end of the carbonyl dipole.

q: A Grignard reagent (R–MgBr, met in Organometallics) has a C–Mg bond. Why does the carbon carry the partial negative charge?
e: Even though carbon is usually the less electronegative partner compared to oxygen or nitrogen, it is considerably more electronegative than a metal like magnesium, reversing the usual polarity seen in most organic bonds.

q: Which is more polar: S–H or O–H?
e: Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur (despite being in the same group), giving O–H a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity than S–H.

q: The greater the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms, the more polar that bond generally is.
e: Electronegativity difference is essentially a direct proxy for bond polarity — bigger gaps mean more unequal electron sharing and a more polar bond.

q: Chloromethane (CH3Cl) is an overall polar molecule mainly because:
e: With only one strongly polar C–Cl bond and three much weaker C–H dipoles that don't offset it, the molecule ends up with an unbalanced, net dipole moment overall.

q: Which bond is essentially nonpolar due to a very small electronegativity difference: C–H or O–H?
e: The electronegativity difference between carbon and hydrogen (about 0.4) is much smaller than between oxygen and hydrogen (about 1.2), making C–H nearly nonpolar by comparison.

q: Why is a C=O bond more polar overall than a typical C–O single bond?
e: Roughly: the double bond puts two shared pairs between the same two atoms, so there is more electron density for the oxygen to pull on, and the pi electrons are held loosely and shift easily. The measured dipole of a C=O is larger than that of a C–O.

q: Dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂, is tetrahedral. Is it polar?
e: Symmetry is what cancels dipoles, not the tetrahedral label. In CCl₄ four identical dipoles point at four corners and sum to zero. Replace two chlorines with hydrogens and the two remaining C–Cl dipoles point to the same side of the molecule, so they add rather than cancel and the molecule has a net dipole of about 1.6 D.

q: Which of these bonds would you expect to be purely (or nearly) nonpolar: H–H, H–Cl, or H–F?
e: H–H connects two identical atoms with zero electronegativity difference, making it the only purely nonpolar bond among these three options.

q: A chemical bond must be classified as either purely covalent or purely ionic, with no middle ground between the two.
e: Bonding actually exists along a continuous spectrum, with nonpolar covalent and ionic bonds as the two extremes and polar covalent bonds occupying the wide middle ground.

q: Why does water (H2O) have a net dipole moment even though it is made of individual polar O–H bonds pointing in specific directions?
e: Because water is bent (not linear), the two O–H dipoles reinforce rather than cancel each other, summing into a single net molecular dipole pointing toward the electronegative oxygen.

q: Which functional group is CH3CH2OCH3?
e: An oxygen with a carbon on each side and no C=O anywhere near it is an ether. An ester would need a carbonyl next to that oxygen.

q: CH3COOCH2CH3 contains which group?
e: Find the C=O: one neighbor is CH3, the other is O–CH2CH3. Carbon on one side and O–carbon on the other is an ester (ethyl acetate). The extra O rules out ketone; the C=O rules out ether.

q: What distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?
e: Both are a C=O with carbon attached. An aldehyde has at least one H on that carbon, so it sits at the end of a chain; a ketone has carbon on both sides.

q: CH3CH2CH2NH2 is what kind of amine?
e: Count carbons bonded to the nitrogen, not to any carbon: one carbon on N, so primary. The three-carbon chain is irrelevant.

q: (CH3)2CHOH is what kind of alcohol?
e: The carbon carrying the OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is a secondary carbon and the alcohol is secondary.

q: Which of these contains an amide?
e: An amide is a nitrogen bonded to a C=O. Only CH3CONHCH3 has a carbonyl next to its nitrogen; the first and last are amines and the third is a nitrile.

q: Which group has a C≡N?
e: A nitrile is R–C≡N. A nitro group is R–NO2 (nitrogen bonded to two oxygens), and amines and amides have single bonds to nitrogen.

q: An OH directly on a benzene ring is a:
e: The same OH on a saturated carbon would be an alcohol. On an aromatic carbon it is a phenol, which is far more acidic.

q: Which piece of a molecule is the spectator in most reactions?
e: C–C and C–H bonds are close to nonpolar and carry no lone pairs, so they have no electron-rich or electron-poor site to react through. The functional groups are where the action is.

q: HCOOCH3 is best described as:
e: The carbonyl carbon carries an H and an O–CH3. O–carbon on the carbonyl makes it an ester; the H on the same carbon is what an aldehyde needs, but the O–carbon outranks it, and this compound is the ester of formic acid.

q: CH3COCl belongs to which family?
e: Chlorine on a carbonyl carbon is an acid chloride. In an alkyl halide the chlorine is on an sp3 carbon with no C=O.

q: (CH3CO)2O is:
e: Two C=O groups joined through one oxygen: an anhydride (acetic anhydride). An ester has one carbonyl next to its oxygen; an anhydride has two.

q: (CH3)3C–NH2 is what kind of amine?
e: Count carbons on the nitrogen: one. The tert-butyl carbon has three carbon neighbors, which would make a tertiary alcohol if it carried an OH, but the amine rule counts carbons on N.

q: (CH3)3C–OH is what kind of alcohol?
e: The carbon carrying the OH has three carbon neighbors. Alcohols are classified by that carbon, so tertiary.

q: CH3CH2CHO contains which group?
e: A CHO written at the end of a condensed formula is an aldehyde: the carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen.

q: Which molecule contains an ester but no ether?
e: CH3CH2COOCH3 has a C=O with O–CH3 on it and nothing else oxygen-containing. CH3COCH2OCH3 has a ketone plus an ether, and CH3OCH2CH3 is a plain ether.

q: Acetaminophen, HO–C6H4–NH–CO–CH3, contains which groups?
e: The OH is on the ring, so phenol; the nitrogen is bonded to a C=O, so amide. Neither an alcohol nor an amine is present.

q: Aspirin, HOOC–C6H4–O–CO–CH3, contains which set of groups?
e: COOH is the acid. The –O–CO–CH3 has a carbonyl next to its oxygen, which makes it an ester rather than an ether, and the C=O has an oxygen neighbor, so it is not a ketone.

q: Why does a carbonyl carbon end up strongly δ+?
e: Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, and the double bond means two bonds pull the same way, so the carbonyl carbon is the most electron-poor carbon in the table.

q: Through which feature does an amine mostly react?
e: The C–N bond is only mildly polar. The nitrogen lone pair is the accessible pair of electrons, and it is what an amine uses.

q: C=C has no polar bond. Why is it still a functional group?
e: Uneven electron density is one way for electrons to be available; exposed is the other. π electrons sit outside the bond axis, held only by sideways p-orbital overlap.

q: Which formula contains a nitro group?
e: A nitro group is R–NO2, nitrogen bonded to two oxygens. CH3CN is a nitrile, CH3NH2 an amine, CH3CONH2 an amide.

q: Which of these is a thiol?
e: A thiol is R–SH, sulfur carrying a hydrogen. CH3SCH3 is a sulfide (the sulfur analog of an ether).

q: How many distinct functional groups are in HO–CH2CH2–COOCH3?
e: The OH on a saturated CH2 is an alcohol. The COOCH3 is one ester group, which should not be split into an ether and a ketone.

q: CH3CH2CH(CH3)Br is what kind of alkyl halide?
e: The carbon carrying Br is bonded to two other carbons (the ethyl and the methyl), so it is secondary.

q: Ibuprofen is (CH3)2CHCH2–C6H4–CH(CH3)–COOH. How many functional groups does it contain besides the aromatic ring?
e: Everything to the left of the ring and the CH(CH3) to its right are C–C and C–H only. The only group beyond the ring is COOH.

q: A student calls the C=O in CH3COOCH3 a ketone. What is wrong?
e: A ketone requires carbon on both sides of the C=O. With an oxygen on one side, the carbonyl is the ester functional group, not a ketone plus an ether.

q: In R–NO2 the nitrogen has four bonds. What formal charge does it carry?
e: Nitrogen with four bonds and no lone pair has one electron fewer than neutral, so +1. The singly bonded oxygen with three lone pairs carries −1, so the group is neutral overall.

q: Which pair of condensed formulas differ by a single oxygen atom yet belong to different groups?
e: Inserting one O between the carbonyl and the methyl turns the ketone (acetone) into an ester (methyl acetate). The other pairs differ by a carbon, by a sulfur-for-oxygen swap, or by a whole C=O.

q: A skeletal structure is drawn as a zigzag of five line segments. How many carbons?
e: Every vertex and both ends are carbons: four internal vertices plus two ends makes six. Counting the segments instead of the carbons is off by one every time.

q: In a skeletal structure, what does a plain line represent?
e: A line is a bond. The atoms sit at its ends, and if nothing is written there, they are carbons.

q: A carbon at the end of a chain has one line to it. How many hydrogens?
e: One bond drawn, three left over: CH3. Chain ends are the methyl groups of the molecule.

q: Why is an O-H hydrogen drawn when C-H hydrogens are not?
e: The notation keeps what reacts. An O-H hydrogen is acidic, hydrogen bonds and is removed by base; a C-H along a chain almost never is.

q: What does a bare hexagon represent?
e: Six corners, six carbons, two hydrogens on each. Benzene needs three alternating double bonds drawn in, or a circle.

q: How is benzene marked as different from cyclohexane?
e: A bare hexagon is the saturated ring. The alternating double bonds, or a circle for the delocalized system, mark benzene.

q: Lone pairs are usually omitted. What should you do about them?
e: An oxygen drawn with two bonds has two lone pairs whether anyone drew them or not, and arrow-pushing needs them.

q: Which atoms are always written out explicitly?
e: Carbon is the only atom left implied. O, N, S, Cl and the rest are always drawn, and so are their hydrogens.

q: A four-vertex zigzag carries a methyl branch on vertex 2 and a C=C between vertices 3 and 4. How many hydrogens sit on vertex 3?
