e: Count bonds, not lines. Vertex 3 has one bond along the chain to vertex 2 and a double bond — two bonds — to vertex 4. That is three of its four, leaving one hydrogen.

q: Four line segments in a zigzag, no heteroatoms. What is the formula?
e: Four segments means five carbons: pentane. Two CH3 ends and three CH2 vertices gives C5H12.

q: What does skeletal notation deliberately hide?
e: It hides the uninformative half and keeps the skeleton and the functional groups, which is the whole trade.

q: A carbon with four lines to it carries how many hydrogens?
e: All four bonds go to other atoms, so there is no room for hydrogen. This is a quaternary carbon.

q: What is the commonest miscount in reading a skeletal chain?
e: A zigzag of five segments is six carbons, not four. Both ends are carbons and are easy to miss.

q: Which statement about skeletal notation is FALSE?
e: It is the reverse: every atom not drawn is a carbon, so anything written out is something else.

q: What does a drawn ring show that a condensed formula does not?
e: A condensed formula already states connectivity, and the hydrogen count is inferred either way. What the drawing adds is geometry: ring size and shape are visible without decoding anything.

q: An N is drawn with two lines and one H. How many lone pairs?
e: Nitrogen has five valence electrons and three bonds here, leaving one lone pair.

q: A five-vertex zigzag has a methyl branch on vertex 2 and a C=C between vertices 4 and 5. What is its molecular formula?
e: Six carbons: five in the chain plus the branch. Subtracting bonds from four along the chain gives 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 hydrogens, plus 3 on the methyl, which is 12. The one double bond is exactly what separates C₆H₁₄ from C₆H₁₂.

q: What must you work out rather than read off a skeletal drawing?
e: The hydrogen count is inferred by subtracting the drawn bonds from four — that is the trade the notation makes.

q: Which of these descriptions is of a structure that cannot exist?
e: Count to four. Two lines plus three hydrogens is five bonds on carbon, which no structure has; the other three descriptions each come to exactly four. This is the miscount that happens when a vertex is read as a carbon and then labeled as if it were a substituent too.

q: What do wedge and dash bonds add to a skeletal structure?
e: They say which bonds come toward you and which go away, which is what stereochemistry needs.

q: A Cl is drawn at the end of a line. What is on that carbon?
e: The chlorine takes one of the four bonds. Whatever bonds remain after the drawn ones are hydrogens.

q: Why does this notation matter for mechanisms?
e: You have to see the implied carbons and the undrawn lone pairs as clearly as the drawn ones.

q: A hexagon with an OH on one corner. What is the formula?
e: Six ring carbons; the OH replaces one hydrogen, giving five CH2 groups and one CH-OH.

q: A skeletal drawing shows an oxygen with one line to a carbon and a minus sign beside it. What does that oxygen carry?
e: Oxygen has six valence electrons. One bond and a charge of −1 means six unshared electrons, which is three lone pairs, and no room left for a hydrogen. A neutral oxygen with one line would have been drawn OH instead.

q: Resonance structures differ only in the position of:
e: Resonance structures show the same atoms in the same positions — only electron placement (lone pairs/pi bonds) differs.

q: The real structure of a resonance-stabilized species is:
e: The actual molecule is a single resonance hybrid — a weighted average of the contributing structures, not an equilibrium between them.

q: Which resonance structure generally contributes most to the real hybrid?
e: Lower-energy (more stable) resonance structures — full octets, minimized/well-placed formal charges — contribute more to the actual hybrid.

q: Resonance structures must all have the same:
e: Only electrons move between resonance structures — the atoms themselves never move, so connectivity (which atom is bonded to which) is identical in every resonance structure.

q: Drawing multiple resonance structures for a molecule means the molecule rapidly interconverts between two or more distinct forms.
e: This is a common misconception. The molecule has only one real structure, a hybrid of all the contributing structures; it never actually becomes any single drawn structure.

q: In the carbonate ion (CO3^2-), how many equivalent resonance structures contribute to the hybrid?
e: The negative charge and the C=O double bond can each be placed on any of the three equivalent oxygens, giving three equivalent resonance structures that average to give each C–O bond equal, partial double-bond character.

q: Resonance stabilization generally makes a molecule or ion:
e: Delocalizing electrons over more atoms lowers the overall energy of the real hybrid below that of any one localized contributing structure — this is the resonance (delocalization) energy.

q: Which pair of features makes a resonance structure a poor (minor) contributor?
e: Structures with incomplete octets on carbon, or other atoms that normally want 8 electrons, are high in energy and contribute very little to the real hybrid.

q: Placing a negative formal charge on oxygen is generally more favorable than placing it on carbon in a resonance structure.
e: Electronegative atoms like oxygen stabilize negative charge better than carbon does, so resonance structures with negative charge on O are usually major contributors.

q: For an allylic cation (CH2=CH–CH2+), the curved arrow used to draw its second resonance structure moves electrons from:
e: The adjacent pi bond's electrons shift toward the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, moving the double bond over by one position and relocating the positive charge to the far end.

q: Why does an amide (R–CO–NH2) have a C–N bond that is shorter and stronger than a typical amine C–N bond?
e: A resonance structure places the nitrogen lone pair in a pi bond to carbon (with the negative charge moving to oxygen), giving real double-bond character to the C–N bond and restricting its rotation.

q: Rank the following resonance contributors of an enolate (CH2=CH–O^- versus ^-CH2–CH=O) by how much they contribute to the real hybrid.
e: Negative charge is better stabilized on the more electronegative oxygen, so the O-centered structure is the major contributor even though both are valid resonance forms.

q: A nitro group (R–NO2) is often drawn with one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond bearing a negative charge, but both N–O bonds are experimentally found to
e: Two equivalent resonance structures (swapping which oxygen carries the double bond and which carries the negative charge) mean the real structure is a hybrid with both N–O bonds equivalent and of intermediate bond order.

q: Which of the following is a requirement for two structures to be valid resonance forms of each other?
e: Resonance structures share identical atomic connectivity and total electron count; only the positions of pi electrons and lone pairs differ. That difference is allowed to change individual formal charges, and it is allowed to change how many bonds are drawn.

q: Benzene's six C–C bonds are all the same length (intermediate between single and double bond length) because:
e: The two Kekule structures are equal contributors, so the actual molecule has six equivalent bonds with bond order 1.5, not alternating single and double bonds.

q: A curved arrow used to generate a new resonance structure can show a lone pair moving to form a new pi bond, or a pi bond's electrons moving to become a lone pa
e: Both directions are valid ways of redistributing electrons between resonance structures, as long as connectivity and total charge are conserved.

q: Pyrrole is a flat five-membered ring with an N–H whose nitrogen uses its three sp² orbitals for two C–N bonds and the N–H. Pyridine is a flat six-membered ring
e: In pyrrole the N–H leaves the lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps the ring pi system (delocalized), whereas in pyridine the lone pair occupies an in-plane sp2 orbital perpendicular to the pi system and cannot delocalize.

q: Which contributing structure of the carboxylate ion (RCOO^-) is the major contributor?
e: The two oxygens in a carboxylate are equivalent by symmetry, so the two resonance structures (negative charge/double bond swapped between the two oxygens) contribute equally, giving two identical C–O bond lengths.

q: A resonance structure with separated formal charges (+ and -) generally contributes more than one with no charge separation, as long as both satisfy the octet r
e: Minimizing formal charge and charge separation generally increases a structure's stability and contribution; a neutral, fully-satisfied-octet structure is usually favored over one with separated charges.

q: For the allyl radical (CH2=CH–CH2•), resonance predicts that the unpaired electron is:
e: Like allylic cations and anions, an allylic radical has resonance structures that place the odd electron on either terminal carbon, so the true structure has partial radical character spread over both ends.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes resonance structures from isomers?
e: Isomers are distinct, isolable compounds, whereas resonance structures are just different ways of drawing electrons in the one real molecule; you cannot isolate a single resonance structure.

q: In a resonance structure for the phenoxide ion (deprotonated phenol), the negative charge can be placed at the ortho and para ring carbons as well as on oxygen.
e: Pushing electrons from the oxygen lone pair into the ring, and then around the ring pi system, generates resonance structures with negative charge at the ortho and para positions, explaining phenoxide's extra stability and its reactivity there.

q: Comparing a resonance structure where a positive charge sits on oxygen (with three bonds, full octet) to one where it sits on carbon (with only three bonds, inc
e: A complete octet is usually weighted more heavily than minimizing which atom bears a positive charge; an atom with an incomplete octet is a high-energy, minor contributor.

q: Three equivalent contributors of the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) each place one N=O double bond. What is the average N–O bond order in the real ion?
e: Each N–O linkage is double in one contributor and single in the other two, so on average it is (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3. That is why all three N–O bonds are measured at the same length, between a single and a double bond.

q: One anion has a single excellent contributor with full octets and the charge on oxygen. Another has three contributors, all putting the charge on carbon. Which
e: Counting contributors is a rough guide, not a rule, and the ranking criteria say so: a low-energy structure with full octets and the charge on an electronegative atom describes the hybrid better than three high-energy ones do. Exams use this comparison precisely because the count is the tempting answer.

q: Why is it misleading to say a resonance hybrid is a 'mixture' of its contributing structures?
e: A resonance hybrid is one real, single structure; the multiple drawings are just an artificial way of depicting delocalized electron density using the tools of simple bonding diagrams, not a literal equilibrium or blend of separate species.

q: Which of these changes between two drawn Lewis structures would disqualify them from being true resonance structures of each other?
e: Resonance structures never move atoms (including hydrogens) — only electrons move. Moving an atom creates a different molecule (often a tautomer), not a resonance structure.

q: In which of these is an oxygen lone pair delocalized by resonance?
e: Delocalization needs an unbroken run of overlapping p orbitals. Only in the second is oxygen bonded directly to an sp² carbon of the pi bond. In the first an sp³ CH₂ sits in between and breaks the run, and the last two have no pi bond for the pair to reach.

q: In the acetate ion's major resonance structures, what happens to the C–O bond lengths compared to a simple ester's C=O and C–O–R bonds?
e: Because the two equivalent resonance structures contribute equally, the real acetate ion has two identical C–O bonds with bond order about 1.5, not one single and one double bond.

q: A student draws a contributor of acetate in which the carboxyl carbon ends up with five bonds. What is wrong with it?
e: Second-row atoms have four valence orbitals and a hard ceiling of eight electrons. A five-bonded carbon is not a poor contributor to be ranked low, it is not a Lewis structure at all, and the arrow that produced it formed a bond without breaking one.

q: A curved arrow in a mechanism always starts at:
e: Curved arrows track electron movement — they start where electrons already are (a lone pair or an existing bond).

q: Where does a curved arrow’s head point?
e: The arrowhead marks the destination of the moving electron pair — a new bond or a new lone pair.

q: In an acid-base proton transfer, where does the curved arrow showing the base attacking start from?
e: The arrow starts at the electron source doing the attacking — the base’s lone pair — and points to the proton it is grabbing.

q: A curved arrow can legally start from a positively charged atom with no electrons to give.
e: A curved arrow always represents electrons moving, so its tail must start at a source of electron density (a lone pair, a bond, or a negative charge), never at an empty orbital or cation.

q: When a pi bond attacks an electrophile, the curved arrow's tail is placed on:
e: Because both electrons of the pi bond move together as a unit, the tail is drawn from the middle of the double bond line, not from either individual atom.

q: In an SN2 reaction, how many curved arrows are minimally needed to show the nucleophile displacing the leaving group?
e: One arrow shows the nucleophile's lone pair attacking the carbon, and a second arrow shows the C–leaving group bond breaking as electrons move onto the leaving group.

q: A curved arrow starts on a C–H bond, and in the product there is a C=C between that carbon and the one next to it. Where must the arrowhead point?
e: A head pointing at the middle of an existing bond means a new pi bond forms there. The C–H electrons become the second bond between the two carbons, so the head sits on the C–C bond between them rather than on any single atom.

q: Arrow 1 runs from a lone pair on HO⁻ to the H of H–Br. Arrow 2 runs from the H–Br bond to Br. What are the products and their charges?
e: Arrow 1 makes the new O–H bond, so hydroxide (one bond, three lone pairs, −1) becomes water (two bonds, two lone pairs, neutral). Arrow 2 hands the bonding pair to bromine, which ends with no bonds and four lone pairs: 7 − 8 = −1. Charge in −1, charge out −1.

q: If you draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on oxygen toward a neighboring carbon, but that carbon already has four bonds and no leaving group departing, what i
e: Carbon can never exceed four bonds (an octet at most); forming a new bond to carbon requires that carbon simultaneously break an existing bond (a leaving group departing) unless it already has room, such as being cationic.

q: In drawing a mechanism step, the tail of a curved arrow can be placed on a formal negative charge even if no explicit lone pair is drawn.
e: A formal negative charge implies an unshared pair at that atom, so a tail drawn there is still starting on a lone pair — one that simply was not redrawn. It is accepted shorthand rather than a third kind of tail, and the test does not change: you must still be able to name the pair the tail is standing on.

q: Which of these is an invalid use of a curved arrow?
e: A bare proton (H+) has no electrons to donate, so an arrow can never start from H+; instead, the arrow starts from the base's lone pair and points to the H, while a separate arrow shows the H–X bond breaking.

q: When two curved arrows are drawn for a single mechanistic step, they must be drawn simultaneously to represent a concerted process, not as two separate sequenti
e: Multiple arrows within one mechanism arrow-pushing 'step' (one structure to the next) represent bond-breaking and bond-forming events happening at the same time, i.e., concertedly.

q: For an intramolecular ring-closing step where a nucleophile inside the same molecule attacks an electrophilic carbon, how many curved arrows are typically neede
e: As in any nucleophilic substitution, one arrow shows the nucleophile (even if intramolecular) attacking, and a second shows the leaving group departing, regardless of whether the nucleophile is in the same molecule.

q: A curved arrow's tail placed in between two atoms on a bond line, rather than directly on an atom, specifically indicates:
e: Placing the tail on the bond line itself (rather than on an atom's lone pair) shows that the whole bonding pair associated with that bond is the electron source.

q: In the mechanism for acid-catalyzed protonation of an alkene, the curved arrow showing the alkene attacking H+ starts from the pi bond and points to:
e: The pi electrons act as the nucleophile and are shown attacking the electrophilic proton; the arrowhead lands on the H atom that is being bonded.

q: Why can you not draw one continuous curved arrow from the breaking C–leaving group bond straight to where the nucleophile will bond?
e: Two electron pairs are in play and they are not the same pair. One starts as the nucleophile's lone pair and ends in the new bond; the other starts as the C–LG bonding pair and ends on the leaving group. A single arrow can only describe one pair going from one place to one other place.

q: A curved arrow used to show a carbocation rearrangement (1,2-hydride shift) has its tail on:
e: The electrons of the adjacent C–H bond shift to fill the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, so the tail starts on that C–H sigma bond and the head points to the cationic carbon.

q: Which statement about curved arrows and formal charge is correct?
e: Since formal charge tracks an atom's electron count relative to its neutral state, moving electrons away from an atom (tail) raises its formal charge while electrons arriving (head) lower the formal charge at the destination.

q: Preview of a later chapter: in an E2 elimination a base removes a hydrogen, a C=C forms, and a leaving group departs, all in one step. Three curved arrows are d
e: E2 is a single concerted step: base removes the beta-hydrogen, those electrons form the new pi bond, and simultaneously the leaving group departs with the sigma bond electrons — three synchronized arrows.

q: Every curved arrow tail must originate exactly where the electrons physically are before the step, and every arrowhead must point to exactly where they end up a
e: Curved arrows are a precise bookkeeping tool: tails mark the electrons' starting location and heads mark their ending location, corresponding exactly to the bonding changes between the starting and product structures.

q: A student draws an arrow from a lone pair on a neutral amine nitrogen pointing toward a proton on a neutral water molecule, forming an ammonium ion and hydroxid
e: The amine's lone pair is the base's electron source (tail), and it forms a new bond to the acidic proton (head); a second arrow would then show the O–H bond breaking, with electrons going to oxygen.

q: Why can't a curved arrow ever have its head pointing at a plain, unlabeled blank space with no atom or bond present?
e: An arrowhead marks the destination of electron density — either a new bond (so it points between two specific atoms) or a new lone pair (so it points at a specific atom) — never an arbitrary empty location.

q: One arrow takes a C=C pi bond to a proton and nothing else is drawn. The starting alkene is neutral and has no leaving group. Which rule does this break?
e: Charge in is +1 from the proton and charge out is +1 on the carbocation, so nothing is unbalanced. Carbocations are electron-deficient but not illegal: six electrons on carbon is exactly what an empty p orbital looks like. Only more than eight would be impossible.

q: When two separate curved arrows point to the same single atom in one mechanistic step, that atom would end up with too many bonds unless something simultaneousl
e: If two new bonds or lone pairs are being added to one atom in the same step without anything leaving, that atom would exceed its normal valence (e.g., carbon exceeding four bonds), which is why such steps require a compensating departure.

q: Preview of a later chapter: a Grignard reagent is R–MgBr, whose C–Mg bond is polarized so that carbon is nucleophilic. That carbon attacks the carbon of a keton
e: The polarized C–Mg bond's electrons attack the electrophilic carbonyl carbon (first arrow), and the pi electrons of C=O simultaneously shift onto oxygen to avoid carbon exceeding four bonds (second arrow), generating an alkoxide.

q: A curved arrow can start from a sigma bond between two carbons (a C–C bond) in certain rearrangement or fragmentation mechanisms.
e: While less common in introductory reactions than lone pairs or pi bonds, C–C sigma bonds can act as electron sources in rearrangements (such as carbocation rearrangements where an alkyl group shifts), so this is valid.

q: Which best describes the overall direction curved arrows flow in virtually every organic mechanism?
e: Curved arrows track the flow of electron density, and electrons always flow from a source with available density toward a site that can accept it (an electrophile), never the reverse.

q: Preview of a later chapter: an alcohol adds to an aldehyde under acid catalysis (the product is called a hemiacetal). Using only the four arrow patterns, the ve
e: Under acid catalysis, the mechanism usually begins with protonation of the carbonyl oxygen (its lone pair attacks H+), which increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon before the alcohol attacks.

q: If a curved arrow's tail is drawn on an atom with no lone pairs, no negative charge, and no bond to break from that position, the arrow is invalid.
e: Every arrow tail needs a genuine electron source at that exact location — a lone pair, a bond, or charge implying available electrons; an atom with none of these cannot be a valid tail location.

q: In the reaction of a carboxylic acid with a base, which is the correct single curved arrow showing the acid donating its proton to the base, assuming the O–H bo
e: The base supplies the electrons that form the new bond to the proton, so the arrow tail sits on the base's lone pair and the head points at the hydrogen; a separate arrow then shows the O–H bond breaking toward oxygen.

q: A nucleophile is best described as:
e: Nucleophiles ("nucleus-loving") are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair to form a new bond.

q: Which factor generally makes a species a better nucleophile in a polar protic solvent?
e: In a protic solvent every anion sits in a shell of hydrogen bonds, and the small charge-dense ones are held tightest. A large, polarizable anion such as I⁻ is barely caged and is free to attack, so size wins here. In a polar aprotic solvent there is no cage to strip and the order reverses.

q: Methanol is a mediocre nucleophile and sodium methoxide is a strong one. What single change does that, and why does it work?
e: Deprotonation leaves the same oxygen with the same nuclear charge but an extra unshared pair and no bond holding it. That pair sits higher in energy than any pair in the neutral alcohol, so it has less distance to climb to reach the transition state, which is what a faster attack means.

q: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as a nucleophile?
e: A bare proton has no electrons to donate and is instead a classic electrophile; true nucleophiles must have a lone pair, negative charge, or pi bond available to donate.

q: Nucleophilicity and basicity measure exactly the same property and always rank species in the same order.
e: Basicity is thermodynamic (affinity for a proton at equilibrium), while nucleophilicity is kinetic (rate of attack on an electrophilic carbon); steric bulk and solvent can make the two rankings diverge, as with bulky bases that are poor nucleophiles.

q: Going down a column of the periodic table (F⁻ to Cl⁻ to Br⁻ to I⁻), nucleophilicity in a polar protic solvent generally:
e: Two things change together down the column: the anion gets larger and more polarizable, and it gets less tightly solvated by hydrogen bonds. Both free it to attack, so iodide is the best nucleophile of the four in water or methanol — and the worst of the four once the solvent is aprotic.

q: In a protic solvent like water or methanol, I- is typically a better nucleophile than F-, but in a polar aprotic solvent like DMSO, the order can reverse.
e: Protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to small, localized-charge anions like F-, caging it and lowering its reactivity; in aprotic solvents with no hydrogen bonding, F- is not solvated as heavily and its small size/high charge density can make it more nucleophilic than I-.

q: Which of these is the best nucleophile in a protic solvent, assuming all are similarly charged halides?
e: In protic solvents, strong solvation (hydrogen bonding) cripples small, charge-dense nucleophiles like F-; the large, weakly solvated, highly polarizable I- is freest to attack and is the best nucleophile.

q: A bulky nucleophile like tert-butoxide (tBuO-) is generally a weaker nucleophile (in the SN2 sense) than a less hindered one like methoxide (CH3O-), even though
e: Steric bulk around the nucleophilic atom hinders its ability to approach and bond with an electrophilic carbon in an SN2-type attack, reducing nucleophilicity even when basicity (proton affinity) remains high.

q: Why is a thiolate (RS-) generally a stronger nucleophile than an alkoxide (RO-), even though alkoxide is the stronger base?
e: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, so its lone pairs deform easily and can begin forming a bond at longer range. It is the weaker base for a related but separate reason — the charge is spread over a much bigger atom, and H–S is a weaker bond than H–O — which is exactly why the two rankings come apart here.

q: An uncharged species such as ammonia (NH3) can never act as a nucleophile because it carries no negative charge.
e: Neutral species with an available lone pair (like NH3, H2O, or amines) are common, effective nucleophiles; a negative charge increases nucleophilicity but is not required.

q: Rank CH3O-, CH3NH2, and CH3COO- in order of decreasing nucleophilicity toward a simple alkyl halide (all else being similar solvent conditions).
e: A localized, non-resonance-stabilized alkoxide is a stronger nucleophile than a neutral amine, and the resonance-stabilized, delocalized carboxylate is the weakest of the three because its negative charge is spread out and less available.

q: A pi bond, such as the C=C of an alkene, can act as a nucleophile even though it carries no lone pair or formal negative charge.
e: The electron density of a pi bond is available to attack an electrophile (as in addition of HBr to an alkene), making alkenes legitimate, if relatively weak, nucleophiles.

q: Which factor does NOT generally increase nucleophilicity?
e: Higher electronegativity means an atom holds its electrons more tightly, making it less willing to donate them to an electrophile, which generally decreases (not increases) nucleophilicity.

q: Why does resonance delocalization (as in a carboxylate or enolate) generally reduce nucleophilicity compared to a non-delocalized anion of similar charge?
e: When charge is shared across several atoms via resonance, less electron density sits at any one reactive site, so the species is both more stable (weaker base/nucleophile) and slower to attack an electrophile.

q: Between H2O and OH-, which is the better nucleophile, and why?
e: Removing a proton from water to give hydroxide increases the electron density around oxygen without adding extra nuclear charge to hold it, making the anion considerably more reactive as a nucleophile (and stronger base).

q: A good nucleophile must always also be a good leaving group in the reverse reaction.
e: Good nucleophiles and good leaving groups tend to have opposite characteristics (strong nucleophiles are typically poor leaving groups, like amines or alkoxides, and vice versa, like halides or sulfonates), so this statement is false in general.

q: Which statement best explains why cyanide (CN-) is an effective nucleophile despite carbon (not nitrogen) usually being the attacking atom?
e: Although formal charge considerations might suggest nitrogen, the carbon atom of cyanide is the kinetically preferred nucleophilic site in most SN2-type reactions due to its orbital characteristics and accessibility.

q: You want substitution rather than elimination on a primary alkyl bromide. Which reagent choice fits that goal?
e: Substitution needs a species that attacks carbon; elimination needs one that grabs a proton from the carbon next door. Iodide is large, polarizable and a very weak base, so it does the first and not the second. The other three are chosen for how well they remove protons, which is the wrong job here.

q: An sp3-hybridized nitrogen lone pair (as in a trialkylamine) is generally a better nucleophile than an sp2-hybridized nitrogen lone pair (as in pyridine), all e
e: An sp3 lone pair has less s-character than an sp2 lone pair, so it sits farther from the nucleus and is held less tightly, making it somewhat more available to donate; this fits pyridine's sp2 nitrogen being a weaker nucleophile and base than a typical sp3 trialkylamine.

q: What makes a carbanion (such as an acetylide ion, HC≡C-) an especially strong nucleophile?
e: Because carbon is not very electronegative, a negative charge on carbon is poorly stabilized and very reactive, making carbanions some of the strongest nucleophiles (and bases) encountered in introductory organic chemistry.

q: Which best describes an 'ambident' nucleophile like the cyanide or enolate ion?
e: Ambident nucleophiles (like enolates, which can react through carbon or oxygen, or cyanide through carbon or nitrogen) have more than one potential reactive atom, and which one reacts can depend on conditions.

q: In general, across a single row of the periodic table (e.g., comparing C, N, O, F anions of similar charge), nucleophilicity tends to decrease as electronegativ
e: Moving right across a period, atoms hold electron density more tightly due to increasing electronegativity, so their lone pairs are less available to donate, generally reducing both basicity and nucleophilicity.

q: Why does steric hindrance near the nucleophilic atom matter more for SN2 reactivity than for simple proton-transfer basicity?
e: Because an SN2 nucleophile must approach a tetrahedral, often crowded carbon from a specific backside angle, bulky substituents on the nucleophile or substrate create steric clashes that aren't nearly as significant when a small, exposed proton is simply being removed by a base.

q: Azide ion (N3-) is generally considered a good nucleophile in SN2 reactions.
e: Azide is a small, negatively charged, relatively unhindered nucleophile commonly used in SN2 substitutions to introduce a nitrogen functional group, later reducible to an amine.

q: Which change would most directly increase a nucleophile's reactivity toward a given alkyl halide substrate, without changing the nucleophile's identity or charg
e: Polar aprotic solvents cannot hydrogen-bond to and cage anionic nucleophiles the way protic solvents do, leaving the nucleophile's electron density more exposed and reactive.

q: Which of the following pairs correctly identifies the stronger nucleophile based primarily on charge alone, holding the rest of the structure constant?
e: A negative charge raises the electron density on the donor atom, so the anion of a conjugate pair is always the better nucleophile. Going the other way is worse than it looks: protonating an amine consumes the lone pair entirely, so the ammonium ion is not a weak nucleophile but no nucleophile at all.

q: Triethylamine is routinely used as a base but is a poor nucleophile toward a crowded carbon. What explains the difference?
e: Both jobs use the same nitrogen lone pair, so the difference is not electronic. Taking a proton means reaching a bare hydrogen on the outside of a molecule; attacking a carbon means reaching an atom already surrounded by three other groups. Three ethyls barely hinder the first and badly hinder the second.

q: A hydride ion (H-) delivered from a reagent like NaBH4 or LiAlH4 acts as a nucleophile in reducing a carbonyl. What is it attacking?
e: Hydride attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon, with its electron pair forming a new C–H bond while the C=O pi electrons shift onto oxygen, ultimately giving an alkoxide (and after protonation, an alcohol).

q: Why is water generally considered a weaker nucleophile than hydroxide, yet water is still used as a nucleophile in many SN1 and addition reactions?
e: Neutral nucleophiles like water are weaker than their anionic counterparts but are still perfectly capable nucleophiles, especially toward highly reactive electrophiles such as carbocations formed in SN1 pathways.

q: An electrophile is best described as:
e: Electrophiles ("electron-loving") are electron-poor and accept an electron pair to form a new bond.

q: A carbonyl carbon (C=O) is a good electrophile because:
e: Oxygen’s electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, giving carbon a δ+ that nucleophiles attack.

q: Which of these is typically NOT a good electrophile?
e: Hydroxide is electron-rich (a nucleophile/base), not electron-poor — it seeks to donate electrons, not accept them.

q: Which carbon of ClCH₂–CH₂–CO–CH₃ is the most electrophilic?
e: The carbonyl carbon is bonded twice over to oxygen, so it is the most polarized carbon in the molecule, and it needs no leaving group because the pi bond can break onto the oxygen instead. The CH₂Cl carbon is a genuine second site — δ+ and carrying a group that departs — but it is the less electron-poor of the two.

q: An electrophile must always carry a full positive formal charge.
e: Many electrophiles are neutral but electron-poor (such as the carbon of a carbonyl group, or boron in BF3), so a full positive charge is not required, only a deficiency of electron density at the reactive atom.

q: Why is the carbon of an epoxide ring a good electrophile even though the molecule overall is neutral?
e: The electronegative oxygen pulls electron density from the ring carbons (inducing partial positive charge), and the strained three-membered ring geometry adds extra driving force for nucleophiles to open the ring at carbon.

q: Rank BF3, CH4, and CH3Cl in order of decreasing electrophilicity at their central/relevant carbon or boron atom.
e: BF3's boron has an empty p orbital and no octet, making it a very strong electrophile (Lewis acid); CH3Cl's carbon is moderately electrophilic due to the polar C–Cl bond; CH4 has no polarized bonds and is essentially non-electrophilic.

q: Which has the more electrophilic carbonyl carbon, CH₃CHO or CF₃CHO?
e: Induction from three fluorines strips further electron density out of the carbonyl carbon and deepens its δ+. Electron-withdrawing neighbors sharpen an electrophile and electron-donating ones such as alkyl groups blunt it, which makes the methyl compound the milder of the two.

q: Adding an electron-withdrawing group (such as a second carbonyl or a halogen) near a carbonyl carbon generally makes that carbonyl carbon:
e: Electron-withdrawing groups intensify the positive character at the carbonyl carbon by further depleting its electron density, which is why acid chlorides and anhydrides are more electrophilic (more reactive to nucleophiles) than simple ketones or esters.

q: A carbocation is generally considered one of the strongest electrophiles in organic chemistry because it has an empty orbital and carries a full positive charge
e: Carbocations are highly electron-deficient, with an empty p orbital and a full positive charge on carbon, making them extremely reactive toward any available nucleophile or pi bond.

q: Why is the carbon attached to a leaving group in an alkyl halide (e.g., the carbon in CH3–Br) considered electrophilic even though it is tetravalent and neutral
e: The polar C–Br bond leaves carbon partially positive (δ+), and because Br- can leave as a stable anion, a nucleophile can attack that carbon while the C–Br bond breaks, as in SN1/SN2 reactions.

q: Which halogen-containing species acts as the electrophile when Br2 reacts with an alkene in a bromination addition reaction?
e: As the alkene's pi electrons approach Br2, they induce a dipole in the Br–Br bond, making one bromine electrophilic; the alkene attacks it, displacing bromide and forming a bromonium ion intermediate.

q: A Lewis acid such as AlCl3 is classified as an electrophile because it:
e: Aluminum in AlCl3 has only six electrons around it (no octet), giving it a strongly electron-accepting empty orbital, which is the hallmark of a Lewis acid/electrophile used to activate other electrophiles in reactions like Friedel-Crafts.

q: Protonation of an alcohol by a strong acid converts the alcohol's oxygen region into a better leaving group, but does this make the adjacent carbon a better or
e: Protonating the oxygen gives it a formal positive charge, which pulls even more electron density away from the attached carbon through the sigma bond, increasing that carbon's electrophilicity and making it far more reactive to nucleophilic attack or departure as a leaving group.

q: Which of the following carbonyl-containing compounds has the most electrophilic carbonyl carbon, making it the most reactive toward nucleophiles?
e: Chlorine is a strong electron-withdrawing group and a poor electron donor by resonance, leaving the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon the most electron-poor and electrophilic; amides are the least electrophilic because nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl most effectively, reducing electrophilicity.

q: A carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is generally a poor electrophile at its carbonyl carbon.
e: The negative charge and resonance delocalization in a carboxylate actually increase electron density at the carbonyl carbon (compared to a neutral ester or acid), making it a very poor electrophile and resistant to nucleophilic attack.

q: Why can a simple, unactivated alkane like ethane not act as an electrophile under ordinary conditions?
e: Without a polarized bond, an empty orbital, or a good leaving group, there is no electron-poor site available, so simple alkanes are essentially unreactive toward nucleophiles under standard conditions.

q: In an SN1 mechanism, which species formed as an intermediate is the actual electrophile attacked by the incoming nucleophile?
e: Once the leaving group departs in the first (rate-determining) step, a planar carbocation intermediate forms with an empty p orbital, and this highly electrophilic cation is what the nucleophile subsequently attacks.

q: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is generally more electrophilic than a ketone's carbonyl carbon because:
e: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating and bulky; a ketone has two of them stabilizing and shielding the carbonyl carbon, while an aldehyde's single alkyl group (plus a small hydrogen) leaves it more electrophilic and more accessible to nucleophiles.

q: An aromatic ring undergoing electrophilic aromatic substitution reacts with an electrophile such as Br+ generated from Br2 and a Lewis acid catalyst.
e: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a Lewis acid (like FeBr3) helps generate a highly electrophilic species (such as Br+) that the electron-rich aromatic ring then attacks as the nucleophile.

q: Which statement correctly relates electrophile strength to reaction rate with a given nucleophile?
e: Just as nucleophile strength affects rate, a more electron-deficient and accessible electrophile is attacked more readily and rapidly by a given nucleophile, since there is a greater driving force for electron transfer.

q: In a protonated ketone the plus sign is drawn on oxygen. Which atom does a nucleophile attack?
e: A drawn charge is formal bookkeeping, not a measure of electron deficiency. Oxygen with three bonds and a plus still has lone pairs and a full octet; the carbon is the atom that is short, and the minor contributor placing the positive charge on it says so. Hunt for the deficient atom, not the symbol.

q: Why does conjugation of a carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond (as in an enone, an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) create a second electrophilic site at the
e: A resonance structure of an enone shows the C=C pi electrons shifting all the way to the very electronegative oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the beta carbon; this explains why nucleophiles can add either directly to the carbonyl carbon or to this more remote beta carbon (conjugate addition).

q: Which of the following best explains why CO2 (carbon dioxide) reacts readily as an electrophile with strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents?
e: The two electronegative oxygens withdraw significant electron density from the central carbon, making it quite electrophilic; Grignard reagents readily attack this carbon to eventually form a carboxylic acid after workup.

q: Why does protonating a ketone's oxygen make its carbon a far better electrophile?
e: A protonated carbonyl has two contributors: one with the plus on oxygen and every octet full, and one with the plus on carbon and only six electrons there. The second is minor but real, and its share of the hybrid is what deepens the carbon's positive character. That is why so many carbonyl reactions are run under acid.

q: A terminal alkyne's acidic proton can be removed by a strong base. In this acid-base reaction, which species is acting as the electrophile?
e: The acidic C–H proton is the electrophilic site being attacked by the base's lone pair; the carbon framework itself is not what is directly attacked in this proton-transfer step.

q: What makes sulfonate esters (like tosylates, R-OTs) useful electrophiles in substitution reactions, much like alkyl halides?
e: Like halides, the oxygen in a sulfonate ester polarizes the attached carbon (making it electrophilic), and the resulting sulfonate anion is exceptionally stable (weak base) due to extensive resonance and charge delocalization, making it depart easily as a leaving group.

q: In general, increasing the number of electron-donating alkyl substituents directly on an electrophilic carbon tends to:
e: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (by induction/hyperconjugation) and also physically block approach, so more substitution at a potentially electrophilic carbon generally reduces how strongly and how accessibly electrophilic it is (this is part of why more substituted carbonyls are less reactive toward nucleophiles).

q: A tertiary carbocation forms more readily than a primary carbocation.
e: Alkyl groups donate electron density to an adjacent positive charge, so a tertiary cation sits lower in energy than a primary one and the ionization that produces it is easier. Every carbocation remains a strong electrophile once formed; this comparison is about how readily they appear, not how hungry they are.

q: Which best explains why methyl iodide (CH3I) is often used as a model electrophile in SN2 reactions despite iodine being a relatively weak inductive electron-wi
e: Even though the C–I bond is only modestly polarized, the weak, long C–I bond breaks easily and iodide is a very stable, weakly basic leaving group, so the overall reaction is fast even if carbon itself is not the most electron-poor among the halomethanes.

q: A good leaving group is generally one that is:
e: Good leaving groups are stable as the departed anion/molecule — i.e., weak bases, since weak bases are comfortable holding the extra electron density.

q: Which of these is typically the best leaving group?
e: Iodide is a large, very weak base — very stable once it leaves — making it an excellent leaving group, unlike OH⁻, NH₂⁻, or CH₃⁻ which are strong bases.

q: An alcohol does not react with NaBr, but the same alcohol with HBr gives the alkyl bromide. What does the acid change?
e: Nothing was wrong with the nucleophile: bromide is the same species in both flasks. The blocked step was the departure, because hydroxide (pKaH 15.7) will not leave a carbon. Protonation changes the departing species to neutral water (pKaH −1.7), and the reaction goes.

q: A good leaving group should be the conjugate base of a:
e: Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, which are exactly the conjugate bases of strong acids (like HI, HBr, or TsOH); weak bases hold their extra electron pair loosely and leave readily.

q: Which reagent turns R–OH into a substrate with an excellent leaving group without strong acid?
e: TsCl with pyridine converts the alcohol to a tosylate under mild, neutral conditions. Sulfuric acid also activates the OH, by protonation, but every acid-sensitive group in the molecule then has to survive it; the other two reagents do nothing useful here at all.

q: Rank Cl-, Br-, and I- in order of decreasing ability to act as a leaving group.
e: Leaving group ability tracks with anion stability (weak basicity); I- is the weakest base of the three halides and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group, followed by Br- then Cl-.

q: Why is F- generally a poor leaving group compared to the other halides even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen?
e: F- is a much stronger base than the other halide ions because its small size concentrates negative charge, making the C–F bond strong and fluoride reluctant to depart with the electron pair, unlike the larger, more stable, weaker-base halide ions.

q: A tosylate group (OTs-, the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid) is considered an excellent leaving group for the same general reason that halides are, nam
e: The negative charge on a sulfonate leaving group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance (and stabilized further by the electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group), making it a very weak base and thus an excellent, stable leaving group.

q: Amide ion (NH2-) is generally considered one of the worst common leaving groups in organic chemistry.
e: NH2- is the conjugate base of ammonia, an extremely weak acid, making amide ion an extremely strong base that holds on tightly to its electrons and essentially never leaves under normal conditions.

q: Why does protonating the oxygen of an alcohol (forming R-OH2+) convert a poor leaving group into a good one?
e: Once protonated, the group that leaves is neutral water rather than negatively charged hydroxide; water is a much weaker base (conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+) and leaves far more easily, which is why acid catalysis activates alcohols for substitution/elimination.

q: Which of the following is generally NOT a good leaving group under typical SN1/SN2 conditions?
e: A carbanion like CH3- is an extraordinarily strong base (conjugate base of methane, an exceedingly weak acid) and essentially never acts as a leaving group under normal conditions, unlike halides or neutral water.

q: Resonance stabilization of the departing anion (as in a sulfonate or carboxylate leaving group) generally makes that group a better leaving group.
e: Delocalizing the negative charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the anion, making it more stable (a weaker base) and thus more willing to depart, which is exactly why sulfonate esters are popular synthetic leaving groups.

q: In the reaction of an epoxide with a nucleophile under basic conditions, what effectively serves as the leaving group when the ring opens?
e: As a nucleophile attacks a ring carbon, the strained C–O bond breaks and the oxygen (now bearing the electron pair) becomes an alkoxide leaving group still attached elsewhere in the molecule, relieving ring strain.

q: Why is it generally true that weaker bases make better leaving groups?
e: Base strength measures how strongly a species wants to grab and hold a proton (or, analogously, electron density); weak bases are inherently stable on their own and 'happy' to leave with the bonding electron pair, which is the core reason leaving group ability and base strength are inversely related.

q: Which species would you predict to be a better leaving group: the conjugate base of acetic acid (CH3COO-, pKa of acid ≈ 4.8) or the conjugate base of ethanol (C
e: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), meaning acetate is a much weaker base than ethoxide and therefore a considerably better leaving group.

q: A carbocation can be thought of as having 'lost' a leaving group from the original substrate. Which best describes the leaving group's role right before departu
e: Because the leaving group departs with the bonding electrons, its ability to stabilize that extra electron density (i.e., be a weak, stable base) directly controls how readily ionization occurs and therefore the rate of SN1/E1 reactions.

q: Converting an alcohol's -OH into a mesylate (OMs) or tosylate (OTs) group before a substitution reaction is a common strategy because:
e: Sulfonate esters are prepared under mild, non-acidic conditions and then provide a highly stabilized, weak-base leaving group, giving chemists a practical alternative to strongly acidic activation of alcohols.

q: A proposed mechanism has a nucleophile attacking a carbon while hydroxide is pushed off that same carbon. What is wrong with it?
e: Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKaH 15.7, so it is a strong base and does not depart from carbon on its own. The missing piece is an activation step — protonate the OH, tosylate it, or convert it to a halide — and only then can something leave.

q: Which leaving group would most likely make an SN2 reaction proceed fastest, all else being equal: Cl-, Br-, or a tosylate (OTs-)?
e: Tosylate's negative charge is spread over three oxygens and stabilized further by the adjacent aromatic sulfonyl group, making it one of the best common leaving groups, generally outperforming simple halides.

q: An amine (R–NH₂) is a poor leaving group, but it can depart once its nitrogen carries a positive charge, as in R–NH₃⁺ or R–NR₃⁺, because what leaves is then a n
e: The amide anion ⁻NH₂ is far too strong a base to leave a carbon. Put a positive charge on the nitrogen first, by protonation or by alkylation to a quaternary ammonium, and the departing species is a neutral amine rather than an anion, which is a much cheaper thing to become.

q: Why does pKa of the leaving group's conjugate acid serve as a useful predictor of leaving group ability?
e: Since leaving groups are conjugate bases, the pKa of their conjugate acid directly reflects base strength: a low pKa (strong acid) means a weak, stable conjugate base, and therefore a good leaving group.

q: Which of these would you predict to be the best leaving group based on its conjugate acid's strength: leaving group X whose conjugate acid has pKa 9, or leaving
e: A conjugate acid pKa of -7 corresponds to an extremely strong acid (such as HI), meaning its conjugate base is extremely weak and stable — exactly the profile of an excellent leaving group, far better than one with a conjugate acid pKa of 9.

q: Cyanide ion (CN-) is generally a poor leaving group.
e: HCN is only a moderately weak acid (pKa around 9), making cyanide a fairly strong base relative to halides or sulfonates, so it does not readily depart as a leaving group under typical substitution conditions.

q: In a Grignard or organolithium reagent, the carbon bonded to the metal behaves as a strong nucleophile/base. If this carbon were instead asked to act as a leavi
e: Because strong bases/nucleophiles and good leaving groups are generally opposite ends of the same stability spectrum, a reactive carbanion (strong base) is a very poor leaving group — it simply does not want to depart and take the electron pair in an already-stable low-energy form elsewhere.

q: Which best explains why water (H2O) can act as a leaving group in acid-catalyzed reactions but hydroxide (OH-) generally cannot under the same mild acidic condi
e: Protonation shifts the leaving species from hydroxide (conjugate base of water, pKa ≈ 15.7, a fairly strong base) to water itself (conjugate base of H3O+, pKa ≈ -1.7, a very weak base), dramatically improving its willingness to leave.

q: Which reagent would you supply to convert an alcohol directly into an alkyl bromide in one step?
e: Bromide on its own cannot displace hydroxide, and deprotonating the alcohol makes the leaving group worse rather than better. PBr₃ converts the OH into a good leaving group and delivers bromide in the same operation, which is why it is the standard one-step route.

q: Phosphate groups (such as those in ATP) are biologically important leaving groups. Why are they effective leaving groups despite carrying a full negative charge
e: Like sulfonates and carboxylates, phosphate leaving groups spread their negative charge over several oxygen atoms via resonance, lowering their basicity and making them effective leaving groups despite the formal negative charge, which is central to many biochemical substitution reactions.

q: Which of the following best ranks typical leaving group ability from best to worst: I-, OH-, OTs-?
e: Hydroxide is a strong base and a poor leaving group, so it is clearly last. Tosylate and iodide are both conjugate bases of very strong acids and belong to the same top tier; measured substitution rates put tosylate marginally ahead of iodide, which is the order keyed here. Getting the tiers right matters more than the order inside one.

q: A trifluoromethanesulfonate group (triflate, OTf-) is considered one of the best leaving groups known, even better than tosylate, largely because of the strongl
e: The three highly electronegative fluorine atoms further withdraw electron density and help delocalize/stabilize the negative charge on the departing sulfonate oxygen, making triflate an exceptionally weak base and outstanding leaving group, even better than a simple tosylate.

q: If a leaving group is a poor one (a strong base) in a proposed SN1 mechanism, what is the most likely consequence for the reaction?
e: Since SN1 rate depends on how readily the substrate ionizes, a poor leaving group (strong base, high-energy anion) makes that ionization step slow or unfavorable, often requiring the substrate to be activated first (e.g., protonation or conversion to a sulfonate) before substitution can proceed.

q: An electron-rich atom in a mechanism tends to act as a(n):
e: Electron-rich atoms have extra electron density to donate, making them nucleophilic.

q: Why is the carbon of C=O electron-poor while the oxygen is electron-rich?
e: The electronegativity difference polarizes the pi bond, making O δ− (electron-rich) and C δ+ (electron-poor).

q: In a C–Mg bond (as in a Grignard reagent), which atom is electron-rich?
e: Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making it electron-rich (and strongly nucleophilic/basic).

q: An electron-poor atom in a mechanism generally acts as a(n):
e: Electron-poor atoms lack sufficient electron density and therefore seek it out from an electron-rich partner, which is exactly the defining behavior of an electrophile.

q: A carbon bonded directly to a highly electronegative atom like oxygen, nitrogen, or a halogen is generally electron-poor relative to a carbon bonded only to oth
e: Electronegative substituents pull electron density away from the attached carbon through the polar sigma bond (an inductive effect), leaving that carbon partially positive (δ+) relative to one surrounded only by similarly electronegative C and H.

q: In CH₃–CH₂–O–CH₂–CH₂–Cl, which carbon does a nucleophile attack?
e: Oxygen (3.44) is more electronegative than chlorine (3.16), so the carbons flanking the ether oxygen are polarized at least as strongly as the Cl-bearing one. What decides it is the second condition: only the chlorine-bearing carbon holds a group that will actually depart. Electron-poor makes a carbon a candidate; a leaving group makes it the answer.

q: In an enolate, the negative charge is delocalized between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen. Which site is more electron-rich in the major resonance cont
e: The resonance structure placing the negative charge on oxygen is the larger contributor to the hybrid, since oxygen is far better suited to stabilize a negative charge than carbon is — making the oxygen the more electron-rich site overall.

q: An aromatic ring substituted with an electron-donating group, such as an amine or alkoxy group, becomes more electron-rich overall, making it more reactive towa
e: Electron-donating substituents push additional electron density into the aromatic ring (by resonance and/or induction), increasing the ring's overall nucleophilicity and accelerating electrophilic aromatic substitution.

q: Which atom in a hydrogen halide (H–X, such as H–Cl) is electron-poor and thus reacts as the acidic proton source?
e: The halogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling bonding electron density toward itself and leaving hydrogen partially positive (δ+), which is why H–X compounds act as proton (acid) sources.

q: A nitro group (-NO2) attached to an aromatic ring makes the ring more electron-rich due to strong electron donation by resonance.
e: The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance, since nitrogen is positively charged with electronegative oxygens), making an attached ring more electron-poor, not electron-rich.

q: Why does an alkene substituted with several alkyl groups (a more substituted alkene) tend to be more electron-rich and thus a better nucleophile than a less sub
e: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (through hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C bonds and simple induction), so each additional alkyl substituent on a double bond increases the electron density of the pi bond, making the alkene a better nucleophile.

q: Comparing a C–F bond to a C–I bond, which carbon is more electron-poor (more δ+)?
e: Fluorine's very high electronegativity creates a strongly polarized C–F bond, pulling substantial electron density away from carbon, more so than the much less electronegative iodine does in a C–I bond, even though the C–I bond is actually weaker and breaks more easily.

q: A carbanion is an example of an electron-rich carbon species, while a carbocation is an example of an electron-poor carbon species.
e: A carbanion carries a full negative charge and a lone pair (electron-rich, nucleophilic), while a carbocation has an empty orbital and a full positive charge (electron-poor, electrophilic) — they sit at opposite ends of the electron-density spectrum.

q: In an enol (the tautomer of a ketone with a C=C–OH arrangement), which carbon is electron-rich and acts as the nucleophilic site?
e: A resonance structure of the enol places a lone pair from oxygen into the pi system, shifting electron density to the terminal (alpha) carbon and giving it significant nucleophilic, electron-rich character, which is why enols react with electrophiles at that carbon.

q: Why is the nitrogen of an amide less electron-rich (less basic/nucleophilic) than the nitrogen of a simple amine?
e: Conjugation of the nitrogen lone pair with the carbonyl pi system pulls electron density away from nitrogen toward the electronegative oxygen, leaving the amide nitrogen considerably less electron-rich than an isolated amine nitrogen.

q: Which of these atoms, all found within a molecule of acetonitrile (CH3-C≡N), is the most electron-rich and would be expected to act as a nucleophile/base site?
e: The nitrogen of a nitrile carries a lone pair in an sp orbital and, despite nitrogen's electronegativity pulling some density toward it within the triple bond, this lone pair is the most electron-rich, available site for interacting with electrophiles or protons.

q: An amino group on a benzene ring makes the ring more reactive toward electrophiles, though nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon. Which effect explains i
e: The two effects point opposite ways in this molecule. Induction pulls density out of the ring, because nitrogen is the more electronegative atom, while resonance pushes a whole lone pair in. A relocated pair beats a tilted one, so resonance wins and the ring ends up electron-rich.

q: Between the carbon and the boron atom in a carbon-boron bond (as found in certain organoborane reagents), which atom is electron-rich?
e: Boron's electronegativity is lower than carbon's, so the shared electrons in a C–B bond sit closer to carbon, making that carbon somewhat electron-rich, similar to the polarization seen in Grignard C–Mg bonds though less pronounced.

q: Inductive electron withdrawal through sigma bonds (as from a nearby halogen) typically has its strongest effect on the immediately adjacent atom and weakens rap
e: Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off quickly with distance, so a halogen's electron-withdrawing influence is strongest on the carbon it's directly attached to and becomes much weaker two or three carbons away.

q: Why does protonation of a carbonyl oxygen (under acid catalysis) make the attached carbonyl carbon even more electron-poor than it already was?
e: Adding a full positive charge directly onto the already electronegative oxygen dramatically increases its pull on the shared electrons, making the attached carbon even more electron-deficient and far more reactive to nucleophilic attack.

q: Which species is more electron-rich at its reactive carbon: a simple alkene (C=C) or an enolate ion (C=C–O-)?
e: The negatively charged oxygen of an enolate strongly donates its extra electron density through resonance into the adjacent carbon, making the enolate's nucleophilic carbon considerably more electron-rich (and thus more reactive) than a simple, unactivated alkene carbon.

q: A sulfur atom in a thiol (R-SH) is generally considered more electron-rich and nucleophilic than the oxygen in a comparable alcohol (R-OH), even though oxygen i
e: Although oxygen holds its own electrons more tightly (higher electronegativity, stronger base), sulfur's larger, more polarizable, more loosely held electron cloud makes it more willing to donate electron density in bond-forming reactions, so it behaves as more nucleophilic/electron-rich in a reactivity sense.

q: In the molecule CH3-CH2-Cl, which carbon carries the greater partial positive charge (is more electron-poor)?
e: The carbon directly bonded to the electronegative chlorine experiences the strongest inductive pull of electron density, making it the most electron-poor carbon in the molecule; the effect diminishes sharply at the next carbon over.

q: Why is the oxygen of a carboxylic acid's hydroxyl group (the O–H oxygen, not the carbonyl oxygen) considered relatively electron-poor compared to the oxygen of
e: One of the hydroxyl oxygen's lone pairs conjugates with the carbonyl pi system, pulling electron density toward the carbonyl oxygen; this depletion of electron density on the OH oxygen is part of why the O–H bond is more acidic (and the oxygen less basic) than in a simple alcohol.

q: A carbon at the end of a polarized C≡N (nitrile) triple bond is generally electron-poor and can act as an electrophile toward strong nucleophiles like Grignard
e: Nitrogen's higher electronegativity polarizes the triple bond, leaving the nitrile carbon partially positive and electrophilic, which is why Grignard and organolithium reagents can add to nitriles to eventually form ketones after hydrolysis.

q: Which best explains why the alpha carbon of an alkyl halide (directly bonded to the halogen) is electron-poor, yet the beta carbon (one carbon further away) sho
e: Inductive (sigma-bond) electron withdrawal falls off rapidly with each bond, so while the alpha carbon feels the halogen's pull strongly, the beta carbon experiences only a faint residual effect.

q: Why can an enamine's beta carbon (the carbon two atoms from nitrogen, across the double bond) be considered especially electron-rich and strongly nucleophilic?
e: Just as an enolate's oxygen lone pair activates the alpha carbon through resonance, an enamine's nitrogen lone pair conjugates through the C=C pi system to make the beta carbon unusually electron-rich and nucleophilic, a key feature exploited in many carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

q: Both inductive and resonance (conjugative) effects can make a given atom more electron-poor or more electron-rich, and in some molecules these two effects can a
e: A classic example is a halogen substituent on an aromatic ring: it withdraws electron density inductively (making the ring somewhat electron-poor overall) while donating electron density by resonance at the ortho/para positions (making those specific positions more electron-rich), so the two effects can genuinely pull in opposite directions.

q: Which contributor of CH₂=CH–CHO puts a positive charge on the beta carbon, and what does it predict?
e: Push the C=C electrons into the central C–C bond and the carbonyl pi electrons onto oxygen, and the result carries a minus on oxygen and a plus on the far, beta carbon. That contributor is a genuine part of the hybrid, which is why nucleophiles add at the beta position — conjugate addition.

q: A bromonium ion intermediate (formed when Br2 adds to an alkene) carries its formal positive charge on bromine, so it is bromine itself, not either ring carbon,
e: Although bromine formally bears the positive charge in the strained three-membered bromonium ring, the nucleophile actually attacks one of the electrophilic ring carbons from the backside, displacing bromine and opening the ring; formal charge location does not always mark the exact site of nucleophilic attack.

q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Count the row: six carbons, and the methyl is a one-carbon branch that cannot extend any path, so the parent is hexane. From the left the methyl is on C3, from the right on C4; 3 beats 4. 3-methylhexane.

q: A student names CH₃CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ as 2-ethylbutane. What is the correct name?
e: Trace from the far end of the ethyl through the branch carbon and along the row: two ethyl carbons, the branch carbon, then two more is five. The row was only four. So the parent is pentane, and the carbon left over (the near end of the row) is a methyl on C3. An ethyl on C2 can never be right, because the route through it always beats the row by one.

q: Which of these names cannot be correct as written?
e: An ethyl on the second carbon of a chain always extends it: two ethyl carbons plus C2 plus the rest of the chain is one longer than the chain itself. 2-ethylbutane is really 3-methylpentane. The other three describe a molecule where the row is genuinely the longest path.

q: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. How many carbons are in the parent chain?
e: Three arms leave the branch carbon: three carbons to the left, three in the propyl, two to the right. A chain joins the two longest arms through that carbon: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane. Counting every carbon in the molecule (nine) as one chain would need the path to pass through the branch carbon twice.

q: How is the parent chain defined?
e: The longest unbroken path of carbons, turning as many corners as it needs to. It is very often not the row lying across the page, which is why every end has to be checked.

q: Two seven-carbon paths run through a molecule. One carries a single ethyl group, the other carries two methyls. Which is the parent?
e: A tie on length is broken by the number of substituents, and the chain with more wins. It reads backwards, but a name should put as much of the molecule as possible into numbered prefixes instead of hiding it inside a big branch name.

q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. Which name is right?
e: Two five-carbon chains tie. The one along the row carries a methyl and an ethyl (two substituents); the one through the ethyl carries a single isopropyl. More substituents wins, so the parent is the row with methyl at C2 and ethyl at C3. Then the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl.

q: From one end a chain’s substituents fall at {2, 2, 5}; from the other at {2, 5, 5}. Which numbering is right?
e: Compare term by term and stop at the first difference. Both open with 2; then 2 beats 5. That settles it without looking at the third term.

q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Seven carbons in the row and nothing longer through a methyl. From the left the methyls are at {2, 5}; from the right at {3, 6}. 2 beats 3 at the first term. Two methyls take di- and two locants: 2,5-dimethylheptane.

q: A chain of six carbons is drawn with how many bonds between them?
e: Always one fewer bond than carbons. Counting the line segments and calling a hexane a pentane is the standard off-by-one, and it is the same miscount as forgetting the ends of a skeletal structure.

q: A student writes 1-methylpentane. What is wrong with it?
e: A methyl on the end carbon is one more carbon in a straight line, so the chain is six long, not five. A name with a 1-alkyl locant on an unbranched chain is a sign the parent was chosen wrongly.

q: Which condensed formula is 2,3-dimethylpentane?
e: Pentane is five in a row; put methyls on the second and third. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,4-dimethylpentane, CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,2-dimethylpentane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ has six carbons in the row (2,3-dimethylhexane).

q: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: The longest path runs through one of the two end methyls: six carbons, hexane. The other methyl is the branch, on C2 counting from that end (C5 from the other). Isopropylbutane buries two chain carbons in the branch name.

q: Which condensed formula is 4-ethylheptane?
e: Seven in a row with a two-carbon branch on the fourth. CH₃CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is a hexane (3-ethylhexane), CH₃CH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ has two methyls on one carbon, and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-methylheptane.

q: CH₃CH₂C(CH₂CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃. A student rejects the name 3,3-diethylpentane, saying the longest chain must run through an ethyl. Who is right?
e: Four two-carbon arms leave the central carbon, so every route through it is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. All the candidate chains tie at five with the same two substituents, and the name is 3,3-diethylpentane. The longest-chain rule only changes an answer when an arm is longer than the ones it competes with.

q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Eight in the row. From the left the methyls are at {3, 5}, from the right at {4, 6}; 3 beats 4. The ethyl name has the wrong parent, since an ethyl on C2 would extend the chain.

q: A structure is drawn as a five-carbon row with an ethyl on the middle carbon. What is the parent?
e: Three ends: the two row ends and the ethyl end. Row end to row end is five. Ethyl end to either row end is two, plus the middle carbon, plus two: also five. Nothing is longer than the row, so it stays the parent.

q: That same structure, a five-carbon row with an ethyl on the middle carbon, is correctly named what?
e: Pentane parent, two-carbon branch on C3 from either end. The ethyl survives as an ethyl because every route through it ties the row instead of beating it.

q: A molecule is drawn as a Y: three arms of 3, 3 and 2 carbons leave one central carbon. What is the parent?
e: A chain is a path and cannot pass through the same carbon twice, so only two arms can be joined: the two three-carbon arms plus the center is seven. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane.

q: Why is choosing the parent chain the highest-stakes step in a name?
e: Pick the wrong parent and the numbering, the locants and the substituent names that follow are all wrong too. It is the step where a name goes wrong earliest and most completely.

q: Which name shows the modern IUPAC placement of the locant?
e: Current IUPAC puts a locant immediately before the part of the name it refers to. Older texts write 2-butene, so read both; write the first.

q: A molecule has two eight-carbon paths and nothing longer. What decides between them?
e: When chains tie on length, the one carrying more substituents is the parent. If that ties too, the numbering rule decides: the chain whose substituents get the lower locants.

q: A decane’s substituents fall at {2, 7, 8} from one end and {3, 4, 9} from the other. Which numbering is right?
e: First point of difference: 2 against 3, decided at once. The totals (17 against 16) point the other way, which is exactly why adding locants up is not the rule.

q: A molecule is drawn as a horizontal five-carbon row with a three-carbon branch on the second carbon. What is the parent?
e: From the branch carbon: one carbon to the left, three in the branch, three to the right. Join the two longest arms through it: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The leftover carbon is a methyl: 4-methylheptane.

q: Which condensed formula is 2,2-dimethylbutane?
e: Four in a row with two methyls on the second carbon, which gives a carbon bearing three methyls at one end. The first is 2-methylpentane, the third 2,2-dimethylpentane, the last 2,3-dimethylbutane.

q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. A student writes 3,4-dimethylhexane. Is that right?
e: Six in the row, methyls on the middle two carbons. From either end the set is {3, 4}: the molecule is symmetric, so there is no direction to choose and the name is simply 3,4-dimethylhexane.

q: Which of these is the same compound as 3-methylhexane, under a wrong name?
e: Number the same chain from the other end and the methyl lands on C4. Same structure, wrong direction. The other three are genuinely different molecules.

q: Which of these is a correctly punctuated name?
e: Comma between the two numbers, hyphen between the numbers and the word, and no space anywhere inside the name of a single compound.

q: Two candidate parents are the same length and carry the same number of substituents. What decides?
e: After length and substituent count, the numbering rule is the next tie-break: take the chain whose substituents get the lower set of locants at the first point of difference.

q: Which condensed formula is 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane?
e: Hexane row, methyl on C2, ethyl on C3. Check the parent: from C3 the arms are 2 (left), 2 (ethyl) and 3 (right), so the six-carbon row is the longest and the ethyl is a real branch. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylhexane.

q: A branch –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ hangs off a parent chain. Which group is it?
e: Attached through a CH₂, then a CH carrying two methyls: a three-carbon chain attached at its end with a methyl on its second carbon. That is isobutyl. sec-Butyl attaches through the branch point itself.

q: Which group attaches through its middle carbon?
e: Isopropyl, systematically propan-2-yl, attaches at C2 of a three-carbon fragment. Propyl and butyl attach at an end; isobutyl attaches at the end of a branched three-chain.

q: What is the systematic name of the tert-butyl group, (CH₃)₃C–?
e: The attached carbon carries three methyls: a propane chain attached through its middle carbon with a methyl on that same carbon, so propan-2-yl with a 2-methyl. Almost nobody says it aloud, but you should be able to decode it.

q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)– attached to the parent through the CH. What is its common name?
e: Four carbons, attached through the second one: butan-2-yl, called sec-butyl. Isobutyl attaches through a CH₂; tert-butyl through a carbon bearing three methyls.

q: How is a halogen named in a systematic name?
e: fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo. A halogen is a prefix wherever it sits and is not a suffix, but it ranks equally with alkyl groups for numbering, so a chloro can claim the low locant over a methyl on first-point-of-difference terms.

q: CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: An ether has no suffix; it is an alkoxy prefix on the longer chain. Propane is the parent, and the –OCH₃ is methoxy on C1, numbered from the end nearer it.

q: CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Two methyls on C2 of a pentane. Each substituent keeps its own locant even when they share a carbon: di- promises two numbers, and the repeated 2 is the only thing saying where the second methyl is.

q: CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. Which name is right?
e: Six in the longest row; from either end the branch carbon is C3 or C4, and 3 wins. Both substituents sit on C3, and the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl. The numbers being equal does not change the word order.

q: CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: From the left: chloro 2, methyl 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: methyl 3, chloro 5, so {3, 5}. 2 beats 3, and the halogen and the alkyl are equals in that comparison. Then chloro before methyl alphabetically.

q: A hexane carries an ethyl on C4 and two methyls on C2. Which is the correct name?
e: Ignore di- when alphabetizing: you are comparing ethyl with methyl, and e comes before m, so ethyl is cited first despite its higher locant. di- needs two locants, which rules out “4-ethyl-2-dimethylhexane”, and a name cannot run two prefixes together without locants, which rules out “2,2,4-dimethylethylhexane”.

q: Under which letter does tert-butyl file when substituents are alphabetized?
e: The italic, hyphenated tert- is ignored, so the name files under b. The typography is the tell: hyphenated italic prefixes are skipped, prefixes joined to the word are counted.

q: A parent carries a tert-butyl, an isopropyl and two methyls. In what order are they written?
e: File each name: tert-butyl under b (tert- ignored), isopropyl under i (iso counts), dimethyl under m (di- ignored). b, i, m.

q: sec-Butyl and ethyl are both substituents on one parent. Which is cited first?
e: sec- is an italic hyphenated prefix and is ignored, so sec-butyl files under b, ahead of ethyl under e. Locants play no part in the order of the words.

q: A hexane has methyls on C2 and C4 and an ethyl on C3, numbering already fixed. Write the name.
e: Collect the two methyls as 2,4-dimethyl, then alphabetize with di- ignored: ethyl before methyl. Identical substituents are always gathered under one multiplying prefix.

q: Which structure is tert-butyl chloride?
e: Common halide names are alkyl group plus halide: the chlorine sits on a carbon bearing three methyls. Systematically, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. The others are isobutyl, sec-butyl and butyl chloride.

q: An octane carries an ethyl on C3 and a methyl on C6 counting from the left; from the right the methyl is on C3 and the ethyl on C6. What is the name?
e: Both directions give {3, 6}: a genuine tie, and the one situation where the alphabet touches the numbering. The substituent cited first (ethyl) takes the lower locant. 6-ethyl-3-methyloctane numbers the wrong way.

q: In what order do the rules apply when naming a substituted alkane?
e: First number for lowest locants; then, only on an exact tie, give the alphabetically first substituent the lower number; last, write the substituents in alphabetical order whatever their numbers.

q: Locants are fixed as bromo-4, methyl-2, propyl-5 on an octane. How is the name written?
e: Alphabetical order sets the order of the words: bromo, methyl, propyl. The numbers travel with their substituents, so they end up out of numerical order, which is normal.

q: A branch is itself branched. How is its name written?
