e: Parentheses tell the reader that the number inside counts along the branch, from its attaching carbon, and not along the parent chain.

q: A complex substituent is numbered from where?
e: The attaching carbon is C1 of the substituent, always. So –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ is (2-methylpropyl), with the methyl on the branch’s own C2.

q: A branch –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ on a parent chain is named, in parentheses, as:
e: Numbered from the attachment point, the CH₂ is C1 and the CH bearing the methyl is C2; the branch is three carbons long. This group is also called isobutyl.

q: The same group is called (2-methylpropyl) or isobutyl. Under which letter does each name file?
e: A complex substituent files under the first letter of its complete name, m. The common name files under i, because iso is joined to the word. Which name you use can change where the group sits in a longer name.

q: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br is commonly called what?
e: Alkyl group plus halide: the bromine is on the end carbon of a three-chain, so propyl bromide (1-bromopropane). Isopropyl bromide would put it on the middle carbon.

q: Which condensed formula is 4-isopropylheptane?
e: Heptane row, with a three-carbon group attached through its middle carbon on C4. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-propylheptane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH(CH₃)₂)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ puts the branch on C3, and (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2-methyloctane.

q: sec-Butyl attaches through which carbon?
e: sec-Butyl is butan-2-yl. C1 of a four-chain is butyl; C2 of a three-chain is isopropyl; a carbon bearing three methyls is tert-butyl.

q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃. What is the name?
e: Five in the longest row, methyls on C2, C3 and C4 from either end. Three identical substituents take tri- and three locants; they are never split between two prefixes. A methyl on C1 would extend the chain.

q: BrCH₂CH₂CH₂Cl. What is the name?
e: From either end the locant set is {1, 3}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes the lower number. Bromo before chloro, so the bromine gets 1. The words are then written in that same order.

q: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Seven in the longest chain (the route through the ethyl also gives seven, with the same two substituents). From the left: methyl 3, ethyl 5. From the right: ethyl 3, methyl 5. Both {3, 5}, so ethyl, cited first, takes the 3.

q: Which statement about alphabetizing substituents is correct?
e: Ignore di-, tri-, tetra- and the italic sec-, tert-. Do not ignore iso, neo or cyclo, which are joined to the word and count as part of it.

q: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂Cl: systematic name, and common name?
e: Propane parent with a methyl on C2 and a chlorine on C1, cited alphabetically: chloro before methyl. The group carrying the chlorine is –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, isobutyl, so the common name is isobutyl chloride.

q: CH₃COCH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
e: Ketone outranks alcohol, so the suffix is -one and the OH is demoted to hydroxy-. The ketone claims the lower locant: C2 from its end, which puts the OH on C4.

q: Which of these groups has the highest priority?
e: acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne. The acid and its derivatives are the top block.

q: ClCH₂CH₂CO₂H. What is the name?
e: The acid carbon is C1 by necessity and needs no locant; count from it and the chlorine sits on C3. Halogens are prefixes in every name.

q: An –OH is outranked by a ketone in the same molecule. What prefix does it take?
e: A demoted alcohol becomes hydroxy-. Nothing about the oxygen changed; its rank did. oxo- is a demoted ketone, carboxy- a demoted acid.

q: A ketone is outranked by a carboxylic acid. What prefix does it take?
e: The IUPAC prefix is oxo-, not keto-. A compound chemists call a keto acid has no mention of a ketone in its systematic name.

q: HOCH₂CH₂CHO. What is the name?
e: Aldehyde outranks alcohol: suffix -al, C1 is the CHO and no locant is written for it. The OH is hydroxy- on C3.

q: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CO₂H. What is the name?
e: The acid wins the suffix and is C1. Counting from it, the OH is on C3. The acid needs no locant; writing -1-oic is redundant.

q: NCCH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
e: Nitrile outranks alcohol, so -nitrile is the suffix and the nitrile carbon is C1 (four carbons in the parent, including it). The OH is hydroxy- on C4. Nitrile begins with a consonant, so the e of butane stays.

q: H₂NCH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
e: Alcohol outranks amine: suffix -ol, OH on C1. The NH₂ is demoted to amino- on C3.

q: Aldehyde outranks ketone in the priority order. What is the basis of that ranking?
e: An aldehyde carbon and a ketone carbon are at the same oxidation level, two bonds to oxygen each; the aldehyde’s extra C–H is why it can be oxidized further, but it does not make it a higher level. The order within that pair, like the order within the acid-derivative block, is convention.

q: How do the functional carbons of an acid, an ester, an amide and a nitrile compare in oxidation level?
e: Each has three bonds from carbon to oxygen or nitrogen (the nitrile’s are all to one nitrogen), so all four sit at the same level. The order within the block is a convention that happens to run with their reactivity.

q: Once a principal characteristic group is present, which feature gets the lowest locant first?
e: The principal group claims the low number before multiple bonds or substituents are considered at all. The old lowest-locants-to-substituents rule was only ever for molecules with nothing to outrank them.

q: A heptane has an OH reachable at C3 from one end and a methyl at C2 from the other. What is the name?
e: The alcohol takes the lower locant first: number from its end, OH at C3. The methyl is then C6, whatever it would have been the other way. Giving the methyl the 2 out of habit is the commonest error here.

q: The longest chain in a molecule does not contain the –OH. What is the parent?
e: Priority beats length. The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, so you take the longest chain that does, even when a longer one exists.

q: Why does a carboxylic acid need no locant?
e: The functional carbon is necessarily at the end of a chain, so it is C1 by construction. Butan-1-al is redundant for the same reason.

q: Propane plus the -ol suffix is spelled how?
e: When the suffix begins with a vowel the parent’s final e is dropped. Before a consonant it stays: propanenitrile.

q: HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH. What is the name?
e: Two alcohols take -diol with two locants, and because di- begins with a consonant the e of butane is kept. Both OH groups are principal, so neither is demoted to hydroxy-.

q: OHC–CH₂–CO–CH₃. What is the name?
e: Aldehyde outranks ketone: suffix -al, the CHO is C1. The ketone is demoted to oxo- on C3. keto- is not an IUPAC prefix.

q: What is the systematic name for acetone?
e: Three carbons with the C=O on the middle one. Acetone is a retained name and cannot be read back into a structure; propan-2-one can.

q: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. What is the name?
e: Find the C=O and count its chain: three carbons, so the acid part is propanoate. The carbon on the single-bonded oxygen is the alcohol part: methyl. Two words, alcohol part first.

q: In ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, which fragment is the "ethyl"?
e: The first word of an ester name is the alcohol’s carbon chain, attached through the single-bonded oxygen. The second word is the acid’s chain, counted from the C=O. Here both happen to be two carbons, which is why the example is worth checking.

q: A cyclohexane ring has a C=O as one ring carbon and a methyl two carbons away from it. What is the name?
e: The ketone takes the suffix and C1; the ring is the parent. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries a –COOH. What is the name?
e: The acid carbon cannot be part of the ring, so it is not counted in the parent: the ring is cyclohexane and the group is the suffix -carboxylic acid. The e is kept because the suffix begins with a consonant.

q: What does "principal characteristic group" mean?
e: It is chosen by the fixed priority order, not by size, position or interest, and it is the one group named as the suffix.

q: Where do double and triple bonds sit in the priority order?
e: Alkenes and alkynes rank below every group in the list, so a functional group always claims the lower locant over a multiple bond.

q: CH₃OCH₂CH₂NH₂. What is the name?
e: An ether can never be a suffix, so the amine wins by default: -amine on C1 of a two-carbon parent, and methoxy- on C2.

q: CH₂=CHCH₂OH. What is the name?
e: The alcohol outranks the double bond and takes C1. The double bond then starts at C2. Both suffixes appear, the multiple bond first and with its e dropped before -ol.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries a –CHO. What is the name?
e: Like the acid, the aldehyde carbon hangs off the ring and cannot be part of it, so the ring is the parent and the group becomes -carbaldehyde. Formyl- is the prefix for a demoted aldehyde, and nothing outranks it here.

q: Why is the naming priority order worth knowing beyond naming?
e: The top of the list is close to the reactivity ladder of the Carboxylic Acids chapter: an acid or acyl chloride converts to an ester, an ester to an amide. Going back up is not a direct step; an ester or amide is hydrolyzed to the acid first.

q: CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Five carbons, double bond between C2 and C3 counting from the nearer end. Only the lower of the two carbons is cited; the reader infers the bond runs to the next one.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries one ethyl group. What is the name?
e: The ring has six carbons to the chain’s two, so the ring is the parent. With only one substituent there is nowhere else it could be, and no locant is written.

q: How does numbering a ring differ from numbering a chain?
e: You choose both the starting carbon and the direction, subject to the same priority rules as a chain: principal group at C1, then lowest locants.

q: A three-carbon chain is attached to a cyclohexane ring. Which name is right?
e: Six ring carbons beat three chain carbons, so the ring is the parent and the chain is a propyl substituent. One substituent needs no locant.

q: A cyclohexane ring is attached to the end of an eight-carbon chain, with no functional groups. What is the parent?
e: With no higher-priority group present, the parent is whichever has more carbons. Eight beats six, so the ring becomes a cyclohexyl substituent: 1-cyclohexyloctane.

q: A cyclopentane ring is attached to a five-carbon chain, with no functional groups. What is the parent?
e: Five against five is a tie, and on a tie the ring is the parent: pentylcyclopentane. Current IUPAC recommendations go further and prefer the ring whatever the chain length, but exams count carbons.

q: A benzene ring bonded to the parent directly through one of its ring carbons is called what?
e: Phenyl is C₆H₅–, the ring itself. Benzyl is the ring plus a CH₂, attached through the CH₂; confusing the two changes the molecule by a carbon.

q: C₆H₅CH₂– as a substituent is called what?
e: A benzene ring attached through an extra CH₂ is benzyl. Phenyl is the bare ring, and benzoyl is C₆H₅CO–.

q: CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: A triple bond takes -yne and one locant, the lower of the two carbons: from the nearer end the bond runs from C2. Nothing else about the procedure changes.

q: CH₂=CHCH₂C≡CH. What is the name?
e: From the left the double bond is at 1 and the triple at 4; from the right it is the other way round. The locant sets tie, so the double bond takes the lower number. The suffix order is fixed, en before yne, and the e of ene is dropped before the y.

q: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the name?
e: Five carbons, double bond starting at C1 from the nearer end. The locant is needed because pent-2-ene is a different compound, and only the first of the two carbons is cited.

q: Which carbon number is cited for a double bond?
e: By convention the locant is the lower-numbered of the two carbons the bond joins; the reader infers that the bond runs to the next carbon along.

q: CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₃. What is the name?
e: Two double bonds take -diene with two locants, one per bond, from the end that gives the lower set: {1, 3} beats {2, 4}. The a in penta- is kept before the consonant d.

q: A six-carbon chain has an OH at C1 and a double bond starting at C5. What is the name?
e: The alcohol outranks the double bond and claims the lower locant, even though that gives the double bond a 5 rather than a 1. The e of ene is dropped before the vowel of -ol.

q: CH₃CH=CH–C≡CH. What is the name?
e: From the left: ene at 2, yne at 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: yne at 1, ene at 3, so {1, 3}. The lower set wins regardless of which bond it favors, so the triple bond gets the 1 here; the double bond only gets preference on an exact tie.

q: A name contains both a double bond and an alcohol. Which suffix is written first?
e: Both appear, the multiple bond first and the principal group last: hex-5-en-1-ol. The order of suffixes is fixed whatever the locants.

q: 1,2-dimethylbenzene is also called what?
e: Xylene is the retained name for dimethylbenzene, and adjacent methyls are ortho: o-xylene. Toluene is methylbenzene.

q: A benzene ring carries chlorines at positions 1 and 3. What is the name?
e: One ring carbon between the two substituents is the 1,3 relationship, meta. The numbers and the word say the same thing, and both are in constant use.

q: Two substituents at positions 1 and 4 of a benzene ring are described by which prefix?
e: Straight across a six-membered ring is three bonds away, the 1,4 relationship: para. Adjacent is ortho (1,2) and one apart is meta (1,3).

q: CH₂=C(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃. A student uses the longest chain and writes 3-methylidenehexane. What does the textbook rule say?
e: The six-carbon chain misses the double bond, so it is not the parent; the longest chain through the C=C is five, starting at the CH₂. The double bond takes C1 and the two carbons left over are an ethyl on C2. The 2013 IUPAC rules relaxed this, but textbooks and exams still apply it.

q: Why can the name but-2-ene describe two different compounds?
e: The two alkene carbons cannot rotate, so the methyls are fixed either on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans). The name needs a prefix to say which.

q: (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. What is the name?
e: The longest chain through the double bond is four carbons, with a methyl on one of the alkene carbons. The double bond is at 2 from either end, a tie; the methyl then takes the lower number, 2 rather than 3.

q: A double bond in a ring is numbered so that its two carbons are which?
e: The double bond takes the lowest possible pair of locants before substituents are considered; only the direction round the ring is left for them to decide.

q: A cyclohexene ring has an OH on the carbon next to one of the alkene carbons. What is the name?
e: The alcohol is the principal group and takes C1. Numbering then goes round the way that reaches the double bond soonest, so it starts at C2. The e of ene is dropped before -ol.

q: Which condensed formula is 3-methylbut-1-ene?
e: Four carbons in the parent, double bond starting at C1, methyl on C3. CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂ is 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbut-1-ene, and CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃ is pent-2-ene.

q: A principal characteristic group sits on a ring, and the ring is attached to a longer chain. What must the parent be?
e: The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, and that overrides the more-carbons rule exactly as it overrides the longest-chain rule.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries an ethyl and a methyl on adjacent carbons. What is the name?
e: Either direction gives {1, 2}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes C1. Ethyl before methyl. Locants are needed because the two groups could also be 1,3 or 1,4.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries three methyls. Numbered one way they fall at {1, 2, 4}; the other way at {1, 3, 4}. Which set is used?
e: First point of difference: both start at 1, then 2 beats 3. On a ring you try every starting carbon and both directions, and {1, 2, 4} is the lowest set this arrangement can give.

q: A cyclohexane ring carries an OH, with a methyl on the carbon two positions away. What is the name?
e: The alcohol takes the suffix and C1. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

q: What does the prefix in cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane tell you?
e: The locants already say the methyls are adjacent. cis and trans on a ring say whether the two groups are on the same face or opposite faces, which are different compounds; the full treatment is in Stereochemistry.

q: When an acid donates a proton, what is left behind called?
e: After losing H⁺, the acid becomes its conjugate base (one less proton, one more negative/less positive charge).

q: A mechanism step shows R–OH₂⁺ handing a proton to a chloride ion. Which assignment of roles is right?
e: Follow the proton. It leaves R–OH₂⁺, so that species is the donor, which is the definition of the Brønsted acid. It lands on chloride, so chloride is the acceptor, the Brønsted base. The fact that the acid is a cation rather than a bottled reagent is what makes this look unfamiliar, and it is also why it works so readily: losing the proton neutralizes the positive charge instead of creating a negative one, which is worth about seventeen pKa units. R–OH₂⁺ sits near pKa −2 while the alcohol it came from sits near 16. Chloride is a very weak base (HCl, pKa −7), so this particular transfer is not especially favorable, but it happens constantly in mechanisms because both species are present and proton transfers are fast.

q: Which species is the Bronsted base in the reaction NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-?
e: NH3 accepts a proton from water to form NH4+, making it the Bronsted base while water acts as the acid.

q: The curved arrow that forms the new bond in a proton transfer starts on the acidic hydrogen.
e: False, and this is the single most common arrow mistake in the chapter. A curved arrow always starts on the electrons that move, and a proton has none — it is a bare nucleus. The electrons that make the new bond are supplied entirely by the base, so the arrow starts on the base’s lone pair and ends on the hydrogen. The second arrow starts on the old X–H bond and ends on the atom that keeps the pair, which is what leaves the conjugate base with its negative charge. Draw the arrow from the hydrogen and you have said the hydrogen donated electrons it does not have.

q: What is formed when a Bronsted base accepts a proton?
e: Accepting H+ turns a base into its conjugate acid, which now carries one more proton.

q: Which of the following best describes HCl dissolving in water?
e: HCl hands its proton to a water lone pair, giving H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻. That makes HCl the Brønsted acid and water the base — the same water that acts as an acid toward ammonia, which is what amphoteric means. The transfer is essentially complete because HCl (pKa −7) is a far stronger acid than H₃O⁺ (pKa −1.7): the equilibrium constant is about 10⁵. It is also the reason water cannot tell HCl, HBr and HI apart. All three are leveled to hydronium, and their quoted pKa values come from measurements in other solvents.

q: Diluting glacial acetic acid with water makes it a weaker acid.
e: False. Strength and concentration are different properties and the exam rewards keeping them apart. Acid strength is pKa: a fixed property of the molecule, set by how stable its conjugate base is. Acetic acid has pKa 4.76 whether the bottle is neat or millimolar. Concentration is how much of the substance is present per litre. Diluting lowers the concentration, which lowers the pH of the resulting solution — fewer protons overall — but changes nothing about the molecule. Hence the two combinations students find surprising: glacial acetic acid is concentrated and weak, while dilute hydrochloric acid is dilute and strong.

q: In the reaction CH3COOH + NH3 → CH3COO- + NH4+, identify the Bronsted acid.
e: Acetic acid donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the proton donor (acid) in this transfer.

q: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + HO⁻, what role does water play, and what role would it play with HCl instead?
e: Water gives a proton to ammonia, so here it is the acid and hydroxide is its conjugate base. Put water with HCl instead and the proton moves the other way: water accepts it to become H₃O⁺, so there it is the base. A species that can do both is amphoteric, and water is the standard example. The point is that "acid" and "base" are roles in a particular reaction, not permanent labels on a bottle. Which role a species plays is decided by the partner: water is more acidic than ammonia (15.7 against 38) so it donates, and far less acidic than HCl (15.7 against −7) so it accepts.

q: HSO4- (bisulfate) can act as both a Bronsted acid and a Bronsted base depending on what it reacts with.
e: HSO4- can donate its remaining proton to become SO4^2- (acid) or accept a proton to become H2SO4 (base), making it amphoteric.

q: Which pair does NOT represent an acid and its conjugate base?
e: The conjugate base of HCl is Cl-, formed by loss of H+; OH- is not related to HCl by a single proton loss.

q: When a carboxylic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate, what role does bicarbonate play?
e: Bicarbonate accepts the proton from the carboxylic acid, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2 and water), acting as a Bronsted base.

q: 4-Hydroxybutan-2-one is CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH₂–OH. One equivalent of sodium hydride is added. Which proton is removed?
e: Scan the sites and give each one a pKa. The O–H is an ordinary primary alcohol at about 16. The C–H bonds on either side of the carbonyl — the acetyl methyl and the CH₂ — are alpha hydrogens at about 20, acidic for carbon because the anion is an enolate delocalized onto oxygen. The C–H bonds on the carbon carrying the OH have no such help and sit near 50. Sodium hydride is comfortably strong enough for any of this: its conjugate acid is H₂ at pKa 36. Lowest pKa wins, so the O–H comes off, and it beats the alpha positions by roughly four units — ten thousand to one. This is the comparison students most often get backwards, because a hydrogen next to a carbonyl feels activated and is: by thirty orders of magnitude relative to an alkane, and still not enough to beat an alcohol.

q: Moving a proton between two oxygen atoms is usually the slow step of a mechanism.
e: False, and the opposite is close to a rule. Proton transfers between electronegative atoms — O to O, O to N, N to O — are among the fastest reactions known, often limited only by how quickly the two molecules diffuse together. That has a practical consequence you will use constantly: in a multi-step mechanism you may shuffle protons between heteroatoms freely, and a mechanism is not wrong for including such a step. What is genuinely slow is removing a proton from carbon, because the carbanion left behind is high in energy and the geometry has to reorganize. That is why enolate chemistry needs its own treatment and why proton transfers to and from carbon are the ones worth drawing carefully.

q: Sodium acetate is added to a solution of phenol. Acetic acid has pKa 4.76 and phenol has pKa 10. What happens?
e: Name the acid on each side. On the left the acid is phenol, pKa 10. On the right it would be acetic acid, pKa 4.76. The equilibrium always favors the side holding the weaker acid, that is the higher pKa, so it favors the left, where phenol keeps its proton. Quantitatively, K ≈ 10^(4.76 − 10) = 10^−5.2, which is about one part in 160,000. Acetate is simply too weak a base to take a proton from phenol. To deprotonate phenol you need a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa comfortably above 10 — hydroxide, at 15.7, does it easily, which is why phenols dissolve in sodium hydroxide but not in sodium bicarbonate.

q: Consider HC triple-bond CH (acetylene) reacting with a very strong base like NaNH2. What role does acetylene play?
e: The sp-hybridized C-H of a terminal alkyne is weakly acidic (pKa about 25) and can be deprotonated by a sufficiently strong base like amide ion.

q: A Brønsted base must carry a negative charge.
e: False. A base needs an available electron pair, and a lone pair on a neutral atom is an electron pair. Ammonia, water, alcohols, ethers, amines and the oxygen of a carbonyl are all neutral Brønsted bases, and most of the proton transfers you will draw in mechanisms involve one of them. Charge helps — hydroxide is a far stronger base than water, and alkoxide than an alcohol — because a negative charge makes the pair more available. But helping is not the same as being required. The reliable test is to ask whether the species has a pair it can put on a proton, not whether it has a minus sign.

q: Why can methane (CH4) technically act as a Bronsted acid, even though it essentially never does in practice?
e: Any X-H bond can formally act as a Bronsted acid, but methane's conjugate base (CH3-) is extremely unstable, giving methane an extremely high pKa (about 50) and negligible real-world acidity.

q: Which best explains why ammonia is a stronger Brønsted base than water?
e: Basicity is about how willingly a lone pair is handed to a proton. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it grips its electrons less firmly and gives the pair up more readily — ammonia is the stronger base. The cleanest way to confirm it is to compare conjugate acids: NH₄⁺ has pKa 9.2 and H₃O⁺ has pKa −1.7, so ammonia’s conjugate acid is about eleven orders of magnitude weaker, which means ammonia is about eleven orders of magnitude the stronger base. The other options fail on the facts: nitrogen has one lone pair to oxygen’s two, N–H is less polar than O–H, and size and hindrance are not what separates these two.

q: In the step R–OH + H₂SO₄ → R–OH₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻, which species is the Brønsted base?
e: Track the proton across the arrow. Sulfuric acid starts with two and ends with one, so it is the donor — the acid — and bisulfate is its conjugate base. The alcohol starts with one hydrogen on oxygen and ends with two, so it accepted a proton: it is the base, and R–OH₂⁺ is its conjugate acid. The instinct to reject this is that an alcohol does not feel basic, and on the pKa scale it is a feeble one — its conjugate acid sits near pKa −2. But basicity is relative, and against sulfuric acid an alcohol is quite basic enough. This exact step is how alcohols are activated for substitution and elimination: protonating the oxygen turns a terrible leaving group, hydroxide, into a good one, water.

q: Which of these reactions is a proton transfer?
e: A proton transfer moves one hydrogen nucleus, and nothing else, from one species to another. In the first reaction the O–H hydrogen of acetic acid moves onto hydroxide: acetate and water come out, and no heavy atom has changed partners. The bromination is an addition across a pi bond. The third is a Lewis acid–base reaction — water donates a lone pair to the empty p orbital of a carbocation and a new C–O bond forms, with no proton moving. The last is a nucleophilic substitution at carbon. All four are acid–base reactions in the broad Lewis sense; only the first is Brønsted.

q: In the self-ionization of water (2 H2O → H3O+ + OH-), how many water molecules act as the acid and how many as the base?
e: One water molecule donates a proton (acid) to the other, which accepts it (base), producing hydronium and hydroxide.

q: A student says phenol (C6H5OH) cannot be a Bronsted acid because it contains a benzene ring. What is wrong with this statement?
e: The presence of an aromatic ring does not block the O-H proton from being donated; phenol is a well-known weak Bronsted acid.

q: A carbocation is captured by water during acid-catalyzed hydration, giving R–OH₂⁺. What has to happen next to give a neutral alcohol?
e: Count the charge on R–OH₂⁺. Oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is +1, and the whole species is a cation. The only way to reach a neutral alcohol is to lose a proton, and that is a Brønsted step: another water molecule, acting as the base, takes the proton and leaves as H₃O⁺. Notice how strong an acid R–OH₂⁺ is — pKa about −2 against the alcohol’s 16 — so that step is fast and complete. The sequence is worth remembering as a pattern: a Lewis acid–base step makes the bond and creates a charge, and a Brønsted step removes it.

q: In a molecule carrying both an O–H and an N–H, a base removes the N–H proton first.
e: False, and the order is worth committing to memory because polyfunctional molecules are exam favorites. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it is more comfortable carrying the negative charge left behind, which makes the O–H the stronger acid. The numbers are not close: an alcohol O–H sits near pKa 16 and an amine N–H near 38, twenty-two orders of magnitude apart. Add one equivalent of a base strong enough for the alcohol and the nitrogen is untouched. The reverse question has the opposite answer: ask which site a proton goes to and nitrogen wins, because it holds its lone pair more loosely. Most acidic and most basic are different questions with different answers.

q: Which of these amine-type species acts purely as a Bronsted base and cannot donate an N-H proton at all?
e: Trimethylamine has no N-H bond at all (every substituent is a methyl group), so unlike ammonia or primary and secondary amines, it cannot donate an N-H proton and behaves purely as a Bronsted base.

q: Hydrogens on carbon are generally far less acidic than hydrogens on oxygen or nitrogen.
e: True, and the gap is enormous rather than marginal. An alkane C–H sits near pKa 50, an amine N–H near 38 and an alcohol O–H near 16, so a typical C–H is about thirty orders of magnitude less acidic than a typical O–H. The reason is where the charge ends up: carbon is the least electronegative of the three and is the least willing to hold the pair left behind. That is why the practical rule for finding an acidic proton is to look on oxygen and nitrogen first. The exceptions are the ones worth learning individually — a C–H next to a carbonyl at about 20, a terminal alkyne C–H at 25, a 1,3-dicarbonyl at 9 — and every one of them is explained by something stabilizing the carbanion.

q: Which pair of curved arrows correctly shows methoxide deprotonating acetic acid?
e: Two arrows, and each has a job. The first makes the new bond, so it starts on the electrons that will become that bond — a lone pair on methoxide — and ends on the acidic hydrogen. The second breaks the old bond, so it starts on the O–H bonding pair and ends on the oxygen that keeps it, which is what leaves acetate negatively charged. The answer that runs the acidic H at methoxide and acetic acid’s oxygen at the O–H bond reverses both arrows, and has the hydrogen donating electrons it does not possess. The answer that pushes the C=O bond up onto the carbonyl oxygen breaks the wrong bond: the pi bond has nothing to do with deprotonation. And the answer that sends methoxide at the carbonyl carbon is a real reaction later in the course, but it is nucleophilic addition, not proton transfer.

q: Identify the conjugate acid-base pair among these four species: H2CO3, HCO3-, CO3^2-, H3O+.
e: H2CO3 loses one proton to become HCO3-; they differ by exactly one H+ and are therefore a conjugate acid-base pair.

q: A Lewis acid is defined as a species that:
e: Lewis acids are electron pair acceptors — a broader definition than Brønsted acids, which must involve a proton.

q: Which of these is a classic Lewis acid even though it has no protons to donate?
e: BF₃ has an empty p orbital on boron and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a Lewis acid despite having no acidic protons.

q: Metal cations like Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺ act as Lewis acids in organic reactions mainly by:
e: Metal cations have empty orbitals and coordinate to electron-rich atoms like carbonyl oxygen, pulling electron density away and making the carbon more electrophilic.

q: In the step (CH₃)₃C⁺ + H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺, which species is the Lewis acid and where does the charge end up?
e: The carbocation has six valence electrons at its central carbon and an empty p orbital, so it accepts a pair: it is the Lewis acid. Water supplies the pair from one of its lone pairs, so it is the Lewis base. Now do the formal charges, because this is where the item is really aimed. Before: carbon +1, oxygen 0. After: carbon has four bonds and is neutral, while oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is +1. The charge did not disappear — it moved onto the atom that supplied the electrons and got no share of them back. Drawing the product neutral on both atoms is the classic error here. A separate Brønsted step removes that proton to give the neutral alcohol.

q: Every Bronsted base is also a Lewis base.
e: Accepting a proton requires donating an electron pair to form the new bond, so every Bronsted base (proton acceptor) is necessarily also a Lewis base.

q: Which of the following is a classic example of a Lewis acid used as a catalyst in Friedel-Crafts reactions?
e: AlCl3 has an incomplete octet on aluminum and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a powerful Lewis acid catalyst in Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.

q: BF₃ is a strong Lewis acid primarily because:
e: Boron brings three valence electrons and uses all three in bonds to fluorine, so it ends with six electrons rather than eight and an empty 2p orbital perpendicular to the trigonal planar molecule. That orbital is a genuine hole, and anything with a spare pair can fill it. The fluorines do help by pulling electron density away inductively, which makes boron hungrier, but that is a secondary effect — the empty orbital is what makes BF₃ an acid at all. The claim that fluorine donates density into boron by resonance is true in part and works against the answer: fluorine lone pairs do donate a little into that p orbital, which is exactly why BF₃ is a weaker Lewis acid than BCl₃.

q: Which of these can act as a Lewis base even though it has no lone pair at all?
e: A Lewis base donates an electron pair, and a pi bond is an electron pair. In ethene the two pi electrons sit above and below the plane of the molecule, held loosely and reaching out into space, which makes them available to anything electron-poor. That is why an alkene reacts with Br₂ or with H⁺: the pi pair attacks, exactly as ammonia’s lone pair attacks boron. Chloride, ether and ammonia are all Lewis bases too, but each has lone pairs, so none answers the question as asked. Recognizing the pi bond as the electron source is the single idea that makes the whole of alkene chemistry make sense.

q: Which species below is a Lewis base that donates electron density through pi bond electrons rather than a lone pair?
e: Ethylene has no lone pairs; it donates electron density from its pi bond to electrophiles such as Br2 or H+, a hallmark of alkene reactivity in organic chemistry.

q: In the reaction of a carbonyl oxygen with a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a Lewis acid-base adduct, what is the role of the carbonyl oxygen?
e: The carbonyl oxygen's lone pair coordinates to the electron-deficient boron of BF3, activating the carbonyl toward nucleophilic attack, a common strategy in Lewis acid catalysis.

q: A Lewis acid–base reaction always involves a proton changing hands.
e: False, and the exceptions are the reason the Lewis definition exists. BF₃ plus ammonia forms a B–N bond with no hydrogen involved anywhere; a carbocation capturing water, AlCl₃ pulling chloride off an acyl chloride, and every nucleophilic attack you will draw are all Lewis acid–base events with no proton transfer. The relationship runs the other way: Brønsted chemistry is the subset of Lewis chemistry in which the electron pair happens to be donated to H⁺. So every Brønsted base is a Lewis base, but a Lewis acid needs only somewhere for a pair to land.

q: Which of the following best explains why carbocations are strong Lewis acids?
e: A carbocation's central carbon has only six valence electrons, leaving an empty p orbital that strongly attracts electron pairs from Lewis bases (nucleophiles).

q: Which of these drawn species could act as a Lewis acid?
e: Ask of each one: does it have somewhere for an incoming pair to go? The carbonyl carbon does. Oxygen pulls density out of the C=O pi bond, leaving the carbon with a substantial partial positive charge and a low-lying pi antibonding orbital, so a nucleophile attacks it and the pi pair moves onto oxygen. That is an electron-pair acceptor, which is what Lewis acid means, and it is the single most important example in the second half of the course. The other three are all electron-rich: an ether has lone pairs, an alkene has a pi pair, a chloride has both a charge and lone pairs. All three are Lewis bases.

q: SnCl₄ and BF₃ are both Lewis acids, but they accept an electron pair in different ways. How do they differ?
e: Boron in BF₃ brings three valence electrons and uses all three, so it ends with six and a genuinely empty 2p orbital — a hole waiting to be filled. Tin in SnCl₄ has no such hole; what it has is room. A metal center with four ligands is usually perfectly comfortable with five or six, so a Lewis base simply adds on and the coordination number goes up. FeBr₃, ZnCl₂ and TiCl₄ all work the same way. The definition covers both because it is about where the pair can go, not about how the space is made available — and a carbonyl carbon is a third route again, with a full octet that accommodates the incoming pair by pushing its pi electrons onto oxygen.

q: In the Lewis acid-base adduct formed between NH3 and BF3 (H3N-BF3), what change occurs at boron's geometry?
e: Forming the new B-N bond gives boron four bonding pairs instead of three, changing its hybridization from sp2 (trigonal planar) to sp3 (tetrahedral).

q: A student claims that all Lewis acids are also Bronsted acids. Which example best refutes this claim?
e: BF3 cannot donate a proton since it has none, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid, yet it is a textbook strong Lewis acid, showing the two acid categories are not equivalent.

q: AlCl₃ is added to an acyl chloride, RCOCl. What does it do, and what is produced?
e: Aluminum in AlCl₃ has six valence electrons and an empty orbital, so it is the Lewis acid, and the best pair on offer is a lone pair on the acyl chloride’s chlorine. Coordinating there drains density out of the C–Cl bond until it breaks heterolytically, leaving AlCl₄⁻ and an acylium ion, RC≡O⁺. The acylium ion is a far stronger electrophile than the acyl chloride was — a full positive charge on carbon, stabilized by the oxygen lone pair — and it is powerful enough to attack benzene, which the acyl chloride alone is not. The catalyst did not supply the electrophile; it manufactured one, which is the general job description of a Lewis acid catalyst.

q: A species can simultaneously be a Lewis base toward one reagent and a Lewis acid toward a different reagent.
e: Lewis acid or base character depends on the reaction partner, so the same species can play different roles with different partners depending on which one is electron-rich or electron-poor in that specific interaction.

q: In H₃N: + BF₃ → H₃N–BF₃, which species donates and which accepts?
e: Nitrogen carries a lone pair and boron has an empty orbital, so the pair goes from nitrogen to boron: ammonia is the Lewis base, BF₃ the Lewis acid. One curved arrow, from the nitrogen lone pair to boron, and nothing breaks. The bookkeeping afterwards is the part worth practising. Nitrogen now has four bonds where it normally has three, so it is +1; boron has four bonds and three valence electrons, 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The adduct is neutral overall but carries an internal charge separation, and boron has gone from trigonal planar to tetrahedral. A bond made from a pair supplied entirely by one atom is called dative, though once formed it is an ordinary covalent bond.

q: Which functional group commonly acts as a Lewis base due to its lone pairs, making it useful for coordinating to Lewis acid catalysts?
e: The oxygen of a carbonyl group has lone pairs that readily coordinate to Lewis acids such as BF3 or AlCl3, a common activation strategy in synthesis.

q: A Lewis acid must have a formally empty orbital.
e: False, and the exception is a whole class of reagents. BF₃, AlCl₃ and carbocations do work that way: six valence electrons and a genuine empty p orbital. But FeBr₃, ZnCl₂, TiCl₄ and SnCl₄ are metal centers that accept a pair by expanding their coordination number instead — titanium with four bonds is perfectly comfortable with five or six, so a carbonyl oxygen can simply add on as an extra ligand. A carbonyl carbon is a third case again: it has a full octet, and the incoming pair is accommodated by pushing the pi electrons up onto oxygen. Three different mechanisms, one definition: somewhere for a pair to go.

q: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as a Lewis acid?
e: Chloride ion has a full octet and a lone pair to donate, making it a Lewis base, not a Lewis acid; the other three are classic electron-pair acceptors.

q: Why does adding TiCl₄ make a ketone react faster with a weak nucleophile?
e: Titanium accepts a lone pair from the carbonyl oxygen, expanding its coordination sphere. Once oxygen is donating into the metal it pulls harder on the C=O pi electrons, which drains density off the carbonyl carbon and leaves it more strongly delta positive — a better electrophile. The effect is the same one protonation achieves, and that is the point: a Lewis acid activates a carbonyl under neutral conditions, so a substrate that would not survive strong protic acid can still be activated. Look for the pattern rather than the reagent name: ZnCl₂, BF₃, AlCl₃ and TiCl₄ all do this job.

q: Why can a proton (H+) itself be classified as the simplest possible Lewis acid?
e: A bare proton has no electrons at all, so when it bonds to a base, that bond forms entirely from the base's donated electron pair, the defining behavior of a Lewis acid.

q: Consider a Lewis acid catalyst promoting ring-opening of an epoxide. What is its mechanistic role?
e: By accepting a lone pair from the epoxide oxygen, the Lewis acid withdraws electron density from the ring, weakening the C-O bonds and activating the epoxide carbons for nucleophilic ring-opening.

q: Why is H⁺ often described as the simplest possible Lewis acid?
e: A bare proton is a nucleus with nothing around it, so its 1s orbital is empty and every bond it ever makes is built entirely from a partner’s donated pair. That is the definition of an electron-pair acceptor, and it is why a proton cannot exist free in solution: it binds the first available lone pair instantly. Seeing it this way also settles how the two definitions fit together. A Brønsted base is always a Lewis base, because accepting a proton means donating a pair to it; and a Brønsted acid works by supplying the Lewis acid H⁺ rather than by being one itself.

q: A coordinate covalent (dative) bond, as formed between a Lewis acid and Lewis base, is characterized by:
e: In a Lewis acid-base adduct, the base supplies both electrons of the new bond while the acid simply provides the empty orbital to receive them.

q: Steric bulk around a Lewis acid's empty orbital can reduce its practical effectiveness even if its electronic electron-deficiency is high.
e: Bulky substituents can physically block a Lewis base from approaching the empty orbital, so steric hindrance, not just electronics, influences a Lewis acid's real-world reactivity.

q: An ether is stirred with BF₃ and a complex forms. Which statement about that complex is correct?
e: Oxygen donates one of its two lone pairs into boron’s empty p orbital. Count afterwards: oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, and boron has four bonds and three valence electrons, 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The complex is neutral overall while carrying a charge on each atom, which is exactly what happens with BF₃ and ammonia. Nothing was ionized and no bond broke — that is why “both atoms stay neutral” is tempting — but formal charge counts the electrons each atom can claim, and the donor always loses a claim. Ether–BF₃ complexes are real, isolable substances; BF₃ is sold as its diethyl etherate for this reason.

q: A chemist wants to make a carbonyl react faster but the substrate decomposes in strong acid. What is the standard solution?
e: Protonating a carbonyl oxygen activates the carbon beautifully, but it requires a medium acidic enough to do it, and plenty of substrates — acetals, many protecting groups, acid-sensitive stereocenters — will not survive that. A Lewis acid gives the same activation by a different route: the metal accepts a lone pair from the carbonyl oxygen, density is pulled off the carbon, and the carbon becomes more electrophilic, all under neutral conditions. That equivalence is the practical payoff of the Lewis definition. The base option is wrong in a useful way — deprotonating a carbonyl oxygen is not a thing, since there is no hydrogen there to remove.

q: A lower pKa indicates:
e: pKa and acid strength are inversely related — lower pKa means the acid dissociates more, so it’s stronger.

q: If an acid has a pKa of 5 and a base’s conjugate acid has a pKa of 10, which side does the acid-base equilibrium favor?
e: Proton transfer equilibria favor forming the weaker acid (higher pKa) — the reaction runs toward the more stable, less acidic species.

q: Hydroxide is added to a terminal alkyne (C–H pKa 25). Roughly what is the equilibrium constant for deprotonation?
e: Use K ≈ 10^(pKa of the acid formed − pKa of the acid consumed). The acid consumed is the alkyne, 25. The acid formed is water, 15.7, because that is what hydroxide becomes once it has the proton. So K ≈ 10^(15.7 − 25) = 10^−9.3, about one part in two billion against the product. Hydroxide is simply too weak a base for an alkyne. Swap in sodium amide and the acid formed is ammonia at pKa 38, giving K ≈ 10^(38 − 25) = 10¹³, which is complete — and that is exactly why NaNH₂, not NaOH, is the reagent every textbook specifies for making acetylides.

q: Acid A has Ka = 1 × 10⁻³ and acid B has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁷. How do they compare?
e: pKa = −log₁₀(Ka), so a Ka of 10⁻³ gives pKa 3 and a Ka of 10⁻⁷ gives pKa 7. The larger Ka means the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ sits further to the right, so acid A dissociates more and is the stronger acid — and it has the lower pKa. That is the whole content of the minus sign, and it is the source of most of the confusion on this topic: a bigger Ka and a smaller pKa say the same thing. The four-unit gap means A is about ten thousand times the stronger of the two.

q: Sodium hydride is added to ethanol. What happens, and why is the choice of base a good one?
e: Hydride’s conjugate acid is H₂, pKa about 36. Ethanol is 16. K ≈ 10^(36 − 16) = 10²⁰, which is complete by any standard. There is a second reason NaH is the standard reagent for making an alkoxide: the by-product is hydrogen gas, which bubbles out of the flask, so the reaction cannot run backwards even in principle. Compare the alternatives. NaOH has a conjugate acid at 15.7, slightly below ethanol, so K ≈ 10^−0.3 and you get a mixture. Sodium ethoxide is the same molecule’s own conjugate base, so K = 1 and nothing is achieved at all.

q: Which base will deprotonate a ketone alpha hydrogen (pKa 20) essentially completely?
e: A base removes a proton completely when its conjugate acid has a pKa comfortably above the proton’s — three or four units is a working minimum, and ten is decisive. LDA’s conjugate acid is diisopropylamine at about pKa 36, sixteen units above 20, so deprotonation is quantitative. Hydroxide (conjugate acid water, 15.7) and ethoxide (ethanol, 16) both sit about four units below the alpha hydrogen, so they give only a trace of enolate at equilibrium — which is useful when a trace is what you want, as in an aldol, and useless when you need all of it. Acetate (acetic acid, 4.76) is fifteen units short and does nothing. LDA is also bulky enough not to attack the carbonyl itself, which is the second reason it is chosen.

q: At what pH is a weak acid exactly 50 percent dissociated into its conjugate base, according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship?
e: When pH equals pKa, the concentrations of the acid and its conjugate base are equal, meaning the acid is 50 percent dissociated.

q: Water has a pKa of about 15.7 (based on its autoionization), while ethanol's O-H has a pKa of about 16. What does this comparison show?
e: Both are O–H bonds on a small, unhindered oxygen with no resonance and nothing withdrawing nearby, so the four ARIO factors give the same answer for each and the pKa values come out within half a unit: water 15.7, ethanol 16. The textbook explanation for the small difference is that an alkyl group is weakly electron-donating compared with a hydrogen, which slightly destabilizes the alkoxide. That is usually how it is taught, and it is worth knowing it is not the whole story: in DMSO the order reverses, with ethanol at 29.8 the stronger acid against water at 31.4. The real driver in water is solvation — hydroxide is smaller and easier for water molecules to surround than ethoxide. Either way, treat water and a simple alcohol as effectively equal in acidity.

q: A carboxylic acid has pKa around 4 to 5, while a simple alcohol has pKa around 16 to 18. Approximately how many orders of magnitude more acidic is the carboxyli
e: Since pKa is a log scale, a difference of about 12 pKa units corresponds to roughly 10^12 difference in Ka, reflecting the large stabilizing effect of resonance in the carboxylate compared to the alkoxide.

q: To fully drive deprotonation of a carboxylic acid (pKa approximately 5) forward, the base used should form a conjugate acid whose pKa is:
e: For deprotonation to run to completion, the acid produced has to be weaker than the acid consumed — higher pKa, not lower. Write it as K ≈ 10^(pKa of the acid formed − pKa of the acid consumed): with the carboxylic acid at 5, a base whose conjugate acid sits at 10 gives K ≈ 10⁵ and a base whose conjugate acid sits at 2 gives K ≈ 10^−3. The first goes, the second does not. In practice a carboxylic acid is easy: even bicarbonate, pKaH 6.4, is enough, which is why a bicarbonate wash pulls carboxylic acids out of an organic layer.

q: pKa values can be negative for very strong acids, such as HCl or the first ionization of H2SO4.
e: Since pKa = -log(Ka), an extremely large Ka for a very strong acid produces a negative pKa value.

q: A terminal alkyne C-H has pKa around 25, while a simple alkane C-H has pKa around 50. What does this difference primarily reflect?
e: Higher s-character (sp versus sp3) stabilizes the lone pair left behind in the conjugate base, making sp C-H bonds considerably more acidic than sp3 C-H bonds.

q: Which solvent property most directly affects the experimentally measured pKa of an acid?
e: pKa values are measured in a specific solvent, commonly water, because the degree to which that solvent stabilizes the separated charges through solvation strongly affects the measured equilibrium constant.

q: The pKa of the protonated carbonyl oxygen of a ketone is roughly -7, while the pKa of the same ketone's alpha C-H is roughly 20. What does this 27-unit gap tell
e: A pKa difference of 27 units corresponds to an enormous difference in Ka, showing the oxygen-protonated form is vastly more acidic than the alpha C-H, which needs a much stronger base to deprotonate.

q: A compound has two acidic protons with pKa1 = 3 and pKa2 = 10. At a pH of 7, which species predominates?
e: Use the rule that an acid is mostly protonated below its pKa and mostly deprotonated above it, one proton at a time. pH 7 is four units above pKa1 = 3, so the first, more acidic proton is long gone — better than 99.99 percent of it. pH 7 is three units below pKa2 = 10, so the second proton is still firmly attached, about a thousand to one. The species that dominates is therefore the one that has lost exactly one proton. Sketching a number line with the two pKa values marked and the pH between them makes this a five-second question rather than a calculation.

q: The pKa of a compound is an intrinsic property that is completely independent of the solvent used.
e: pKa values depend on the solvent because solvation stabilizes ions differently in different media; the same acid can show noticeably different pKa values in water versus a solvent like DMSO.

q: A carboxylic acid (pKa 4.76) and a phenol (pKa 10) are dissolved together in ether. Which reagent separates them?
e: Pick a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa between the two compounds. Bicarbonate’s conjugate acid is carbonic acid, pKa 6.4: above the carboxylic acid at 4.76 and below the phenol at 10. So the carboxylic acid is deprotonated, becomes an ion, and moves into the aqueous layer as its sodium salt, while the phenol stays neutral and stays in the ether. Hydroxide would not work: its conjugate acid is water at 15.7, above both, so it deprotonates both and sends both into the water. HCl protonates neither. Brine changes nothing about either. Acidify the aqueous layer afterwards and the carboxylic acid comes back out clean.

q: Which of these will NOT be deprotonated to any useful extent by sodium ethoxide (pKaH 16)?
e: Ethoxide removes a proton well when the substrate’s pKa is below 16, and the further below, the more complete the reaction. Acetic acid at 4.76, a 1,3-diketone at 9 and phenol at 10 are all comfortably below, by eleven, seven and six units, so ethoxide takes all three essentially completely. The terminal alkyne at 25 is nine units above: K ≈ 10^(16 − 25) = 10^−9, about a billion to one against. The diketone is the one worth noticing — its acidic hydrogen is on carbon, and it is still more acidic than phenol, because the anion delocalizes onto two carbonyl oxygens.

q: Protonated amines (ammonium ions, R-NH3+) typically have pKa values around:
e: The conjugate acids of typical alkyl amines have pKa values in the range of about 9 to 11, reflecting amines' moderate basicity.

q: If Ka for acid A is 1 times 10^-5 and Ka for acid B is 1 times 10^-3, what is the approximate difference in their pKa values, and which acid has the higher pKa?
e: pKa = -log(Ka), so a Ka of 10^-5 gives pKa = 5 and a Ka of 10^-3 gives pKa = 3; acid A, with the smaller Ka, has the higher pKa, a difference of 2 units.

q: Why can it be misleading to directly compare a gas-phase acidity measurement to an aqueous-solution pKa for the same compound?
e: In solution, polar solvents like water stabilize charged conjugate bases through solvation, which can significantly change or even reverse relative acidity trends compared to the gas phase, where no such stabilization exists.

q: A pKa value can be used to predict which of two acids will protonate a common base more completely at equilibrium.
e: Comparing the pKa values of two acids against a common base's conjugate acid lets you predict which acid-base pair favors products versus reactants at equilibrium.

q: The pKa of hydronium ion (H3O+) is approximately -1.74. What does this illustrate about the leveling effect in water?
e: Because H3O+ is the strongest acid species that persists in water, stronger acids added to dilute water are converted essentially completely to H3O+, a phenomenon known as the leveling effect.

q: Ethanol (pKa 16) and acetic acid (pKa 4.76) are both treated with one equivalent of sodium bicarbonate (pKaH 6.4). What is the result?
e: Compare each substrate with the base’s pKaH. Acetic acid at 4.76 sits 1.6 units below 6.4, so K ≈ 10^1.6, about forty to one in favor of deprotonation — it goes, and you can see it go, because the carbonic acid produced falls apart into CO₂ and water and the mixture fizzes. Ethanol at 16 sits nearly ten units above, so K ≈ 10^−9.6 and nothing happens. This selectivity is the basis of the standard bicarbonate wash: it removes carboxylic acids from a mixture and leaves alcohols and phenols alone.

q: A student needs to know whether hydroxide will deprotonate a given substrate. What is the fastest reliable test?
e: A base can remove a proton whose pKa is lower than the pKa of its own conjugate acid. Hydroxide’s conjugate acid is water, pKa 15.7, so that is the number to compare against. Below 15.7 and the reaction is favorable; a few units below and it is essentially complete; above 15.7 and it is not happening. The neutral point of water, pH 7, is a property of a solution rather than of a molecule and has nothing to do with this comparison. Having an O–H bond is not enough either: ethanol has one and sits at 16, just above hydroxide’s reach.

q: Two acids differ by 3 pKa units. How different are they in acid strength?
e: pKa is a base-ten logarithm, so each unit is a factor of ten in Ka and three units is 10³, a thousandfold. This is worth converting every time, because pKa differences look deceptively small on the page. Acetic acid at 4.76 and ethanol at 16 look eleven small steps apart and are a hundred billion to one. The practical calibration: one or two units is a real but incomplete reaction, three or four is enough to call a proton transfer complete for synthetic purposes, and anything past six is absolute.

q: Acetic acid has pKa 4.76 and ammonium has pKa 9.2. In CH₃CO₂H + NH₃ ⇌ CH₃CO₂⁻ + NH₄⁺, which side is favored and by roughly how much?
e: Name the acid on each side. On the left it is acetic acid, pKa 4.76. On the right it is ammonium, pKa 9.2, formed when ammonia takes the proton. The equilibrium favors the side holding the weaker acid, that is the higher pKa, so it favors the right. K ≈ 10^(9.2 − 4.76) = 10^4.4, roughly 10⁴ — complete for practical purposes. Notice what the calculation does not require: you never had to decide whether acetate or ammonia is the stronger base. Converting everything to acids and comparing two pKa values answers the same question with the numbers pointing the right way.

q: A reaction needs a base strong enough to deprotonate an alkyne (pKa 25) but must not use anything that attacks a carbonyl elsewhere in the molecule. Which consi
e: Two properties decide whether a base is usable, and they are independent. First, strength: the conjugate acid needs a pKa well above 25, which rules out hydroxide at 15.7 and ethoxide at 16 and points to amide bases at 36 to 38. Second, nucleophilicity, which is largely a matter of steric bulk: a small strong base such as amide ion will also add to a carbonyl, whereas a bulky one such as LDA is too hindered to reach the carbonyl carbon and can only reach a proton. This separation of basicity from nucleophilicity is exactly why LDA exists as a reagent.

q: Trifluoroethanol has pKa 12.4, while ethanol has pKa 16. Which base is strong enough to deprotonate ethanol but not trifluoroethanol?
e: The question contains its own contradiction, which is the point of it. Ethanol at 16 is the weaker acid of the two, so any base able to remove ethanol’s proton will remove trifluoroethanol’s more easily still. Selectivity runs the other way: you can find a base that takes the more acidic proton and leaves the less acidic one alone, but never the reverse. A base whose pKaH is about 14, for instance, would deprotonate trifluoroethanol and not ethanol. Getting this backwards is a common slip, and the fix is to always rank the substrates by pKa first and then ask which end of the range your base can reach.

q: Why is the pKa of HCl usually quoted as about −7 when nobody can measure it in water?
e: Water levels every acid stronger than H₃O⁺. Add HCl, HBr, HI or H₂SO₄ to water and each is converted essentially completely to hydronium, so all four look identical and the solution cannot tell them apart: the strongest acid that can exist in water is H₃O⁺, pKa −1.7. To rank them you have to move to a solvent that is a much weaker base, such as acetic acid or DMSO, measure there, and extrapolate back. The same levelling happens at the basic end — hydroxide is the strongest base water permits — which is why NaNH₂ and LDA have to be used in aprotic solvents like THF.

q: A strong acid has a conjugate base that is:
e: Strong acids give up protons easily because their conjugate base is very stable (weak) once formed.

q: What is the conjugate acid of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH?
e: A conjugate acid is what a species becomes when it gains one proton, so add H⁺ to one of oxygen’s lone pairs. Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair, which is a formal charge of +1, giving the oxonium ion CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. Nothing else about the molecule changes. The ion is a strong acid, pKa about −2, eighteen units below the alcohol it came from — which is exactly why protonating an alcohol is the standard way to turn hydroxide, a terrible leaving group, into water, a good one. CH₃CH₂O⁻ is the conjugate base rather than the acid, and the other two options are different compounds altogether.

q: What is the conjugate base of a terminal alkyne, RC≡CH?
e: Remove the terminal C–H proton and leave the bonding pair behind: the result is an acetylide anion, with the negative charge in an sp orbital on carbon. The alkyne is far more acidic than an ordinary hydrocarbon — pKa 25 against about 50 — because an sp orbital is 50 percent s character, so it holds the pair close to the nucleus and low in energy. The other options change the carbon skeleton rather than just removing a proton, which conjugate relationships never do. Acetylides matter because they are carbon nucleophiles: they attack alkyl halides and carbonyls and make carbon–carbon bonds.

q: A conjugate base always carries a negative charge.
e: False, and the trap catches almost everyone once. "One proton and one unit of charge" means the charge goes down by one, not that it lands on −1. Start from a cation and the conjugate base is neutral: H₃O⁺ gives water, NH₄⁺ gives ammonia, a protonated alcohol gives the alcohol back. Start from a neutral molecule and you do get an anion: water gives hydroxide, ethanol gives ethoxide. The same applies in reverse for conjugate acids, which are not always neutral: the conjugate acid of a neutral amine is an ammonium cation. Write the charge you started with, then add or subtract one.

q: Given that HCN has a pKa of approximately 9.2 and HF has a pKa of approximately 3.2, which conjugate base is the stronger base?
e: Because HCN is a much weaker acid than HF (higher pKa), its conjugate base, cyanide, holds onto protons more strongly and is therefore the stronger base of the two.

q: Which of the following conjugate bases would be expected to be the strongest (best proton acceptor)?
e: Water is a much weaker acid than HCl or acetic acid, so its conjugate base, hydroxide, is a correspondingly much stronger base than chloride or acetate.

q: Which conjugate acid-base pair is correctly matched?
e: NH4+ loses a proton to become NH3, making them a properly matched conjugate acid and conjugate base pair, differing by exactly one H+.

q: The conjugate base of a strong acid is generally a poor base in aqueous solution.
e: Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base has very little affinity for protons and is correspondingly a weak base, such as Cl- from HCl.

q: Which pair is a conjugate acid–base pair?
e: A conjugate pair differs by exactly one proton and by nothing else. Acetic acid loses its O–H proton to give acetate: same carbon skeleton, same atoms apart from that one hydrogen, charge down by one. That is a pair. Acetic acid and ethanol are different compounds with different skeletons. Acetic acid and methyl acetate differ by a methyl group, not a proton — an ester is not a conjugate anything. Acetate and hydroxide are simply the two bases that might appear on opposite sides of some reaction; being on opposite sides of an arrow is the classic reason people pair species that are not conjugates.

q: A ketone can act as both an acid and a base. What are its conjugate acid and conjugate base?
e: Run the definition in both directions on the same molecule. Add a proton to a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen and you get the protonated carbonyl, C=OH⁺ — the conjugate acid, and a strong one at pKa about −7, which is how acid catalysis activates a carbonyl toward nucleophiles. Remove an alpha proton, the one on the carbon next to C=O, and you get the enolate — the conjugate base, from a C–H at pKa about 20, unusually acidic for carbon because the anion delocalizes onto oxygen. Both halves of carbonyl chemistry are on that one line: acid catalysis on the left, enolate chemistry on the right.

q: Which of these is the strongest base?
e: Base strength is read off the conjugate acid, inverted: the weaker the acid, the stronger the base it leaves behind. Methane at pKa 50 is the feeblest acid on the list by a wide margin, so methyl anion is the strongest base — strong enough to deprotonate essentially anything organic, which is why organolithiums and Grignards cannot be used in the presence of water or alcohols. Chloride comes from the strongest acid, pKa −7, so it is a spectator: you can eat sodium chloride. Hydroxide and acetate sit in between and in that order. Note that there is no separate base scale to memorize; one pKa column answers both questions.

q: Why does the acetate ion, the conjugate base of acetic acid, react with water far less extensively than the ethoxide ion, the conjugate base of ethanol?
e: Both anions came from an O–H, so the atom holding the charge is oxygen in each case and factor A is a tie. What differs is what happens next. Acetate spreads its negative charge equally over two equivalent oxygens by resonance, so each carries about half a unit; ethoxide has nowhere to put it and keeps the whole charge on one oxygen. Half a charge is far easier to hold than a whole one, so acetate is the more stable and therefore the weaker, less reactive base — which is the same statement as acetic acid (pKa 4.76) being eleven orders of magnitude stronger an acid than ethanol (pKa 16).

q: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) is amphoteric. As the conjugate base of which species does it form by losing a proton, and as the conjugate acid of which species does it fo
e: Bicarbonate forms when carbonic acid (H2CO3) loses a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate base, and also when carbonate (CO3^2-) gains a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate acid; this dual role is why it is amphoteric.

q: The conjugate acid of a carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is:
e: Adding one proton to a carboxylate ion regenerates the neutral carboxylic acid, its conjugate acid.

q: HCN has pKa 9.2 and HF has pKa 3.2. Which conjugate base is stronger, and what follows for leaving-group ability?
e: HCN is the weaker acid of the two — higher pKa — so its conjugate base, cyanide, holds a proton more strongly and is the stronger base. Fluoride, left behind by the stronger acid, is the weaker and more stable of the two anions. A good leaving group is a weak, stable base, so fluoride is the better leaving group of the pair. That chain of reasoning is worth rehearsing because it is one property under four names: conjugate base of a strong acid, weak base, stable anion, good leaving group. Read the pKa column left to right for acid strength and right to left for everything else.

q: Given the conjugate acids methane (pKa about 50), ammonia (pKa about 38), water (pKa about 15.7), and HF (pKa about 3.2), which of their conjugate bases, CH3-,
e: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the conjugate base; since methane is the weakest acid of the four (highest pKa), methyl anion is the strongest base.

q: Which statement correctly relates acid strength and conjugate base strength within a conjugate pair?
e: Because a weak acid holds onto its proton fairly well, its conjugate base, once formed, has a correspondingly stronger pull on protons, meaning it is a relatively strong base.

q: Rank these bases from strongest to weakest: ⁻NH₂, HO⁻, CH₃CO₂⁻, Cl⁻.
e: Convert every base to its conjugate acid and rank those by pKa: ammonia 38, water 15.7, acetic acid 4.76, HCl −7. The weakest acid leaves the strongest base, so the base order is the reverse of the acid order: amide, then hydroxide, then acetate, then chloride. The spread is enormous — 45 pKa units from top to bottom — and it maps directly onto what each one does in a flask. Amide deprotonates almost anything organic. Hydroxide handles alcohols and carboxylic acids. Acetate manages only strong acids. Chloride does essentially nothing as a base, which is precisely why it is a good leaving group.

q: The conjugate base formed by removing the N-H proton from an amine (giving R-NH-) is a much stronger base than the conjugate base formed by removing the O-H pro
e: Because N-H, with pKa around 35 to 38, is far less acidic than O-H, with pKa around 16 to 18, the nitrogen-based conjugate base holds its electron pair much more tightly and is therefore a much stronger base than an alkoxide.

q: You need to deprotonate a terminal alkyne (pKa 25) essentially completely. Judging each base by its conjugate acid, which one does the job?
e: Choosing a base is a conjugate-acid comparison. A proton transfer runs downhill when the acid you form is weaker — higher pKa — than the acid you consume, and K ≈ 10^(pKa formed − pKa consumed). Sodium amide forms ammonia at 38 from an alkyne at 25, so K ≈ 10¹³ and the deprotonation is complete. Hydroxide would form water at 15.7, which is 9.3 units below the alkyne — uphill by 10⁻⁹·³, so almost no acetylide. Triethylamine at 10.7 and bicarbonate at 6.4 are further uphill still. The working rule is to pick a base whose conjugate acid sits several pKa units above the proton you want, which is why acetylide chemistry is written with NaNH₂ and never with NaOH.

q: What is the conjugate base of an amine, RNH₂, and what does it take to make it?
e: Removing a proton from nitrogen gives the amide anion RNH⁻. The reagent question is what makes this worth asking: the N–H of an amine sits at pKa about 38, so a base whose conjugate acid is well above 38 is needed — butyllithium, whose conjugate acid is butane at about 50, does it. Hydroxide at 15.7 is twenty-two units short and does nothing at all. The contrast with the conjugate acid is the useful part: RNH₃⁺ forms whenever an amine meets any ordinary acid, because its pKa is only about 10.7. Same molecule, one proton either side, wildly different difficulty.

q: Hydroxide is often called a strong base and water a weak one. How can both be true?
e: Every base inherits its strength from its own conjugate acid, and these two have different partners. Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKa 15.7 — a weak acid, so hydroxide is a strong base. Water is the conjugate base of hydronium, pKa −1.7 — a strong acid, so water is a weak base. The seventeen-unit gap between the two conjugate acids is exactly the gap between the two basicities. This is also why "is this a conjugate base?" is not a well-formed question: the answer always requires naming the other party, the way "is this a sibling?" does.

q: Identify both conjugate pairs in CH₃CO₂H + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CO₂⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺.
e: Pair each species with the one it turns into, which means reading vertically down the equation rather than diagonally across the arrow. Acetic acid loses a proton to become acetate: one pair. Methylamine gains that proton to become the methylammonium ion: the other pair. The diagonal readings — pairing acetic acid with methylammonium, or methylamine with acetate — are the classic error, and so is pairing the two species that merely sit on the same side of the arrow. Acetate and methylamine are not conjugates; they are simply the two species that end up on opposite sides. Every proton transfer has all four roles filled at once, and the test for a pair is always the same: do these two differ by exactly one H and one unit of charge, and by nothing else?

q: A carboxylate RCO₂⁻ is treated with dilute HCl. What forms, and what is it called?
e: Adding a proton to a base gives its conjugate acid, so the carboxylate picks up H⁺ on one of its oxygens and becomes the neutral carboxylic acid. The charge goes from −1 to 0, which is the "one unit of charge" half of the definition. This is not a theoretical step: it is the second half of every acid–base extraction. Wash an organic layer with bicarbonate and the carboxylic acid is converted to its salt and pulled into the water; acidify that aqueous layer and the conjugate acid reforms, comes out of solution and can be collected. Nothing was reduced and no chlorine was installed — dilute HCl here is only a proton source.

q: Given that HI has pKa around -10, H2O has pKa around 15.7, and NH3 has pKa around 38, how should their conjugate bases I-, OH-, and NH2- rank from weakest to st
e: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base; since HI is the strongest acid (most negative pKa) and NH3 is the weakest (highest pKa) of the three, their conjugate bases rank I- as weakest, then OH-, then NH2- as strongest.

q: Which statement about an acid and its conjugate base is correct?
e: The relationship is a strict inverse, and it is not a separate fact to memorize — it follows from what the words mean. An acid is strong precisely because it lets go of its proton readily, which requires that whatever is left behind is comfortable holding the electron pair and has little appetite for the proton back. Comfortable holding it is the definition of a weak base. Run it the other way and the same logic applies: ammonia is a vanishingly weak acid at pKa 38, so amide ion is one of the strongest bases in the course. Every species has a conjugate base, however feeble an acid it is; methane’s is the methyl anion.

q: Identify the two conjugate acid-base pairs in the reaction HCN + OH- → CN- + H2O.
e: Every proton transfer contains exactly two conjugate pairs, and you find them by pairing each species with what it turns into. HCN loses its proton to become CN⁻: one pair. Hydroxide gains that proton to become water: the other pair. Read the equation vertically, not diagonally — HCN and water are simply the two species that happen to sit on opposite sides, and pairing them is the standard mistake. Which way does it run? Left acid HCN, pKa 9.2; right acid water, pKa 15.7. The higher pKa is on the right, so the equilibrium favors the products by about 10⁶.5.

q: Ethanol has pKa 16 and pentane-2,4-dione has pKa 9, even though the acidic hydrogen of the diketone is on carbon. Which factor decides it?
e: Run ARIO and watch two factors disagree. A favors ethanol: its anion puts the charge on oxygen, while the diketone’s puts it on carbon, and oxygen is far more electronegative. R favors the diketone by a mile: the anion sits between two carbonyls and delocalizes onto both oxygens, so the charge spends most of its time on oxygen anyway and on two of them, while ethoxide has nowhere to put it. R wins, and not narrowly — seven pKa units, ten million to one. This is the case that shows the ARIO order is a search order, not a ranking of strengths: A is checked first because it settles most comparisons quickly, not because it always wins.

q: Across a period, as electronegativity of the atom bearing the negative charge increases, acidity of the H attached to it:
e: More electronegative atoms stabilize the extra negative charge of the conjugate base better, increasing acidity (e.g., HF > CH₄ in acidity trend logic, comparing across a period).

q: Acetic acid has pKa 4.76 and trifluoroacetic acid has pKa 0.5. Which factor accounts for the difference?
e: Both anions are carboxylates, so resonance is identical on both sides and the atom holding the charge is oxygen in each case. What the three fluorines do is pull electron density toward themselves through the sigma framework, which helps spread the carboxylate’s negative charge and stabilizes it. That is induction, and here it is worth 4.3 pKa units — about twenty thousand fold. Two properties of induction are worth carrying away from this: it is cumulative, so three fluorines do far more than one, and it dies quickly with distance, so moving the fluorines three carbons away would leave almost nothing of the effect.

q: Which anion is the most stable?
e: Rank the conjugate acids and invert, because a stable anion is the one left behind by a strong acid. Acetic acid 4.76, ethanol 16, an amine N–H about 38, an alkane about 50. So acetate is by far the most stable of the four and the propyl carbanion the least, spanning 45 pKa units. The reasons stack in the expected order: acetate gets both the electronegative atom and resonance over two equivalent oxygens; ethoxide gets the atom but no resonance; the amide anion is on a less electronegative atom; the carbanion has nothing at all going for it. A stable anion, a weak base and a good leaving group are three names for the same property.

q: Down a column of the periodic table, such as F, Cl, Br, I, acidity of the corresponding H-X bond generally:
e: Acidity increases down the column: HF 3.2, HCl −7, HBr −9, HI −10, so HI is about thirteen orders of magnitude stronger than HF. The explanation this course uses is size and polarizability — iodide spreads one unit of charge over a vastly bigger, floppier electron cloud than fluoride can, and that dilution stabilizes the anion far more than the loss of electronegativity costs. A second effect points the same way and some textbooks lead with it: the H–X bond also gets longer and weaker down the group, from about 570 kJ/mol for H–F to 300 for H–I. Both are real; size is the one to quote, with bond strength reinforcing it.

q: Cyclopentadiene has pKa 16, comparable to an alcohol, although its acidic hydrogen is on carbon and no heteroatom is involved. Resonance onto carbon alone can t
e: True, and this corrects an over-simple version of the rule. It is true that delocalizing onto an electronegative atom is worth more per atom — acetate, on two oxygens, beats phenoxide, on three carbons. But "onto carbon does not count" is wrong, and the counterexamples are all standard: allyl anion at pKa 43 against propane at 50, triphenylmethane at 31, phenol at 10 against an alcohol at 16, and cyclopentadiene at 16 against a normal alkane at 50 — thirty-four units from delocalization onto carbon alone. Cyclopentadienyl is the extreme case because its anion is also aromatic, six pi electrons in a planar ring, and aromatic stabilization is resonance in its strongest available form.

q: Which is the stronger acid: ethanethiol (CH₃CH₂SH) or ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH)?
e: Only factor A differs here, and it is the down-a-group case rather than the across-a-period one. No resonance in either anion, nothing withdrawing in either molecule, both atoms sp³. Oxygen is more electronegative, which would favor ethanol — but sulfur is much larger, so the thiolate spreads one unit of charge over a far bigger, more polarizable electron cloud, and that dilution beats the loss of electronegativity. Measured: ethanethiol 10.6, ethanol 16, so the thiol is about 250,000 times the stronger acid. The same logic runs down the halogens, where HI beats HF by thirteen orders of magnitude.

q: Pent-4-yn-1-ol is HC≡C–CH₂CH₂CH₂–OH. One equivalent of sodium hydride is added. Which proton comes off?
e: Give every site a pKa and take the lowest. The O–H is an ordinary primary alcohol at about 16. The terminal alkyne C–H is 25 — remarkably acidic for carbon, because the pair left behind sits in an sp orbital with 50 percent s character, but still nine units above the alcohol.
