The CH₂ groups have nothing stabilizing their anions and sit near 50. So sodium hydride, pKaH about 36, takes the O–H: it is comfortably able to, and the nine-unit gap means the alkyne is untouched. To deprotonate the alkyne instead you would need a base above 25, such as NaNH₂ at 38 — and it would take the O–H first, so you would need two equivalents.

q: Why is cyclopentadiene, with pKa around 16, remarkably acidic for a simple hydrocarbon C-H bond?
e: Removing that specific proton produces a fully conjugated, aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion, whose resonance and aromatic stabilization dramatically lowers the pKa compared to a typical alkane C-H, around 50.

q: Which factor best explains why an alkyne C-H (sp carbon, pKa about 25) is more acidic than an alkene C-H (sp2 carbon, pKa about 44), which is in turn more acidi
e: Orbitals with more s-character are lower in energy and hold electron density closer to the nucleus; since sp has the most s-character of the three, its conjugate base is the most stabilized, making the alkynyl C-H the most acidic.

q: A base is stronger when its own conjugate acid has a lower pKa.
e: False — it is the other way round, and this is the single most common inversion on the topic. A base inherits its strength from its conjugate acid by inversion: the weaker that acid is, the higher its pKa, and the stronger the base. Amide ion is a ferocious base because ammonia is a feeble acid at pKa 38. Chloride does essentially nothing as a base because HCl is a very strong acid at −7. The working rule for any "which is the stronger base" question is to convert both bases to their conjugate acids, look up the two pKa values, and pick the higher one. There is no separate base scale to memorize.

q: Chloroacetic acid (pKa about 2.87) is more acidic than acetic acid (pKa about 4.76). What is the dominant factor responsible for this difference?
e: Chlorine's high electronegativity withdraws electron density through the sigma bond framework, helping stabilize the adjacent carboxylate anion and thus increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted acetic acid.

q: Trichloroacetic acid has pKa 0.65, chloroacetic acid 2.86 and acetic acid 4.76. What does the series show about induction?
e: Take the differences rather than just the direction. The first chlorine is worth 1.90 pKa units, the second 1.57 and the third only 0.64. So the effects do add — three chlorines take the acid from 4.76 to 0.65, about four orders of magnitude — but each one buys less than the one before, because each finds less charge density left on the carboxylate to pull on. Resonance is not the explanation: both anions are ordinary carboxylates with the same delocalization over two oxygens, and the chlorines are not conjugated to anything. Only the sigma-framework pull differs.

q: Phenol (pKa about 10) is far more acidic than a simple alcohol like tert-butanol (pKa about 18), despite neither having a strong electron-withdrawing substituen
e: Both acids give up an O–H, so the atom carrying the charge is oxygen in each case and A is a tie. The difference is what the anion can do next. Phenoxide pushes its charge into the aromatic ring, reaching the two ortho positions and the para position — three extra carbons to share it with, and the C–O bond picks up double-bond character in the process. tert-Butoxide has nowhere to send it. That is worth eight pKa units here, phenol 10 against tert-butanol 18. It is real stabilization and still less than acetate gets, because acetate’s charge lands on a second oxygen rather than on carbon.

q: Which will the stronger base be: ethoxide (from ethanol, pKa 16) or acetate (from acetic acid, pKa 4.76)?
e: A basicity question is an acidity question read backwards, and the translation is one line: the stronger base is the one whose conjugate acid has the higher pKa. Ethanol at 16 is the weaker acid, so ethoxide is the stronger base, by the full 11.2-unit gap. Structurally it is the same resonance argument seen from the other side — acetate’s charge is spread over two equivalent oxygens and is therefore comfortable and unreactive, while ethoxide’s sits entirely on one oxygen and is looking for somewhere to go. This is why you can keep sodium acetate in a bottle and buy it by the kilogram, and why sodium ethoxide has to be kept dry.

q: Why is H₃O⁺ (pKa −1.7) so much more acidic than H₂O (pKa 15.7), when both give up a proton from oxygen?
e: Compare what each deprotonation creates. Water starts neutral and ends as hydroxide, so a full negative charge has to be invented and found a home. Hydronium starts at +1 and ends neutral, so the charge is simply canceled — nothing new has to be stabilized. That is worth about seventeen pKa units here, and the same pattern holds for every pair you meet: NH₄⁺ at 9.2 against NH₃ at 38, a protonated alcohol at about −2 against an alcohol at 16. Charge is the largest single lever in the whole table, and it is why acid catalysis works: protonating a substrate manufactures a strong acid out of a weak one.

q: Formic acid (pKa about 3.75) is somewhat more acidic than acetic acid (pKa about 4.76). What is the best explanation for this difference?
e: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating by induction compared to a hydrogen atom, which slightly destabilizes the negative charge on acetate's conjugate base relative to formate, making formic acid marginally more acidic.

q: The order C–H < N–H < O–H < H–F across the second period is explained by the H–X bond getting weaker from left to right.
e: False. Bond strength is the argument for going down a group, not across a period, and here it points the wrong way: H–F is the strongest bond of the four and HF is by far the most acidic. What changes across a row is electronegativity, and with the atoms all about the same size that is what decides how comfortably the leftover charge is held. Fluorine holds it best, carbon worst, and the pKa values run 50, 38, 15.7, 3.2. Keep the two trends separate: electronegativity across, size and polarizability down, with the weakening H–X bond helping in the second case only.

q: Rank CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and HF from least to most acidic, and name the factor responsible.
e: These four hydrides are all second period, so the atoms are of similar size and the size argument has nothing to work with. What changes across the row is electronegativity, and it changes a lot: carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine. The more electronegative the atom, the more willingly it holds the negative charge left behind, so the anion is more stable and the acid is stronger. The pKa values are about 50, 38, 15.7 and 3.2 — nearly fifty orders of magnitude from one end to the other. Size only takes over when you go down a column instead, where HF at 3.2 is beaten by HI at −10 despite fluorine being the more electronegative.

q: A student argues that since fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, HF should always be the most acidic hydrogen halide. Why is this reasoning flawed?
e: Electronegativity is the right tool across a period, where the atoms are all about the same size: C–H, N–H, O–H, H–F run 50, 38, 15.7, 3.2 and the most electronegative atom does hold the charge best. Down a group the atoms change size dramatically and that becomes the dominant term. Iodide spreads one negative charge over a far bigger, more polarizable cloud than fluoride can, and the weaker H–I bond helps, so HI (pKa −10) beats HF (3.2) by thirteen orders of magnitude. Two different trends, two different reasons, and applying the period rule to a group comparison gets the answer exactly backwards.

q: Protonated ketones are far more acidic than the same ketone's alpha C-H protons.
e: The O-H formed by protonating a carbonyl oxygen has a pKa around -7, vastly lower than a typical alpha C-H, which has a pKa around 20, because oxygen stabilizes the resulting species far better than an unstabilized carbanion at carbon.

q: Malonic acid, CH2(COOH)2, has a notably lower pKa1 (about 2.83) than acetic acid, despite having no halogen substituents. What effect explains this?
e: The second carbonyl-containing group, while not a halogen, is still electron-withdrawing by induction since carbonyl carbons are electron-poor, and its proximity to the first carboxylic acid group stabilizes the conjugate base, lowering pKa1 relative to acetic acid.

q: Ethanethiol has pKa 10.6 and acetic acid 4.76. Which factor decides which is the stronger acid?
e: This is a genuine conflict between the first two factors. A favors the thiol: its charge lands on sulfur, which is large and polarizable and spreads one negative charge over a much bigger cloud than oxygen can — that is exactly why ethanethiol at 10.6 beats ethanol at 16. R favors the acid: acetate delocalizes over two equivalent oxygens while the thiolate has nowhere to send its charge. R wins by six units, ten to the sixth. So checking A first and stopping would give the wrong answer here. The order in ARIO is a search order, and when two factors disagree you have to draw both anions and weigh them.

q: Methanol has pKa 15.5 and tert-butanol 18 in water, although both are simple alcohols. What explains the gap?
e: None of the four structural factors separates these two: the charge is on oxygen in both, neither anion has resonance, neither has an electron-withdrawing group and both oxygens are sp³. What differs is bulk, and bulk matters because every pKa in the table was measured in a solvent. Water molecules can crowd round a small, compact methoxide and stabilize it; three methyl groups keep them away from tert-butoxide, so it is stabilized less and its parent acid is weaker. The proof is what happens when the solvent is removed: in the gas phase the order reverses and tert-butoxide is the more stable anion. Treat solvation as a reminder rather than a fifth factor — structure explains the anion, the solvent has the last word on the number.

q: Which of these C–H bonds is the most acidic?
e: Every option is a hydrogen on carbon, so A is fixed and the differences are all about what stabilizes the resulting carbanion. The 1,3-diketone wins at pKa 9: its anion delocalizes onto two carbonyl oxygens, so the charge spends most of its time on the most electronegative atoms available. A simple ketone’s alpha C–H manages 20 with only one oxygen to delocalize onto. A terminal alkyne is 25 — no resonance at all, but the pair sits in an sp orbital with 50 percent s character and is held close to the nucleus. An alkene C–H is sp² and about 44. A hydrogen on carbon as acidic as phenol is worth noticing: it is why 1,3-dicarbonyls are the workhorse nucleophiles of enolate chemistry.

q: When ranking acidity among compounds that differ in multiple structural ways at once, for example one has extra resonance stabilization while another has a stro
e: Acidity is ultimately about conjugate base stability, and multiple factors often operate simultaneously, so a careful comparison must weigh all of them together rather than applying a single rule in isolation.

q: Rank these O–H acids from strongest to weakest: acetic acid, ethanol, phenol, trifluoroethanol.
e: Take the four conjugate bases and ask which is most comfortable. Acetate, 4.76, is best off: full resonance over two equivalent oxygens. Phenoxide, 10, delocalizes into the ring but only onto carbons, so it gets real help and less of it. Trifluoroethoxide, 12.4, has no resonance at all but three fluorines pulling density away through the sigma bonds — pure induction, and worth 3.6 units against ethanol. Ethoxide, 16, has nothing: one charge, one oxygen, no help. So the order is resonance onto oxygen, then resonance onto carbon, then induction, then nothing, and it spans eleven pKa units.

q: Placing an electron-withdrawing group two carbons further from the acidic proton usually leaves the acidity almost unchanged.
e: True, and the distance dependence is the fingerprint that distinguishes induction from resonance. Induction is transmitted through the sigma framework and fades sharply with each additional bond: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is pKa 2.86, 3-chlorobutanoic 4.06 and 4-chlorobutanoic 4.52, against butanoic acid itself at 4.82. By the third carbon almost nothing is left. Resonance behaves quite differently: it runs the length of a conjugated system losing very little, so a nitro group four bonds away across a benzene ring still moves phenol’s pKa by nearly three units. When an exam asks which effect is operating, ask what happens when you move the group further away.

q: Resonance and induction both stabilize a conjugate base. Which is generally the larger effect, and how safe is that generalization?
e: Resonance usually wins, because it delocalizes the actual charge onto extra atoms rather than merely shifting density along sigma bonds. But "usually" is doing real work in that sentence and an exam will test it. Phenol against an alcohol is six units from resonance; trifluoroacetic against acetic acid is 4.3 units from induction, and trichloroacetic is four units — comparable. Three fluorines beat the aromatic ring in phenoxide. The reliable approach is the one the ARIO order encodes: work down the list, stop at the first factor that differs, and when two factors point opposite ways draw both anions and weigh them rather than applying a slogan.

q: Which base is stronger: ethylamine (conjugate acid pKa 10.7) or ammonia (conjugate acid pKa 9.2)?
e: Convert both bases to their conjugate acids and compare pKa: ethylammonium 10.7, ammonium 9.2. The higher pKa belongs to the weaker acid, and the weaker acid leaves the stronger base, so ethylamine is the stronger base — by 1.5 units, about thirty fold. Two traps sit beside it. Saying “ammonia, because its conjugate acid is the weaker one” uses the right logic on a backwards fact: ammonium at 9.2 is the stronger acid, not the weaker. And size is not what separates these two — the ethyl group is weakly electron-donating and pushes density onto nitrogen, which is the structural reason ethylamine wins, not a steric one. Converting the base to its conjugate acid first is the habit that stops these going backwards.

q: In a Newman projection, the front atom’s bonds are drawn from:
e: The front atom is represented as a point with three lines radiating out; the back atom is the circle behind it.

q: A Newman projection down the C2–C3 bond of butane shows the front methyl pointing straight up and the back methyl 60° away from it. Which conformation is this,
e: Sixty degrees between the reference groups is gauche, and gauche is staggered — every front bond sits in a gap, so there is no torsional strain at all. The 0.9 kcal/mol is purely the two methyls bumping into each other at that angle: steric strain with nothing else mixed in.

q: Using the per-interaction values (H/H eclipsed ≈ 1.0, H/CH₃ eclipsed ≈ 1.4 kcal/mol), estimate the rotational barrier of propane about its C1–C2 bond.
e: Sight down C1–C2: the front carbon carries three hydrogens and the back carbon carries two hydrogens and a methyl. Eclipsing lines up three pairs, and only one of them involves the methyl — 1.4 + 1.0 + 1.0 = 3.4 kcal/mol, which is the measured barrier. The point of the per-interaction values is exactly this: you can price a conformer you have never seen.

q: In a Newman projection, the back atom's bonds are drawn from:
e: The front atom sits at the center (its three bonds radiate from the center dot), while the back atom is represented by the circle itself, so its bonds are drawn from the circle's edge.

q: The dihedral (torsion) angle in a Newman projection is measured between:
e: The dihedral angle describes the angular relationship, looking straight down the C-C bond, between a substituent on the front carbon and one on the back carbon.

q: In the staggered conformations of ethane, the dihedral angles between front and back hydrogens are 60 degrees, 180 degrees, and 300 degrees.
e: Staggered conformations space the front and back substituents as far apart as possible, giving dihedral angles of 60 degrees, 180 degrees, and 300 degrees around the full rotation.

q: The anti conformation about a C-C single bond corresponds to a dihedral angle of:
e: Anti means the two largest groups point in exactly opposite directions when viewed down the bond, which is a 180 degree dihedral angle.

q: The gauche conformation about a C-C single bond corresponds to a dihedral angle of approximately:
e: Gauche conformers are staggered but have the two reference groups only 60 degrees apart, rather than fully opposite as in the anti conformer.

q: In ethane, eclipsed conformations are always higher in energy than staggered conformations.
e: Eclipsing bonds forces electron pairs in the C-H sigma bonds closer together, raising energy through torsional strain, so every eclipsed form of ethane is less stable than every staggered form.

q: The higher energy of eclipsed ethane compared to staggered ethane is best attributed to:
e: Torsional strain. The modern account of it is hyperconjugation: in a staggered arrangement each filled C–H sigma orbital lines up with an empty C–H antibonding (sigma*) orbital on the neighboring carbon, which is worth real stabilization, and eclipsing destroys that alignment. Ethane's hydrogens are far too small to be bumping into each other, so nothing steric is involved.

q: Conformers interconvert so rapidly at room temperature that individual staggered or eclipsed forms generally cannot be isolated as separate pure compounds.
e: Rotation barriers around single C-C bonds are typically only a few kcal/mol, so at room temperature molecules rotate through all conformations far too quickly to separate them.

q: How many H-H eclipsing interactions exist in the fully eclipsed conformation of ethane?
e: Each of the three hydrogens on the front carbon lines up directly with one hydrogen on the back carbon, giving three separate eclipsing interactions.

q: For 1,2-dibromoethane, which conformation about the C–C bond is lowest in energy?
e: Anti and gauche are not words about methyl groups — they describe the dihedral angle between whichever pair you have nominated as the reference, conventionally the two largest. Here that is the two bromines, so the anti conformer at 180° puts them as far apart as rotation allows and is the minimum.

q: A molecule has four different substituents spread over the two carbons of a rotating bond. Can its conformations still be called anti and gauche?
e: Anti means the two reference groups are 180° apart and gauche means 60°. Which pair counts as the reference is a choice you announce, and the convention is to pick the two largest groups because those are the ones whose clash sets the energy. Say which pair you are tracking and the vocabulary works on any molecule.

q: The gauche conformation of butane is higher in energy than the anti conformation mainly because of steric (van der Waals) strain between the two methyl groups.
e: Even though gauche butane is staggered and free of torsional strain, the two methyl groups are close enough at 60 degrees apart to experience unfavorable steric crowding.

q: Ethane's rotational energy barrier (about 3 kcal/mol) arises purely from torsional strain with no steric component, whereas butane's anti-to-gauche energy gap i
e: Butane's methyl groups are much bulkier than ethane's hydrogens, so in addition to any torsional effects, gauche butane suffers extra steric strain that small hydrogens in ethane never experience.

q: Viewed down the C1-C2 bond of propane in a Newman projection, the back carbon (C2) bears which substituents?
e: C2 of propane is bonded to C1 (the front atom in this view), C3 (a methyl group), and two hydrogens, so in the Newman projection the back atom shows a methyl group and two hydrogens.

q: For n-butane, which ranking of the three staggered conformers from lowest to highest energy is correct?
e: Anti butane is the global energy minimum because the methyls are farthest apart, while the two gauche conformers are mirror-image-like and therefore equal in energy to each other, both higher than anti.

q: The two gauche conformations of butane have equal energy to one another.
e: The two gauche conformers are related by reflection (one has the methyl rotated +60 degrees, the other -60 degrees from anti) and are otherwise structurally equivalent, so they have identical energy.

q: 2-Methylbutane is sighted down its C2–C3 bond. How many staggered conformers are there, and how much gauche CH₃/CH₃ strain does the best one carry?
e: The front carbon (C2) carries two methyls and a hydrogen; the back carbon (C3) carries one methyl and two hydrogens. Rotating the back carbon gives three staggered arrangements. Putting the back methyl between the two front methyls gives two gauche CH₃/CH₃ pairs; the other two arrangements give one each. So the best conformers cost about 0.9 kcal/mol, and — unlike butane — there is no conformer with no gauche strain at all.

q: An eclipsed CH₃/CH₃ pair costs far more than three times an eclipsed H/H pair. What accounts for the excess?
e: Eclipsing costs torsional strain whatever the groups are. Two methyl groups brought to 0° are also pushed into each other through space, so they pay van der Waals repulsion as well. Eclipsed conformers carry steric strain on top of torsional strain, which is why the syn conformer is the highest point on butane's curve rather than merely another eclipse.

q: Over a full 360 degree rotation of the C2-C3 bond in butane, how many distinct energy maxima (eclipsed conformations) occur, and are they all the same height?
e: Rotating 360 degrees passes through three eclipsed arrangements; the one eclipsing both methyl groups is distinctly higher than the other two, which eclipse a methyl with a hydrogen and are equal to each other.

q: In a full 360 degree rotation profile of n-butane, the number of energy minima equals the number of energy maxima, but the minima are not all equal in energy to
e: There are three minima (anti plus two gauche) and three maxima (one methyl-methyl eclipsed plus two methyl-hydrogen eclipsed), but anti is lower than the two equal-energy gauche minima.

q: Why is the rotational barrier in ethane attributed almost entirely to torsional strain rather than steric strain?
e: Ethane's substituents are hydrogen atoms, which are small enough that at 0° they are still not pressing into one another — so there is no steric component to subtract. What remains is the loss of the hyperconjugative overlap that staggering allows, worth about 1 kcal/mol per eclipsing pair and 2.9 kcal/mol for all three. Butane's barrier is larger precisely because its methyl groups add a steric term that ethane has not got.

q: In the anti conformation of 2,3-dimethylbutane about the central C2-C3 bond, are there any gauche-type interactions present?
e: Each central carbon bears two methyl groups; fixing one pair anti to each other still leaves the remaining methyl groups positioned gauche to groups on the neighboring carbon, contributing extra strain beyond simple butane.

q: Butane is anti roughly 70% of the time at room temperature, even though the anti-to-gauche gap is only 0.9 kcal/mol. What does that show?
e: Populations follow ΔG = −RT ln K, and at room temperature RT is about 0.59 kcal/mol — so 0.9 kcal/mol is already more than one factor of e. Note the second ingredient: there are two gauche conformers and one anti, so the count works in gauche's favor, and anti still wins. Small energy differences buy large population differences.

q: As the substituents on a rotating C-C bond get larger (ethane to propane to butane), the eclipsed-conformation energy barriers generally:
e: Bulkier substituents add steric strain on top of the intrinsic torsional strain present even in ethane, so rotational barriers tend to rise as the groups attached to the rotating bond get larger.

q: A Newman projection carries CH₃, H and H on the front dot, and CH₂CH₃, H and H on the back circle. What compound is it, and which bond is being sighted down?
e: Read it back out as a chain. The front carbon is bonded to a methyl, two hydrogens and the back carbon; the back carbon is bonded to an ethyl, two hydrogens and the front carbon. Strung together that is CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ — pentane — and the bond joining the dot to the circle is C2–C3.

q: The energy penalty for rotating butane from anti into gauche comes entirely from torsional (eclipsing) strain, with no contribution from steric strain.
e: Anti and gauche butane are both staggered conformations, so there is no eclipsing (torsional) strain difference between them; the energy gap is due to steric strain from the methyl groups being closer together in the gauche form.

q: For 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane, rotation about the central C2-C3 bond has an unusually high barrier compared to simple butane mainly because:
e: With three methyl groups on each central carbon, there is no way to rotate the molecule into a conformation free of substantial steric clash, so all conformers, even the most staggered one, carry extra strain compared to butane.

q: Why is the chair conformation of cyclohexane the most stable?
e: The chair avoids angle strain (near-tetrahedral angles) and torsional strain (fully staggered), unlike boat or planar forms.

q: The boat conformation of cyclohexane is higher in energy than the chair mainly due to:
e: The boat has eclipsing interactions along its sides and a steric clash between the two "flagpole" hydrogens.

q: Besides chair and boat, what is another possible (higher-energy) conformation of cyclohexane?
e: The twist-boat is a slightly lower-energy variant of the boat that partially relieves the flagpole steric clash, but it’s still well above the chair in energy.

q: In the chair conformation of cyclohexane, the carbon-carbon-carbon bond angles are close to:
e: About 111 degrees — within two degrees of the ideal tetrahedral 109.5, so the angle strain is essentially nil. The chair is not quite perfect on angles; what makes it remarkable is that it gets that close while also staggering every ring bond, which a flat hexagon at 120 degrees cannot do.

q: Ring strain is not guessed from a drawing but measured. Which experiment gives it?
e: Burn a cycloalkane completely and it releases a measurable amount of energy. A strain-free CH₂ group releases 157.4 kcal/mol, so multiply that by the ring size to get what the ring ought to give. Anything it releases above that figure was energy stored in its strained bonds, and that excess is the ring strain quoted in the table.

q: In the boat conformation of cyclohexane, the main source of steric strain comes from:
e: The boat has several eclipsed C-H bonds along its sides (torsional strain) plus two hydrogens at the flagpole positions that point toward each other and clash sterically.

q: The half-chair conformation of cyclohexane is a stable, isolable conformer that molecules spend significant time resting in at room temperature.
e: The half-chair is actually a high-energy transition state along the ring-flip pathway, not a resting conformation; molecules pass through it only briefly while interconverting between other forms.

q: Ranking the main cyclohexane conformations from lowest to highest energy gives:
e: Chair is the global minimum; twist-boat is next lowest because twisting relieves some strain present in the regular boat; boat is higher still; and the half-chair, a transition state, is highest in energy.

q: Twisting the boat conformation into the twist-boat (skew-boat) conformation lowers its energy mainly by:
e: The twist partially un-eclipses the ring C-C bonds that were aligned in the regular boat and pulls the flagpole hydrogens slightly apart, so twist-boat sits lower in energy than boat.

q: The chair conformation of cyclohexane is planar.
e: The chair is a non-planar, puckered arrangement with alternating carbons above and below an average plane; this puckering is exactly what allows ideal tetrahedral angles and staggered bonds.

q: Which conformation of cyclohexane has essentially zero angle strain and zero torsional strain?
e: The chair holds its C–C–C angles at about 111 degrees, within two degrees of tetrahedral, and sighting down any ring bond gives a perfectly staggered Newman projection. Near-ideal angles and no eclipsing at the same time is what no smaller ring can manage.

q: Cyclopropane and cyclobutane have similar total ring strain (27.5 and 26.3 kcal/mol), but cyclobutane puckers while cyclopropane cannot. What does cyclobutane g
e: A planar cyclobutane would have 90° angles; the puckered one has about 88°, which is worse. It accepts that in exchange for partly staggering its C–H bonds. A molecule that trades angle strain away to buy torsional relief is telling you torsional strain is not a small effect — which is the lesson cyclohexane then applies at a ring size where it can escape both.

q: The energy difference between the chair and the boat conformation of cyclohexane is approximately:
e: Experimentally, the boat conformation sits roughly 6 to 7 kcal/mol above the chair, reflecting the substantial torsional and flagpole steric strain present in the boat.

q: Two isomers have the same formula, one noticeably more strained than the other. Which releases more heat on complete combustion?
e: Both isomers burn to the same products, so they finish at the same energy. The strained isomer starts higher up, and the heat released is the drop between start and finish — so it gives out more. This is exactly why 'which isomer has the higher heat of combustion' is answerable at all, and why a conformational difference of a kcal or two is a measurable quantity rather than a bookkeeping device.

q: Rank cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane and cyclohexane by total ring strain, highest first.
e: 27.5, 26.3, 6.2 and essentially 0 kcal/mol. The interesting feature is the cliff between four carbons and five: cyclopropane and cyclobutane are locked into badly wrong angles, while cyclopentane already has near-ideal 108° angles and only has eclipsing left to deal with. By six carbons a ring can pucker its way out of both problems at once.

q: The half-chair conformation of cyclohexane is best described as:
e: The half-chair is a saddle point on the conformational energy surface, the highest-energy structure molecules pass through while ring-flipping from one chair-related form to another.

q: The 'flagpole' hydrogens in the boat conformation of cyclohexane are located on which carbons?
e: The boat conformation has two carbons that point upward out of the main ring plane; the hydrogens on these two 'tip' carbons point toward each other and are called flagpole hydrogens.

q: Cycloheptane and cyclooctane carry 6.2 and 9.7 kcal/mol of strain even though their bond angles are close to ideal. Where does it come from?
e: Transannular means 'across the ring'. A seven- or eight-membered ring is loose enough for its two sides to fold toward each other and too tight for the hydrogens on those sides to get out of each other's way. Small rings are too taut to suffer it and rings of a dozen carbons and up are floppy enough to avoid it, which makes the medium rings the most strained sizes after the small ones.

q: A conformation of cyclohexane is described as a genuine but shallow energy minimum that a molecule briefly occupies. Which one is it?
e: A transition state is a peak: passed over in a single vibration and never occupied. The half-chair is one, and so is the symmetric boat, which sits between two twist-boats. The twist-boat itself is a dip — shallow, short-lived, but a real conformation. Knowing which of the four is a dip and which are peaks is the distinction the energy ladder is drawn to make.

q: The twist-boat conformation is lower in energy than the ordinary chair conformation of cyclohexane.
e: The chair remains the global energy minimum; twist-boat is only the lowest-energy member of the boat family, still several kcal/mol above the chair.

q: Why does twisting the boat conformation into a twist-boat actually lower its energy rather than raise it?
e: The twist partially un-eclipses ring bonds and separates the flagpole hydrogens, producing a net stabilization relative to the symmetric boat, even though a slight new strain is introduced by the twist itself.

q: Cyclopentane's angles in a planar form would be 108°, essentially ideal, yet it still puckers into an envelope. Why?
e: Angle strain is not cyclopentane's problem — 108° is within a degree and a half of tetrahedral. Planarity is: every adjacent C–H pair would be eclipsed. Puckering bends the angles down to around 104°, which is cheap, and buys a large amount of torsional relief, which is not. The residual 6.2 kcal/mol is what is left over after that compromise.

q: In one complete chair-to-chair ring flip pathway (going through the boat family), how many half-chair transition states are crossed?
e: The ring flip proceeds chair to half-chair to twist-boat to half-chair to chair, so two distinct half-chair transition states are crossed in a single flip.

q: The pattern of eclipsed ring C-C bonds in the boat conformation is identical to the pattern found in the half-chair transition state.
e: The boat and half-chair are distinct geometries with different numbers and arrangements of eclipsed bonds and ring puckering; they are not interchangeable descriptions of the same structure.

q: Why is unsubstituted cyclohexane essentially free of ring strain, unlike cyclopropane or cyclopentane?
e: The chair's puckering is a geometric solution unique to a six-membered ring that allows perfect bond angles with no eclipsing, whereas smaller rings like cyclopropane are forced into angle strain and cyclopentane into some torsional strain regardless of puckering.

q: A student argues that cyclohexane is strain-free because six-membered rings are simply immune to strain. What is wrong with that?
e: A planar cyclohexane would have 120° angles and twelve eclipsed C–H pairs — a great deal of strain. What is special about six carbons is that a pucker exists which fixes both at once: 111° angles and a perfectly staggered Newman projection down every ring bond. The strain is absent because of a shape the molecule adopts, not because of an exemption it enjoys.

q: The interconversion pathway between the two chair forms of cyclohexane proceeds exclusively through the symmetric boat conformation, never through a twist-boat.
e: The actual lowest-energy pathway passes predominantly through twist-boat intermediates, since twist-boat is more stable than the symmetric boat; the plain boat is a higher-energy, less-traveled point on the overall surface.

q: At room temperature, approximately what fraction of cyclohexane molecules exist in a boat or twist-boat conformation at any instant, compared to the chair?
e: Because the chair is several kcal/mol more stable than any boat-family conformation, the equilibrium population strongly favors the chair, leaving only a tiny fraction in higher-energy forms at any given moment.

q: Angle strain is the dominant reason the boat conformation of cyclohexane is higher in energy than the chair.
e: Both chair and boat keep bond angles reasonably close to tetrahedral; the boat's extra energy comes mainly from torsional strain (eclipsed bonds) and flagpole steric strain, not from angle strain.

q: Compared to cyclohexane, cycloheptane and cyclooctane generally retain some residual strain even in their best conformations. What does this suggest about the c
e: The chair's near-total absence of both angle and torsional strain is a special geometric outcome of the six-membered ring; larger and smaller rings typically cannot fully escape some strain in any conformation they adopt.

q: In a cyclohexane chair, equatorial substituents point:
e: Equatorial positions point outward around the ring’s perimeter, avoiding the 1,3-diaxial interactions that axial groups face.

q: A bulky substituent on cyclohexane is most stable in which position?
e: Equatorial placement avoids steric clashes (1,3-diaxial interactions) with other axial substituents, so bulky groups prefer equatorial.

q: A chair carries a methyl that is axial and pointing up on C1. Where must a second substituent sit to be cis to it and equatorial?
e: Cis means the same face, so the second group must also point up. Axial directions alternate, so C2's axial points down — which means C2's equatorial bond is the one angled up. Putting the group there makes it up (hence cis) and equatorial at the same time. This is the whole of the 'up is not axial' trap: the face and the label are two separate questions.

q: In a cyclohexane chair, axial bonds point:
e: Axial positions alternate, pointing up on one carbon and down on the next as you go around the ring, all roughly parallel to the ring's main symmetry axis.

q: Methylcyclohexane has an A-value of 1.7 kcal/mol. Using RT ≈ 0.59 kcal/mol at 298 K, what equatorial:axial ratio does that predict?
e: K = e^(ΔG/RT) = e^(1.7/0.59) ≈ 18, which is about 95:5. The relationship is exponential, which is why it is worth running once: tripling the energy gap to tert-butyl's 4.9 multiplies the ratio by more than two hundred rather than by three.

q: A substituent with an A-value of 4.9 kcal/mol is better than 99.9% equatorial. What do chemists use that for?
e: A tert-butyl group does not lock the ring in principle — the flip barrier is barely changed. What it does is make the other chair so sparsely populated that the molecule is, for practical purposes, one conformer. Much of what is known about axial versus equatorial reactivity was measured on rings anchored this way.

q: Axial bonds alternate pointing up and down as you move around the cyclohexane ring from carbon to carbon.
e: Because the ring carbons alternate slightly above and below the average plane, their axial bonds alternate direction, up on one carbon, down on the next, all the way around.

q: In unsubstituted cyclohexane, every ring carbon bears exactly one axial hydrogen and one equatorial hydrogen.
e: Since cyclohexane is CH2 repeated six times, each carbon's two hydrogens occupy the one axial and one equatorial position available on that carbon.

q: An axial substituent on cyclohexane generally experiences more steric strain than the same substituent in the equatorial position because of:
e: An axial group points toward axial hydrogens (or groups) on the carbons three atoms away around the ring (1 and 3 relationship), creating steric clashes called 1,3-diaxial interactions.

q: A 1,3-diaxial interaction is strain between an axial substituent on one ring carbon and substituents on which other ring carbon(s)?
e: Counting around the ring, an axial group at C1 points toward the axial substituents at C3 and C5, which are close enough in space to clash with it.

q: In unsubstituted cyclohexane, axial and equatorial positions are equal in energy because the ring is unsubstituted and symmetric.
e: With only hydrogens attached, flipping the ring just swaps which hydrogens are labeled axial versus equatorial on an otherwise identical molecule, so there is no energy difference.

q: Equatorial C-H (or C-substituent) bonds point roughly:
e: Equatorial bonds radiate outward around the 'equator' of the ring, lying much closer to the average ring plane than the axial bonds do.

q: For methylcyclohexane at equilibrium, approximately what percentage of molecules have the methyl group equatorial?
e: The methyl group's modest A-value (about 1.7 kcal/mol) corresponds to roughly a 95:5 equatorial-to-axial ratio at room temperature, strongly favoring equatorial but not completely excluding axial.

q: Equatorial methylcyclohexane predominates over the axial form mainly because:
e: When axial, the methyl group clashes sterically with the axial hydrogens at the 3 and 5 positions; moving it equatorial removes most of that strain, making the equatorial conformer more stable.

q: Chlorine is a larger and heavier atom than carbon, yet –Cl has an A-value of about 0.5 against –CH₃'s 1.7. What does that tell you A-value is measuring?
e: A halogen is a smooth sphere sitting at the end of a long C–X bond, so it reaches into the 1,3-diaxial space very little. A methyl group is lighter but sticks three hydrogens out sideways at a shorter distance. A-value tracks how much room a group demands near the ring, which is why the ordering follows shape rather than atomic weight.

q: Substituents with larger A-values show a stronger preference for the equatorial position.
e: The A-value is defined as the free energy preference for equatorial over axial, so by definition a larger A-value means a stronger equatorial preference.

q: Which substituent has the larger A-value (stronger equatorial preference): methyl, or isopropyl?
e: Isopropyl is bulkier than methyl, so its 1,3-diaxial clashes when axial are more severe, giving it a larger A-value and a stronger preference for the equatorial position.

q: The steric strain in a 1,3-diaxial interaction is conceptually most analogous to which acyclic interaction?
e: Geometrically, an axial substituent and an axial hydrogen three carbons away around the ring are positioned much like the two methyl groups in gauche butane, so the strain is often compared to a gauche interaction.

q: Isopropyl scores 2.2 and tert-butyl 4.9 — a jump far bigger than the one from methyl (1.7) to isopropyl. What causes it?
e: An axial isopropyl can turn its lone hydrogen toward the 1,3-diaxial space and keep both its methyls pointing away. A tert-butyl group has no hydrogen on that carbon: whichever way it rotates, a whole methyl is aimed into the ring. The cliff between them is about what a group can do to get out of the way, not about how big it is on paper.

q: Why is a 1,3-diaxial interaction described as the ring's version of gauche butane?
e: An axial group on C1 and an axial group on C3 are on the same face and about the same distance apart as the two methyls of gauche butane. The repulsion is identical in kind. The difference is that butane can rotate out of it and a ring cannot: the geometry is held, which is why the cost shows up as a fixed conformational preference rather than a passing arrangement.

q: An axial substituent on C1 clashes with the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5. How many such interactions does it have, and how does that relate to its A-value?
e: Only C3 and C5 carry axial positions on the same face as C1, so there are two clashes, one with each. A methyl's A-value of 1.7 is close to two gauche-butane interactions at about 0.9 each, which is the arithmetic behind the number rather than a coincidence.

q: Fluorine substituted on cyclohexane has a larger A-value (stronger equatorial preference) than a methyl group.
e: Fluorine is a small atom with a short C-F bond, so its 1,3-diaxial clash is mild; its A-value (roughly 0.2 to 0.3 kcal/mol) is considerably smaller than methyl's (about 1.7 kcal/mol).

q: Ranking fluorine, methyl, and tert-butyl substituents on cyclohexane by increasing A-value (increasing equatorial preference) gives:
e: A-value scales roughly with steric bulk: small fluorine has the weakest equatorial preference, methyl is intermediate, and the very bulky tert-butyl group has by far the strongest equatorial preference.

q: Why does the tert-butyl group have such an unusually large A-value compared to a single methyl group?
e: Because tert-butyl is essentially three methyl groups bundled on one carbon, placing it axial would force multiple severe steric clashes simultaneously, vastly exceeding the strain from a single axial methyl.

q: Equatorial substituents on cyclohexane experience absolutely no steric interactions with the rest of the ring.
e: Equatorial substituents still have some gauche-type interactions with neighboring ring bonds; they simply avoid the much larger 1,3-diaxial clashes that axial substituents face, so their strain is reduced, not zero.

q: Which statement best explains, in general terms, why the equatorial position is less strained than the axial position for most substituents?
e: Geometrically, the equatorial orientation directs a substituent away from other ring atoms, while the axial orientation aims it straight at the axial groups on the 1,3-related carbons, which is the structural root of the steric difference.

q: If a hypothetical substituent had an A-value of 0 kcal/mol, the predicted equilibrium ratio of equatorial to axial conformers would be approximately:
e: An A-value of zero means there is no free energy preference between the two positions, which corresponds to an equal, 50:50 population at equilibrium.

q: The total 1,3-diaxial strain on an axial substituent is often compared to roughly two gauche-butane-type interactions, since the substituent clashes with axial
e: Because an axial substituent experiences 1,3-diaxial clashes with both the C3 and C5 positions simultaneously, its total strain is often approximated as about twice that of a single gauche interaction.

q: Which of these would you expect to have the largest A-value?
e: The ordering follows the room a group demands beside the ring. Cyanide is a thin rod pointing straight out and scores about 0.2; bromide is a smooth sphere on a long bond, about 0.5; hydroxyl is 0.9. tert-Butyl at 4.9 is in a different class, because it cannot avoid pushing a methyl group into the 1,3-diaxial space whichever way it turns.

q: An axial chlorine substituent on cyclohexane has a noticeably smaller A-value than an axial methyl group, even though chlorine is a larger atom than carbon. Wha
e: Even though chlorine is a larger atom, its longer carbon-halogen bond moves it farther from the ring, and its roughly spherical shape clashes less than the three hydrogens of a methyl group, giving it a smaller A-value than expected from atomic size alone.

q: During a cyclohexane ring flip, axial substituents become:
e: A ring flip interconverts the two chair forms — every axial position becomes equatorial and vice versa.

q: After a ring flip, does the molecule’s relative stereochemistry (cis/trans) change?
e: Ring flips are conformational changes, not bond-breaking — cis/trans relationships (configuration) are preserved; only which substituents are axial vs. equatorial changes.

q: For a monosubstituted cyclohexane (one substituent), a ring flip changes the energy of the molecule unless the substituent is:
e: For a single non-hydrogen substituent, axial and equatorial chairs differ in energy (the equatorial is lower); only when the "substituent" is H (unsubstituted cyclohexane) are both chair forms identical in energy.

q: A chair has a bromine axial and pointing up on C1 and a methyl equatorial and pointing up on C3. After a correct ring flip, what are they?
e: A flip swaps axial for equatorial on every carbon and leaves every group on the face it was already on. Both groups started up, so both finish up; both labels reverse. If your redrawn chair changes both the label and the face, you have drawn a different compound; if it changes neither, you rotated the page instead of flipping the ring.

q: A ring flip is a conformational change, not a configurational change, meaning no covalent bonds are broken.
e: Ring flipping only involves rotation about existing sigma bonds to reshape the ring; it never breaks or forms any covalent bonds, unlike a configurational change such as a reaction.

q: Why can a ring flip happen at all without breaking any bonds?
e: Every bond in the ring is a sigma bond, and sigma bonds rotate. Turning them in a coordinated way carries the ring through the half-chair and twist-boat shapes and into the other chair, with the same atoms bonded to the same atoms throughout. That is what makes a flip a conformational change rather than a reaction.

q: When a ring flip occurs, what happens to whether a given substituent is on the 'up' face or the 'down' face of the ring?
e: A substituent's up/down face assignment is a fixed structural (configurational) feature of the molecule; the ring flip changes only whether that same substituent happens to be axial or equatorial in the new chair.

q: Ring flips occur rapidly at room temperature, interconverting the two chair forms many times per second.
e: With a barrier of only about 10–11 kcal/mol, a cyclohexane ring flips roughly 100,000 times a second at room temperature — about a million times slower than an ethane bond rotation, and still far too fast for the two chairs to be seen separately until the sample is cooled to around −90 °C.

q: The high-energy structure that a molecule must pass through partway along a ring flip is the:
e: As the ring flips, it must pass over an energy barrier corresponding to the half-chair geometry before relaxing into the twist-boat and eventually the other chair.

q: For unsubstituted cyclohexane, a ring flip produces a conformer that is identical in energy to the starting conformer.
e: Because all six ring carbons bear only hydrogens, flipping just relabels which hydrogens are axial and which are equatorial on an otherwise indistinguishable structure, so there is no energy change.

q: The ring-flip barrier is about 10–11 kcal/mol against 2.9 for rotating ethane. Roughly how do the two rates compare at room temperature?
e: Rate falls off exponentially with barrier height, so the extra 8 kcal/mol costs roughly five orders of magnitude: ethane spins at 10¹⁰–10¹¹ per second and a ring flips at about 10⁵. A million times slower, and still far too fast to catch — which is why cyclohexane has to be cooled to about −90 °C before NMR sees the two kinds of hydrogen separately.

q: For trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, a ring flip converts the diequatorial arrangement of the two methyl groups into:
e: In the trans-1,4 pattern both methyl groups flip together from equatorial to axial (or vice versa), so the ring flip swaps a diequatorial conformer for a diaxial one.

q: For cis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, a ring flip converts an axial/equatorial arrangement of the two methyl groups into:
e: In the cis-1,4 pattern, one methyl is always axial while the other is equatorial; flipping swaps which carbon has which, but the overall strain, and therefore the energy, stays the same.

q: For which disubstitution pattern does a ring flip convert a diequatorial arrangement into a diaxial one?
e: A flip always reverses both labels, but only some patterns put both groups in the same column to start with. On 1,2 and 1,4 carbons the axial directions are opposite, so a trans (opposite-face) pair lands both equatorial or both axial. On 1,3 carbons the axial directions match, so it is cis that does. Work out the faces first and the pattern falls out of the drawing.

q: For trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, which conformer is more stable at equilibrium?
e: Placing both methyl groups equatorial avoids all the 1,3-diaxial strain that the diaxial alternative would create, making the diequatorial conformer strongly favored.

q: Ring flipping never changes whether two substituents on a ring are cis or trans to each other.
e: Cis/trans relationships are configurational, fixed by which face of the ring each substituent is attached to; a ring flip only changes axial/equatorial positions, never the underlying configuration.

q: Which disubstitution pattern gives two ring-flip conformers that are degenerate (equal in energy) when the two substituents are identical?
e: Cis-1,4-disubstitution always places one substituent axial and one equatorial; flipping just swaps which carbon carries which role, leaving the overall energy unchanged when the two groups are identical.

q: What is the correct order of conformations passed through during one complete ring flip from one chair to the other?
e: The full lowest-energy pathway goes from chair up over a half-chair transition state, down into the twist-boat, back up over a second half-chair, and finally down into the other chair.

q: For a monosubstituted cyclohexane where the substituent is not hydrogen, why does a ring flip change the molecule's overall energy?
e: With any substituent bulkier than hydrogen, the axial conformer suffers 1,3-diaxial strain that the equatorial conformer avoids, so the two ring-flip conformers are no longer equal in energy.

q: Why are the two chairs of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane equal in energy, while those of the trans isomer are not?
e: Cis on adjacent carbons means one group is up and the other is up too — and since the axial directions alternate, one of them has to be axial whichever chair you pick. Flipping just swaps which one pays, so the two chairs tie. Trans can put both equatorial in one chair and both axial in the other, which is a real difference of about 2.5 kcal/mol.

q: For 1,1-dimethylcyclohexane, a ring flip leaves the molecule's overall energy unchanged because the two methyl groups on that single carbon simply trade axial a
e: Since both substituents are identical methyl groups on the same carbon, one is always axial and the other equatorial; flipping swaps which one is which but keeps the total strain, and thus the energy, the same.

q: Trans-1,4-di-tert-butylcyclohexane exists almost entirely in a single, 'locked' conformation because:
e: Because both tert-butyl groups must move together on a ring flip, the only alternative to the diequatorial conformer is a diaxial one with two extremely bulky groups clashing severely, making that conformer vanishingly rare.

q: For cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, a ring flip converts the ax,eq arrangement of the two methyl groups into:
e: Cis-1,2-disubstitution always gives one axial and one equatorial methyl; flipping swaps which ring carbon carries which role, producing a conformer of identical energy to the first.

q: trans-1,4-Di-tert-butylcyclohexane sits almost entirely in one conformation. Which, and why?
e: Trans on 1,4 carbons allows both groups equatorial in one chair, and the flip would make both axial. Two axial tert-butyl groups is about 4.9 + 4.9, far more than thermal energy will pay for. The ring still flips — the barrier is unchanged — but the other chair is never meaningfully populated, which is the conformational-anchor trick in its strongest form.

q: You redraw a chair, and in the new drawing every substituent has kept both its axial/equatorial label and its up/down face. What happened?
e: A genuine flip pushes the raised end of the chair down and the lowered end up, so every axial/equatorial label reverses while every face stays put. If nothing reversed, the ring is in the same conformation and you have only turned the picture. The test is worth doing every time: exactly one of the two properties should have changed.

q: In one complete ring flip from one chair form of cyclohexane to the other, how many separate half-chair transition states must be crossed?
e: The flip passes chair to half-chair to twist-boat to a second half-chair to the other chair, crossing two distinct half-chair energy barriers along the way.

q: The twist-boat conformation encountered during a ring flip is a lower-energy intermediate than the symmetric boat conformation.
e: Twist-boat relieves some of the torsional and flagpole strain present in the symmetric boat, so the ring flip pathway favors passing through twist-boat rather than lingering in the higher-energy plain boat.

q: For cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, a ring flip converts the diequatorial arrangement of the two methyl groups into:
e: Cis-1,3-disubstitution allows both substituents to be equatorial together in one chair; ring flipping moves them both to axial together in the other chair, just as with trans-1,4 and trans-1,2 patterns.

q: When a monosubstituted cyclohexane with a single bulky substituent reaches conformational equilibrium, which ring-flip direction (which chair) is favored?
e: Because axial substituents suffer 1,3-diaxial strain that scales with their size, the equilibrium strongly favors whichever chair places a bulky group equatorial, minimizing that strain.

q: Does adding a bulky substituent such as tert-butyl slow the rate at which a cyclohexane ring flips?
e: A large A-value says how much the two chairs differ in energy, not how high the hill between them is. tert-Butylcyclohexane flips at much the same rate as cyclohexane itself; it simply spends almost all its time on one side. Confusing a population effect with a rate effect is the standard trap here.

q: For a disubstituted cyclohexane, the most stable chair conformation is generally the one with:
e: Placing bulky groups equatorial minimizes 1,3-diaxial strain, giving the lowest-energy conformation.

q: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane: add up both chairs and give the preference.
e: The diaxial chair carries 1.7 + 1.7 = 3.4. The diequatorial chair carries no axial penalty, but its two methyls sit on adjacent carbons and are gauche to each other, worth 0.9. The difference is 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5, against a measured 2.7. Adding A-values alone would have said 3.4; the gauche correction is what brings it into line.

q: When a cyclohexane has two substituents in a 1,2-relationship that are cis to each other, they are found in which combination of positions in the lower energy c
e: For 1,2-disubstitution, cis substituents are one axial/one equatorial (and trans are both axial or both equatorial) — the reverse of the 1,3 relationship.

q: cis-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane. Which chair dominates, and roughly by how much?
e: On 1,3 carbons the axial directions match, so a cis pair goes both-equatorial in one chair and both-axial in the other. The diaxial chair pays two CH₃/H diaxial contacts plus the direct CH₃/CH₃ clash between the two axial methyls, which is worth about 3.7 on its own — roughly 5.4 in total. Simple A-value addition would have predicted only 3.4, so this is the case where the direct-interaction correction matters most.

q: For trans-1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane bearing two different alkyl groups, the preferred arrangement, when possible, is:
e: Trans-1,4 substitution geometrically allows both substituents to be equatorial simultaneously, which is almost always the lower-energy, preferred arrangement.

q: You are given a wedge/dash hexagon with a methyl on a wedge at C1 and an ethyl on a dash at C4. What is the first thing to write down?
e: A wedge comes up out of the page and a hash goes down behind it, so this pair is on opposite faces: trans. Faces are what survives the ring flip and what decides whether both groups can be equatorial at all, so they are recorded first. Only once the groups are placed on their faces in a numbered chair do the A-values have anything to act on.

q: cis-1-tert-Butyl-4-methylcyclohexane. Which chair wins?
e: Cis on 1,4 carbons forces one group axial whichever chair you pick, so the only question is which one pays. Axial tert-butyl costs 4.9; axial methyl costs 1.7; the difference is 3.2 in favor of axialising the methyl. The bulkier group takes equatorial and the smaller absorbs the cost — and the answer comes out of the arithmetic rather than out of a preference for tert-butyl.

q: Why does the pattern reverse between 1,2 and 1,3 rings — trans gives diequatorial on 1,2, but cis gives it on 1,3?
e: Up, down, up, down round the ring. Adjacent carbons therefore have opposite axial directions, so a pair on opposite faces (trans) lands in matching columns. Carbons two apart have the same axial direction, so it is the same-face pair (cis) that matches. Draw the chair and number it and you never have to remember which is which.

q: For trans-1,2-disubstituted cyclohexane, the preferred arrangement, when possible, is:
e: As with trans-1,4, the trans-1,2 relationship allows both substituents to be equatorial together, which is normally the more stable choice.

q: A ring carries an OH (A-value 0.9) and a tert-butyl (4.9) trans on carbons 1 and 4. Predict the dominant conformer and the preference.
e: Trans on 1,4 carbons allows both groups equatorial in one chair, so it does. The flip would put both axial at a cost of 0.9 + 4.9 = 5.8, and 1,4 groups are too far apart for a direct correction. When a diequatorial chair is available the arithmetic barely needs doing — the work is in deciding whether the pattern allows it.

q: When only one of two substituents on a cyclohexane ring can occupy the equatorial position, the general rule is that the conformation chosen places:
e: Because a bulkier group (higher A-value) suffers a larger energy penalty when forced axial, the lowest-energy conformer is the one that places the substituent with the greater A-value in the equatorial position.

q: For cis-1-methyl-4-tert-butylcyclohexane, the most stable conformation places:
e: The cis-1,4 pattern forces one group axial; since tert-butyl's A-value vastly exceeds methyl's, the lower-energy conformer puts the much bulkier tert-butyl group equatorial and accepts methyl axial instead.

q: For trans-1-methyl-4-tert-butylcyclohexane, the most stable conformation places:
e: Because the trans-1,4 relationship allows both groups to be equatorial simultaneously, and both substituents prefer equatorial, this diequatorial conformer is overwhelmingly the most stable.

q: On a cyclohexane ring, which pair of substituents on adjacent carbons can be anti-periplanar to each other?
e: The chair fixes the angles: adjacent equatorial groups are about 60° apart and an axial/equatorial pair about 60° as well. Only the two axial positions on adjacent carbons — one pointing up, one pointing down, because axial directions alternate — reach the 180° that anti-periplanar means. That single geometric fact is what makes conformational analysis predictive about elimination.

q: The chair conformer with the lower total A-value contribution from its axial substituents is the more stable, lower-energy conformer.
e: Since A-values approximate the strain penalty of having a given group axial, the conformation with less total axial strain corresponds to the more stable structure.

q: For cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, the lowest energy conformation places the two methyl groups:
e: The cis-1,3 relationship is the pattern that geometrically permits both substituents to sit equatorial simultaneously, and that diequatorial form is indeed the most stable.

q: For trans-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, the lowest energy conformation necessarily places the two methyl groups:
e: Because trans-1,3 substitution cannot achieve a diequatorial arrangement, both chair conformers have one methyl axial and one equatorial, and the molecule is forced to accept some axial strain either way.

q: Conformational analysis of a polysubstituted cyclohexane generally proceeds by identifying, for each of the two possible chairs, which substituents end up axial
e: This systematic approach, summing A-value-based penalties for axial groups in each chair, is the standard method for predicting which conformer of a multiply-substituted cyclohexane will dominate.

q: If the two chair conformers of a disubstituted cyclohexane happen to have equal total axial-substituent strain penalties, the predicted equilibrium population i
e: When neither conformer has a net strain advantage over the other, there is no free energy difference driving the equilibrium toward one side, giving an approximately equal population.

q: For cis-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane, the two interconverting chair conformers place the ethyl and methyl groups in opposite ax/eq roles from each other. Which c
e: Since ethyl has a somewhat larger A-value than methyl, putting the bulkier ethyl group equatorial (and accepting methyl axial instead) minimizes the total axial strain, making that conformer more stable.

q: Between the two stereoisomers of 1-methyl-4-tert-butylcyclohexane, which one is, at its most stable conformation, lower in overall energy: cis, or trans?
e: The trans isomer enjoys a genuinely diequatorial lowest-energy conformer, avoiding all 1,3-diaxial strain, whereas the cis isomer is stuck with at least one substituent axial no matter which chair it adopts.

q: Using approximate A-values (methyl about 1.7 kcal/mol), the energy difference between the diequatorial and diaxial conformers of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane i
e: The diaxial chair carries two axial methyls: 1.7 + 1.7 = 3.4. The diequatorial chair carries no axial penalty, but its two methyls are on adjacent carbons and therefore gauche to each other, worth 0.9. So the preference is 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5, against a measured 2.7. Adding A-values alone overstates it, and the gauche correction is what closes the gap.

q: Why does cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane show a much smaller energy difference between its two chair conformers than trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane does?
e: For cis-1,2, both interconverting chairs are ax,eq combinations of roughly comparable strain, so the energy gap between them is small; for trans-1,2, one chair is diequatorial (very favorable) and the other diaxial (very unfavorable), producing a much larger gap.

q: A student concludes that any disubstituted cyclohexane can reach a diequatorial conformation. Where does that go wrong?
e: Whether both groups can be equatorial at once is fixed before any energy is considered: it depends on the two faces and the two positions, and a ring flip cannot change either. cis-1,2, cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 rings have one group axial in both chairs, so the question becomes which group pays rather than whether anything has to.

q: Which general rule correctly summarizes when a diequatorial conformation is geometrically available for a disubstituted cyclohexane?
e: The geometric rule is that trans works for the 1,2 and 1,4 relationships while cis works for the 1,3 relationship; the opposite stereochemistry in each case is always forced into a mixed axial/equatorial arrangement.

q: For a 1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane bearing an OH group (small A-value) and a tert-butyl group (very large A-value) in a trans relationship, the predicted domin
e: Because trans-1,4 substitution permits both substituents to be equatorial at once, and both OH and tert-butyl individually prefer equatorial, the diequatorial conformer is strongly favored with no conflict between them.

q: For the same OH and tert-butyl substituents but in a cis-1,4 relationship, the predicted dominant conformer places:
e: Since cis-1,4 substitution forces one group axial, the molecule 'sacrifices' the position of the substituent with the smaller A-value (OH) to keep the much bulkier, higher-A-value tert-butyl group equatorial.

q: In determining the most stable conformer of a polysubstituted cyclohexane, only the single largest substituent matters, and all smaller substituents can be igno
e: While the bulkiest substituent's A-value often dominates the decision, every substituent contributes some strain energy when axial, so a rigorous analysis sums the contributions of all substituents rather than ignoring the smaller ones.

q: What is the structural reason the axial conformer of tert-butylcyclohexane is so strongly disfavored, in terms of the number and severity of steric clashes?
e: Because tert-butyl presents three methyl groups on one carbon, forcing it axial creates multiple simultaneous 1,3-diaxial clashes rather than just one, which is why its A-value is so much larger than a simple alkyl group's.

q: Predicting relative conformer stability using A-values gives only an approximate, not perfectly exact, result because the method does not account for every poss
e: A-values are empirically averaged steric parameters; real molecules can have additional effects (electronic, hydrogen bonding, or unusual geometries) not captured by a simple sum of standard A-values, so predictions are approximate.

q: What condition is required for an alkane to react with a halogen?
e: Br2 and an alkane in a dark flask do nothing at all. The light or heat is what initiates the chain, which is why bromine water distinguishes an alkene from an alkane.

q: How does the halogen bond break in the initiation step?
e: Homolysis sends one electron to each atom, giving two neutral radicals rather than a cation and an anion.

q: What kind of arrow shows the movement of a single electron?
e: Two fishhooks are needed to break one bond, one for each electron. Mixing arrow types is the commonest drawing error here.

q: How do you tell which stage of a chain a step belongs to?
e: Up from zero is initiation, unchanged is propagation, down to zero is termination. The product is not what distinguishes them.

q: A step consumes one radical and produces one. Which stage?
e: The count is unchanged, so the chain can go round again. This is propagation even when the product appears in this very step.

q: Chlorination of propane. Six primary hydrogens, two secondary, and chlorine prefers secondary over primary by about 4 to 1 per hydrogen. What is the product rat
e: Multiply count by rate. Primary: 6 × 1 = 6. Secondary: 2 × 4 = 8. Total 14, so 8/14 ≈ 57% secondary and 6/14 ≈ 43% primary. The four-to-one selectivity nearly cancels against three times as many primary hydrogens, which is why chlorination of propane is a mixture you would have to separate.

q: Why is termination rare while the reaction runs?
e: Two radicals have to collide, and there are very few in the flask at any moment. A single initiation can turn over thousands of molecules first.

q: What is the order of radical stability?
e: Radicals follow the same order as carbocations, and for the same reason: hyperconjugation from neighboring C-H bonds into the half-filled orbital.

q: Per hydrogen, bromination prefers tertiary over primary by roughly what factor?
e: Bromine is highly selective. Chlorine's corresponding figure is only about 5, which is why chlorination gives mixtures.

q: 2-Methylpropane has nine primary hydrogens and one tertiary. Chlorine prefers tertiary over primary by about 5 to 1 per hydrogen. Which product dominates?
e: Primary: 9 × 1 = 9. Tertiary: 1 × 5 = 5. Total 14, so the primary chloride is 9/14 ≈ 64% — the major product comes from the less stable radical. Run the same substrate with bromine (1600 to 1) and the tertiary bromide is about 99%. One molecule, two halogens, opposite answers: that is the whole selectivity story in one calculation.

q: Why is the less reactive bromine radical the more selective one?
e: Abstraction by bromine is endothermic — a C–H at about 98 kcal/mol is traded for an H–Br at 87.5 — so by the Hammond postulate the transition state resembles the products. The radical is essentially fully formed at the top of the barrier, so every kcal/mol of its stability is already showing up in the rate.

q: Bond dissociation energies: a secondary C–H is about 98 kcal/mol, H–Cl is 103 and H–Br is 87.5. What do those numbers say about the two abstraction steps?
e: ΔH is the bond broken minus the bond made. For chlorine, 98 − 103 = −5, downhill. For bromine, 98 − 87.5 = +10.5, uphill. By the Hammond postulate the downhill step has an early, reactant-like transition state where the radical has barely formed, and the uphill one has a late, radical-like transition state where the radical's stability is already priced in — which is exactly the selectivity difference.

q: A radical reaction creates a new stereocenter. What is the outcome?
e: The carbon radical is essentially planar with its electron in a p orbital, so the halogen arrives on either face equally. No conditions make this enantioselective.

q: Propane gives roughly even amounts of two chlorination products. Why?
e: Six primary hydrogens at rate 1 against two secondary at about 4 gives 6 to 8 — close to even, because the counts nearly offset the modest selectivity.

q: How many different monochlorination products can butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, give?
e: Count sets of equivalent hydrogens, not carbons. The two end methyls are equivalent to each other and the two middle CH₂ groups are equivalent to each other, so there are two sets and therefore two products: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane. Finding the sets first is half the marks in any 'how many products' question.

q: Which reagent is used for allylic bromination?
e: N-bromosuccinimide releases bromine slowly and keeps its concentration permanently low.

q: Why does NBS give substitution rather than addition?
e: Adding Br2 to an alkene is faster than the radical chain, but addition needs a reasonable Br2 concentration and the chain does not. Starve it and substitution wins.

q: Why is an allylic hydrogen unusually easy to abstract?
e: The unpaired electron is delocalized across the pi system, which makes the abstraction much easier than the substitution pattern alone would suggest.

q: Allylic bromination often gives two products. Why?
e: Bromine can end up at either end of the delocalized system. Drawing both resonance forms of the radical is how you predict the second product.

q: HBr plus peroxides adds to an alkene with which regiochemistry?
e: The peroxide starts a radical chain, so a bromine radical adds first rather than a proton.

q: Why do peroxides flip HBr addition to anti-Markovnikov?
e: The first species to add is no longer a proton seeking the better carbocation, but a bromine radical seeking the more stable carbon radical — which puts Br on the other carbon.

q: Which of these steps is NOT a termination step?
e: Count radicals across each step. The three terminations go from two radicals to none. The odd one out starts with one radical and ends with one — it consumes a carbon radical and hands back a bromine radical, so the chain carries on. It makes the product, which is exactly why it gets mislabeled; the stage is read off the radical count and never off the product.

q: Bromine water is decolorized by a compound with a double bond but not by an alkane. What is the difference?
e: Radical halogenation of an alkane has to be started, and in a dark flask at room temperature nothing initiates it. A double bond reacts with bromine directly, with no initiation step, which is why the test works. The reaction behind that is taught in the Alkenes & Alkynes chapter — here it matters only as the reason the light in these conditions is not decoration.

q: A step in your radical mechanism produces a charged species. What does that mean?
e: Radical steps move single electrons and give neutral species. A charge means a pair of electrons moved, which is a different mechanism.

q: Fluorine and iodine are not used for radical halogenation of alkanes. What rules each out?
e: It is the same ΔH arithmetic. H–F is 136 kcal/mol, so abstraction by F• is downhill by nearly 40 — unselective to the point of uselessness and often explosive. H–I is only 71, so abstraction by I• is uphill by about 27, a barrier too high to cross at any workable temperature. Chlorine and bromine sit in the narrow window between the two.

q: You need to install a bromine at the single tertiary position of 2-methylpropane, cleanly. Which conditions, and what result do you expect?
e: Bromine is the selective halogen: 1600 to 1 for tertiary over primary per hydrogen, which beats the nine-to-one head start the primary hydrogens have. Light is not optional — without it there is no initiation and no chain. NBS is for allylic positions, where the point is keeping the bromine concentration low, not reaching a tertiary carbon.

q: What makes a chain reaction efficient?
e: Initiation is the slow, expensive step and only has to happen once per chain. That is the whole trick.

q: Why does radical chemistry reappear in mass spectrometry?
e: The molecular ion fragments to leave the most stable radical it can, which is the same stability order you learned here.

q: A carbon radical holds its unpaired electron in which orbital?
e: That planarity is exactly why a new stereocenter formed this way comes out racemic.

q: Radical bromination of butane at C2 creates a new stereocenter. What is the stereochemical outcome, and why?
e: The carbon radical is essentially planar, with its unpaired electron in a p orbital sticking out of both faces equally. Bromine arrives on one face or the other with equal ease, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts. That is a structural fact about the intermediate — no change of solvent or temperature makes a plain radical halogenation enantioselective.

q: A chiral molecule is one that:
e: Chirality means the molecule and its mirror image are distinct, non-superimposable objects — like left and right hands.

q: A molecule with an internal plane of symmetry is generally:
e: An internal mirror plane (plane of symmetry) means the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image — achiral.

q: Which of these is generally considered a chiral object in everyday life?
e: A shoe is a classic macroscopic chiral object — its mirror image (the other foot’s shoe) is not superimposable on the original.

q: A chiral molecule and its mirror image are related as:
e: The defining test for chirality is whether a molecule's mirror image can be rotated and translated to exactly overlap the original. If not, the molecule is chiral.

q: A molecule can be chiral even if it has no tetrahedral stereocenter at all.
e: Chirality is a property of the whole molecule's symmetry, not just of individual carbons. Substituted allenes and certain biphenyls are chiral through axial or restricted-rotation chirality without a classic stereocenter.

q: Which of the following molecules is achiral?
e: Dichloromethane's central carbon carries two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, giving it an internal mirror plane, so it is achiral.

q: Every molecule that contains a carbon bonded to four different groups is necessarily chiral overall.
e: If a molecule has two or more such stereocenters arranged symmetrically, their effects can cancel, producing an achiral meso compound even though individual centers have four different substituents.

q: What physical phenomenon is used experimentally to detect that a sample is chiral (and not racemic)?
e: Chiral compounds (in non-racemic form) rotate the plane of polarized light passing through them; this optical activity is measured with a polarimeter.

q: Which amino acid, unlike the other 19 common amino acids, is achiral?
e: Glycine's alpha carbon bears two identical hydrogen atoms in addition to the amino and carboxyl groups, so it fails the four-different-groups test and is achiral.

q: A chiral stereocenter and a chiral molecule are exactly the same thing.
e: A stereocenter is a single atom whose substituents can be arranged two ways; chirality is a property of the entire molecule's overall symmetry, which can differ from what any one center suggests (as in meso compounds).

q: The two enantiomers of limonene smell different (orange versus lemon/pine) mainly because:
e: Biological receptors are themselves chiral, so they often bind the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule differently, which is why mirror-image compounds can have different biological or sensory effects despite having identical formulas.

q: The thalidomide case is often used to illustrate chirality in pharmacology because:
e: Thalidomide's two enantiomers have very different biological activities, showing why distinguishing and controlling chirality matters in drug development, not just in academic classification.

q: Which symmetry feature, if present in a molecule's lowest-energy conformation or by rapid averaging, guarantees the molecule is achiral?
e: Any internal improper symmetry element, such as a mirror plane or center of inversion, makes a molecule superimposable on its own mirror image, which is the formal definition of achiral.

q: Counting stereocenters is always a completely reliable way to predict whether a specific molecule is chiral.
e: Stereocenter counting is a useful shortcut, but meso compounds show that a molecule with multiple stereocenters can still be achiral overall, so the mirror-image superimposability test is the truly reliable method.

q: Is 3-methylhexane a chiral molecule?
