q: What makes a disconnection legitimate?
e: If you cannot say what reagents would rejoin the pieces, you have drawn a picture rather than planned a synthesis.

q: What is the synthetic equivalent of an acylium synthon RCO+?
e: Which is what makes Friedel-Crafts acylation the forward reaction for that disconnection.

q: What is a retron?
e: Learning to see retrons is most of what makes an experienced chemist fast at this.

q: A beta-hydroxy ketone is the retron for which reaction?
e: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the carbinol carbon: the fragments are an enolate and a carbonyl.

q: A 1,3-dicarbonyl is the retron for which reaction?
e: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the second carbonyl, giving an ester enolate and an ester.

q: A cyclohexene is the retron for which reaction?
e: One disconnection undoing two bonds, which is why it is the highest-value move in the list.

q: A tertiary alcohol is the retron for which reaction?
e: Any C-C bond to the carbinol carbon can be disconnected into a carbanion and a ketone.

q: Which is generally the best place to disconnect?
e: Functional groups are where reactivity lives, so those bonds are the ones you have reactions for.

q: When do you stop disconnecting?
e: A question usually names the permitted starting materials, and that constraint is the real definition of done.

q: Disconnecting 2-phenylbutan-2-ol at the ethyl group gives which pair?
e: The synthons are the carbanion and the ketone; their equivalents are the Grignard and acetophenone.

q: Why write the forward route out at the end?
e: The forward list is a claim: every step has reagents, a product, and a check that it survives the next step.

q: Which disconnection undoes two bonds at once?
e: Cutting across a six-membered ring containing an alkene gives a diene and a dienophile.

q: The synthon RC-C- corresponds to which reagent?
e: Deprotonating a terminal alkyne gives the acetylide, which does SN2 on an alkyl halide.

q: Why is a shorter route usually preferred?
e: Though the arithmetic is worth doing: a longer route of good steps can beat a shorter one of poor steps.

q: What should you do before disconnecting anything?
e: The difference tells you how many C-C bonds must form and what size pieces you need.

q: Roughly how many ways are there to make a C-C bond in an introductory course?
e: Which is what makes synthesis learnable: the skeleton can only be built in a few places.

q: Conjugate addition builds a bond at which carbon?
e: Two positions away from the carbonyl, which is the third attachment point a carbonyl offers.

q: Why is counting carbons the fastest diagnostic?
e: And roughly what size pieces you need, which narrows ten reactions to two or three.

q: Which enolate reactions are essentially one idea?
e: An enolate attacking something electrophilic, differing in what the electrophile is.

q: A carbonyl offers how many distinct attachment points for a new carbon?
e: The carbonyl carbon, the alpha carbon via an enolate, and the beta carbon via conjugate addition.

q: A move up or down the oxidation ladder needs what kind of reagent?
e: Sideways moves within one level are substitutions and need no redox reagent at all.

q: Alcohol to alkyl halide is which kind of move?
e: One bond to an electronegative atom traded for another, with the hydrogen count unchanged.

q: Which conditions give a trans alkene from an alkyne?
e: A dissolving-metal reduction through radical anions, which adopt the less hindered arrangement.

q: How do you make an aldehyde from an ester using only standard reagents?
e: Down two rungs and back up one, because the reduction cannot be stopped halfway.

q: Which sequence gives an anti diol from an alkene?
e: The epoxide is opened by backside attack, putting the oxygens on opposite faces.

q: Why are reagent PAIRS the important thing in this table?
e: Markovnikov against anti-Markovnikov, cis against trans, aldehyde against acid, syn against anti.

q: How do you control where an alkene forms from an alcohol?
e: Acid-catalyzed dehydration gives Zaitsev and can rearrange; E2 on a halide lets you choose.

q: Which groups also destroy a Grignard?
e: Any acidic proton, which is also why the reaction is run in scrupulously dry ether.

q: What protects an alcohol from a Grignard?
e: TBSCl with imidazole replaces the O-H with an O-Si bond, leaving no acidic proton.

q: What protects a ketone from a hydride or Grignard?
e: The acetal has no C=O and no electrophilic carbon, so there is nothing to attack.

q: A molecule has an aldehyde and an ester, and you want to reduce only the ester. Protect?
e: The aldehyde is the MORE reactive of the two, so there is no way to reach the ester selectively.

q: What happens to a Grignard in wet solvent?
e: Water does exactly what an alcohol O-H does, which is why dry ether is essential.

q: What should you do after finishing a retrosynthetic analysis?
e: Errors of order are invisible in a retrosynthetic tree and obvious in a forward list.

q: What is wrong with a route giving a single enantiomer from achiral inputs?
e: Getting one enantiomer needs a chiral reagent, catalyst, starting material, or a resolution.

q: What final check catches an extra carbon in your route?
e: Cyanide, CO2 and formaldehyde routes all add exactly one carbon, so mixing them up is easy.

q: What does the question 'does this product survive the next step' catch?
e: Making an aldehyde and then running a reaction in aqueous base will not leave you with an aldehyde.

q: What should you ask about stereochemistry in a route?
e: If the target has defined stereochemistry, some step has to set it, and you should be able to name it.

q: What is a carbohydrate, in functional-group terms?
e: Every property of a sugar follows from a carbonyl surrounded by alcohols on the same chain.

q: A sugar whose carbonyl is at the end of the chain is called what?
e: Aldehyde at C1. A carbonyl inside the chain, usually C2, makes it a ketose instead.

q: Fructose has its carbonyl at C2. What does that make it?
e: Six carbons and an internal carbonyl: keto- for the position, -hexose for the count.

q: In a Fischer projection, which carbon decides whether a sugar is D or L?
e: One carbon carries the whole label, and it is the one at the bottom of the drawing.

q: Does calling a sugar D tell you which way it rotates polarized light?
e: D fixes one stereocenter's drawn position; the observed rotation is a measured property of the whole molecule.

q: What forms when the C5 OH of glucose adds to its own C1 carbonyl?
e: One alcohol plus one carbonyl gives a hemiacetal; it takes a second alcohol to reach an acetal.

q: Which carbon of the ring form is the anomeric carbon?
e: It was the carbonyl carbon, so after cyclization it holds the ring oxygen and an OH.

q: What are anomers?
e: They differ at the anomeric carbon only, which is the one stereocenter the ring can open and reset.

q: Which anomer of D-glucopyranose dominates at equilibrium?
e: Beta puts the anomeric OH equatorial, and glucose is the sugar that can get every substituent equatorial.

q: What makes a sugar a reducing sugar?
e: The test oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde, so the ring has to be able to open to supply it.

q: Capping the anomeric OH with a second alcohol gives what?
e: Two OR groups on the anomeric carbon is a full acetal, and the sugar-specific name for it is glycoside.

q: What kind of bond joins two sugar units in a disaccharide?
e: One anomeric carbon, two OR groups, made by an alcohol displacing the anomeric OH under acid.

q: Cellulose and amylose are both 1,4 chains of D-glucose. What differs?
e: One stereocenter on one carbon, and the two materials could hardly behave less alike.

q: Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
e: The enzyme reads the configuration at the anomeric carbon, and it only fits alpha.

q: Fructose is a ketose, yet it gives a positive Tollens' test. Why?
e: The test medium is basic, and an alpha deprotonation gives an enediol that can collapse to the aldose.

q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from an acetal at the anomeric carbon?
e: Tollens' oxidizes the free aldehyde a hemiacetal supplies, and an acetal supplies none.

q: Why is beta-D-glucopyranose the most stable common hexose ring?
e: No 1,3-diaxial strain anywhere in the chair, which is a conformational argument, not a new one.

q: Which four groups sit on the alpha carbon of an amino acid?
e: The alpha carbon is defined as the one next to the carboxyl, and it carries the amine.

q: Which L-amino acid has the R configuration?
e: Sulfur outranks the carboxyl carbon in CIP priority, so the ranking around the alpha carbon reshuffles.

q: What is the dominant form of an amino acid near neutral pH?
e: A pKa 2 acid and a pKa 9 base in one molecule transfer the proton to each other.

q: Roughly what is the pKa of an amino acid's carboxyl group?
e: Lower than acetic acid's 4.8, because the nearby ammonium withdraws inductively.

q: Roughly what is the pKa of an amino acid's alpha-ammonium group?
e: Typical for an alkylammonium ion, pulled down slightly by the adjacent carboxylate.

q: What is the isoelectric point?
e: Plus and minus cancel exactly, which is a property of the pH rather than of the molecule alone.

q: For a side chain that does not ionize, how is pI calculated?
e: The two values bracketing the neutral form, which for a simple side chain are the only two.

q: Glycine has pKa values 2.34 and 9.60. What is its pI?
e: Half of the sum. Note it is below 7, so an isoelectric solution is mildly acidic.

q: Alanine has pKa values 2.34 and 9.69. What is its pI?
e: The same average, and the result is close to glycine's because the side chain is inert in both.

q: Aspartic acid has a pI of 2.77. Why so low?
e: Two acidic groups have to be neutralized before the molecule is uncharged, so the balance point drops.

q: Lysine has a pI near 9.7. What does that tell you?
e: A second amine has to stay protonated, so you must go to high pH before the charge cancels.

q: At pH 7, what is the charge on a lysine side chain?
e: The side-chain ammonium has a pKa near 10.5, so at pH 7 it is overwhelmingly protonated.

q: Which class does phenylalanine's side chain belong to?
e: A benzyl group with no heteroatom, so water pushes it into the protein's interior.

q: Which amino acid can form a covalent cross-link in a protein?
e: Two SH groups oxidize to a disulfide, the only covalent link outside the backbone.

q: Where do nonpolar side chains end up in a folded, water-soluble protein?
e: The hydrophobic effect: burying them frees the water that would otherwise be ordered around them.

q: Histidine is the only side chain with a pKa near 6. Why does that matter?
e: A pKa near the working pH means the residue can act as either an acid or a base in a mechanism.

q: How would you separate two amino acids with pI values of 3.2 and 9.7?
e: A pH between the two pI values forces them to opposite signs, so they migrate in opposite directions.

q: Why is an amino acid least soluble in water at its pI?
e: Without a net charge there is no electrostatic repulsion keeping the molecules apart.

q: How many ionizable groups does aspartic acid have?
e: Two carboxyls and one ammonium, so three pKa values and a pI set by the lowest two.

q: What functional group is a peptide bond?
e: A carboxyl joined to an amine with loss of water gives an amide, and nothing about proteins changes that.

q: What does amide resonance do to the C-N bond?
e: The nitrogen lone pair pushes into the carbonyl, so the real bond is between single and double.

q: Roughly how long is the peptide C-N bond?
e: Between a single bond at 1.47 and a double bond, exactly as the resonance picture predicts.

q: Why is rotation about the peptide C-N bond restricted?
e: Rotating would break the overlap that the second resonance structure depends on.

q: Is the peptide nitrogen basic?
e: A lone pair already spent on the neighboring carbonyl cannot also grab a proton.

q: Where is an amide protonated in strong acid?
e: Protonating oxygen keeps the resonance stabilization; protonating nitrogen would destroy it.

q: How does an amide rank among acyl derivatives for reactivity?
e: The strongest lone-pair donation gives the greatest stabilization and the lowest reactivity.

q: What is primary structure?
e: The only level whose structure is its covalent bonds, and the one from which the others follow.

q: What is quaternary structure?
e: Hemoglobin's four subunits are the standard example, and a single-chain protein has none.

q: What contributes most to tertiary structure?
e: Burying nonpolar side chains releases the ordered water around them, which is the large term.

q: Which interaction in a folded protein is covalent?
e: Everything else holding a fold together is noncovalent, which is why folding is reversible.

q: Why does boiling not hydrolyze a protein to amino acids?
e: An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, and 100 C water is nowhere near enough.

q: Why does proline disrupt an alpha helix?
e: No N-H means no hydrogen bond donor at that position, and the ring restricts the geometry.

q: Which level of structure does a single point mutation change directly?
e: It changes one residue in the sequence, and the other levels change only as a consequence.

q: What does hydrolyzing a protein completely give?
e: Every amide is cut, and each residue is released with its own carboxyl and amine restored.

q: Why can any sequence form a beta sheet in principle?
e: Secondary structure is a backbone property, so the side chains only tip the preference.

q: What makes a protein water soluble?
e: The fold puts the polar residues outside and the nonpolar ones in, which is the hydrophobic effect stated the other way round.

q: How is the lipid class defined?
e: It collects the cell components that dissolve in nonpolar solvents, which is why it holds fats and steroids together.

q: Why does a cis double bond lower a fatty acid's melting point?
e: Melting separates molecules, and a bent chain makes much less contact with the next one.

q: Elaidic acid is C18 with one trans double bond and melts near 44 C. What does that show?
e: It is unsaturated and still nearly as high-melting as the saturated acid, because it is still straight.

q: What does heating a triglyceride with aqueous NaOH give?
e: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis three times over, and the excess base deprotonates each acid.

q: Why do phospholipids form bilayers rather than micelles?
e: A one-tailed molecule tapers into a sphere; a two-tailed one is a cylinder and tiles into a sheet.

q: What is the lipid bilayer?
e: Tails inward and heads facing the water on both sides, which is every cell membrane.

q: What does cholesterol do in a membrane?
e: A rigid ring system inserted among flexible chains changes how easily they move.

q: What is partial hydrogenation used for industrially?
e: Removing double bonds straightens chains, so the material packs better and melts higher.

q: Why does partial hydrogenation create trans fats?
e: An alkene that picks up one hydrogen and loses it again does not remember its original geometry.

q: Why does a trans fat behave like a saturated fat physically?
e: The property that sets the melting point is shape, and trans barely bends the chain.

q: What is a wax, chemically?
e: One ester joining two long chains, which is why waxes are hard and very water-repellent.

q: Why are lipids a compact energy store compared with carbohydrates?
e: A more reduced carbon has further to fall on oxidation, so more energy is released per gram.

q: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
e: Sugar plus base is a nucleoside; adding the phosphate ester makes it a nucleotide.

q: What kind of bond joins a base to its sugar?
e: A nitrogen displaces the anomeric OH, which is acetal formation with N in place of O.

q: Which carbon of the sugar bonds to the base?
e: The anomeric carbon is the electrophilic one, exactly as in ordinary glycoside formation.

q: Which OH of the sugar carries the phosphate that a polymerase adds to a growing chain?
e: Polymerases use 5 prime triphosphates, and the 3 prime OH of the chain is the nucleophile that attacks one. A 3 prime monophosphate is a perfectly good nucleotide too, but it is not what gets added.

q: What links one nucleotide to the next?
e: One phosphorus esterified to two different sugars, 3 prime of one and 5 prime of the next.

q: Why are nucleic acids called acids?
e: A row of negative charges on the outside, which is also why they dissolve in water.

q: How many hydrogen bonds join a G-C pair?
e: One more than A-T, and that difference shows up directly in melting temperature.

q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
e: Weak bonds on purpose, because anything read must first be opened without being destroyed.

q: What does denaturing DNA do?
e: Only the hydrogen bonds between bases are undone, which is why the strands can re-anneal.

q: Why does RNA hydrolyze much faster than DNA in base?
e: An intramolecular attack through a five-membered ring is enormously faster than one from solution.

q: Why is DNA rather than RNA used for long-term storage?
e: Removing one hydroxyl removes the internal nucleophile, and with it the built-in self-destruct.

q: What conditions cleave the base from the sugar?
e: It is an N,O-acetal, and acetals are cut by aqueous acid and stable to base. The rate is very uneven: purines depurinate far more readily than pyrimidines.

q: Which part of a nucleotide carries the genetic information?
e: Sugar and phosphate repeat identically along the chain, so only the bases can vary.

q: Why is the carbon of a Grignard reagent nucleophilic?
e: Carbon at 2.55 against magnesium at 1.31, so the bonding electrons sit on carbon.

q: What is umpolung?
e: An alkyl halide's carbon is an electrophile; the Grignard made from it is a nucleophile at the same carbon.

q: Where is carbon's Pauling electronegativity?
e: Magnesium is 1.31, lithium 0.98 and oxygen 3.44, which is why the first two invert the polarity and the third does not.

q: Is the C-Mg bond ionic?
e: A Grignard is not a free carbanion, though it behaves like one and the arrow starts at the C-metal bond.

q: Which organometallic is the most reactive?
e: The widest electronegativity gap gives the most carbanion character and the least selectivity.

q: Which organometallic is the most selective?
e: Copper sits close to carbon, so the bond is barely polar and the reagent can be pointed at one site.

q: What does high reactivity cost an organometallic reagent?
e: The two trade against each other more visibly here than anywhere else in the course.

q: Which nucleophiles has this course mostly used before organometallics?
e: Hydroxide, alkoxides, amines, halides, cyanide — and a heteroatom nucleophile can only attach a heteroatom.

q: Why is a carbon nucleophile needed to build a skeleton?
e: Whatever attacks is what gets attached, so attaching carbon means attacking with carbon.

q: Which two carbon nucleophiles appeared before this chapter?
e: Both are narrow: cyanide brings one carbon with a nitrile attached, and an acetylide must come from a terminal alkyne.

q: How is a Grignard reagent made?
e: The metal inserts into the carbon-halogen bond; nothing is added and nothing leaves.

q: Which reaction gives a magnesium alkoxide WITHOUT forming a new C-C bond?
e: Deprotonating an alcohol gives the same magnesium alkoxide that a Grignard addition does, but the reagent has been spent on a proton and no carbon was joined to anything.

q: Why is an aryl Grignard useful even though aryl halides resist substitution?
e: The metal inserts into the C-X bond rather than displacing the halide from behind.

q: If a substrate has an OH and a ketone, which does a Grignard reach first?
e: Proton transfer is the fastest reaction available, so the reagent is spent before it can add.

q: What is the practical signal that a Grignard preparation has failed?
e: Wet glassware quenches the reagent as fast as it forms, so the metal never gets used up.

q: A Grignard reagent plus formaldehyde gives what after workup?
e: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, so after one R group is added that carbon still carries two.

q: A Grignard plus an aldehyde other than formaldehyde gives what?
e: One hydrogen and one R group were already there; the Grignard adds the second R.

q: A Grignard plus CO2, then acid, gives what?
e: One carbon longer, and it arrives already at the carboxylic acid oxidation level.

q: A Grignard plus an epoxide gives what?
e: The attack is an SN2 at the less hindered carbon, and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.

q: Where does a Grignard attack an epoxide?
e: There is no acid present, so no carbocation character develops and sterics decide.

q: How many equivalents of Grignard does an ester consume?
e: The ketone formed after the first addition is more electrophilic than the ester was.

q: Why can an ester not be stopped at the ketone with one equivalent?
e: The OR group donates into the carbonyl and makes the ester the sluggish one of the pair.

q: What is a Weinreb amide used for?
e: Its chelated intermediate survives until workup, so no second addition can occur.

q: How many carbons does ethylene oxide add to a chain?
e: Which is why it is the standard two-carbon extension. A substituted epoxide adds more, and the attack still goes at the less hindered carbon.

q: Which target is 1-bromopropane plus Mg plus propanone plus acid?
e: A ketone plus a Grignard gives a tertiary alcohol, here with methyl, methyl and propyl.

q: Which is the last resort for an acidic proton in a Grignard substrate?
e: Two extra steps means two extra yields lost, so it is worth it only when the alternatives fail.

q: Why does acetaldehyde sometimes give poor yields with a Grignard?
e: A very strong base and an alpha hydrogen in the same flask is an acid-base reaction waiting to happen.

q: What is the correct order of operations for a Grignard reaction?
e: Having the electrophile present while the reagent forms invites enolization and self-condensation.

q: What class of alcohol comes from a Grignard plus an acyl chloride in excess?
e: Two additions again, but not for the ester's reason: an acyl chloride is the most electrophilic acyl derivative, and the ketone it gives is simply still reactive enough to be attacked as fast as it forms.

q: Which is the correct disconnection for a tertiary alcohol?
e: Each cut gives a carbanion and a ketone, and there are three legitimate choices.

q: Why does RLi plus a carboxylic acid stop at the ketone?
e: The ketone does not exist in the flask, so there is nothing for a second equivalent to attack.

q: What makes LDA useful?
e: That pairing is what allows complete enolate formation without attack on the carbonyl.

q: Why is LDA a weaker base than n-BuLi?
e: An amine pKa near 36 against an alkane near 50, and it is still far more than enough.

q: What distinguishes t-BuLi from n-BuLi in practice?
e: Bulk does slow its approach to a hindered carbonyl, but t-BuLi is still a fine nucleophile and the standard reagent for lithium-halogen exchange. LDA is the reagent for which basic-but-not-nucleophilic actually holds.

q: What is the approximate pKa of a terminal alkyne C-H?
e: An alkene is 44 and an alkane 50, so the alkyne is by far the most acidic of the three.

q: What does Na in liquid NH3 give from an internal alkyne?
e: A dissolving-metal reduction through a vinyl radical anion, which settles trans.

q: Can an organolithium do everything a Grignard does?
e: The extra reactivity is mostly something to manage rather than something to use.

q: Why can an alkyne not be alkylated twice in the same step?
e: Alkylating a terminal alkyne makes it internal, and an internal alkyne has no acidic C-H.

q: What is the intermediate in the RLi plus carboxylic acid reaction?
e: Two negative charges on one carbon's oxygens. It cannot collapse, because that would mean expelling O2- and adding a third charge, so it survives until workup.

q: Which reagent would you choose to form a ketone enolate completely?
e: Hydroxide gives an equilibrium, n-BuLi attacks the carbonyl, and pyridine is far too weak.

q: Where does a Grignard add to an enone?
e: Hard nucleophile, charge control, and the carbonyl carbon carries the most positive charge.

q: What is the product of an enone plus a cuprate?
e: 1,4 addition gives an enolate, which protonates and tautomerizes back to the ketone.

q: Why can a cuprate couple with a vinyl halide?
e: A vinyl carbon is sp2 and its backside is shielded, so substitution is unavailable.

q: Why does an enone have two electrophilic carbons?
e: Resonance puts positive character on the beta carbon as well as the carbonyl carbon.

q: Why can PCC not fix a tertiary alcohol into a ketone?
e: An oxidation at that carbon needs a C-H to remove, and a tertiary alcohol has none.

q: What would a Grignard do to a substrate containing both an enone and an ester?
e: Low selectivity is the cost of high reactivity; a cuprate would leave the ester alone.

q: What kind of control does a soft nucleophile follow?
e: Which points it at the largest LUMO coefficient rather than the largest partial charge.

q: Which metal catalyzes the standard cross-coupling reactions?
e: Copper appears as a cocatalyst in the Sonogashira, but palladium runs the cycle.

q: What are the three steps of the cross-coupling cycle?
e: The first and last names describe what happens to the palladium's oxidation state.

q: Why is palladium a catalyst rather than a reagent?
e: Reductive elimination hands back the Pd(0) the cycle started with, so a few mole percent turns over thousands of times.

q: Which coupling uses no organometallic partner at all?
e: An alkene inserts into the Ar-Pd bond instead, so there is no transmetalation step.

q: Why does a Suzuki coupling need a base?
e: A neutral boronic acid transfers its R group poorly; the four-coordinate borate does it well.

q: Why did the Suzuki coupling displace the Stille industrially?
e: The chemistry of the Stille is at least as good; the toxicity of organotin is what settled it.

q: Why does a convergent route return more material?
e: Ten linear steps at 85% gives about 20%; two five-step branches joined gives about 37%.

q: Which functional groups survive a Suzuki coupling?
e: The reactive carbon is bound to a metal throughout and never exists as a free carbanion.

q: Which bond should signal a cross-coupling disconnection?
e: Neither ring is nucleophilic or electrophilic enough for anything from earlier chapters.

q: Can an aryl Grignard be made from an aryl bromide?
e: Bromides and iodides go readily. Aryl chlorides are sluggish and need heat or activation, and aryl fluorides do not go at all. The trouble with the reagent is what it does afterward, not whether it forms.

q: What is an ylide?
e: Both charges are real and next to each other, which is why the thing is reactive.

q: What drives the Wittig forward?
e: A P=O double bond at around 130-140 kcal/mol, one of the strongest in organic chemistry, formed in the last step.

q: What is the four-membered intermediate called?
e: It falls apart in the one way it can, giving the alkene and the phosphine oxide.

q: How does a Wittig differ from an elimination?
e: An elimination forms the C=C between two carbons already bonded, so Zaitsev chooses where.

q: What does cyclohexanone plus Ph3P=CH2 give?
e: An exocyclic alkene, and the less stable of the two isomers, which is exactly the point.

q: What does an unstabilized ylide give?
e: It adds fast and irreversibly, so the geometry of the transition state is locked in.

q: Which gives the less stable alkene geometry?
e: A fast irreversible step has no time to equilibrate, which inverts the usual intuition.

q: What does a primary amine plus a ketone give?
e: One hydrogen is left on nitrogen after the addition, so the C=N+ cation loses it.

q: What does a tertiary amine plus a ketone give?
e: With no N-H at all there is no way forward, which is why tertiary amines serve as bases here.

q: How is the equilibrium pulled forward?
e: A Dean-Stark trap or molecular sieves; every step of the sequence is reversible.

q: What is reductive amination?
e: NaBH3CN reduces the imine as it forms, avoiding the over-alkylation of direct SN2.

q: What reagent selectively reduces an imine?
e: Mild enough to leave the ketone alone while reducing the more electrophilic iminium.

q: What is the Michael acceptor?
e: An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, with the beta carbon as the electrophilic site.

q: What spacing does a Michael addition leave?
e: Joining the donor alpha carbon to the acceptor beta carbon puts them five apart.

q: Why must the donor be doubly stabilized?
e: Spreading the charge over two carbonyls is what makes the enolate soft rather than hard.

q: What is methyl vinyl ketone used as?
e: Cheap, and the ring its Robinson product gives is the one steroid chemistry needed.

q: Which step makes a Robinson annulation irreversible?
e: Conjugating the alkene with the carbonyl is the stabilization it cannot climb back out of.

q: How do you undo a Robinson annulation on paper?
e: Reverse order: put the water back, break the aldol bond, then cut beta to a carbonyl.

q: Why does a soft nucleophile add 1,4?
e: Orbital control rather than charge control, and the beta carbon has the larger coefficient.

q: Which reaction sequence builds a cyclohexenone from two acyclic pieces?
e: A Diels-Alder builds a ring too, but it gives a cyclohexene rather than a cyclohexenone.

q: What does a malonic ester synthesis give?
e: Malonate has two esters: one carboxyl is lost as CO2 and the other stays as the acid.

q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of diethyl malonate?
e: Delocalizing the carbanion onto two ester oxygens is worth twelve orders of magnitude.

q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of an ordinary ester?
e: Too high for a convenient base, and a strong base would attack the ester instead.

q: Why is the second carbonyl there?
e: It is thrown away once the alkylation is done, which is what an activating group is.

q: Why does the intermediate decarboxylate on heating?
e: A six-membered cyclic transition state reaches from the carboxyl O-H to that second carbonyl. It is a ketone in the acetoacetic route and the other carboxyl in the malonic one, and either works.

q: Would an alpha-keto acid decarboxylate on warming?
e: The geometry needs the second carbonyl exactly beta, whether that carbonyl is a ketone or another carboxyl.

q: What product would ethyl acetoacetate plus benzyl bromide give?
e: A methyl ketone carrying the benzyl group, after hydrolysis and decarboxylation.

q: Which halides would make 2-methylpentanoic acid from malonate?
e: The alpha carbon of the target carries a methyl and a propyl, installed in two rounds.

q: Which target is out of reach for an acetoacetic ester synthesis?
e: All four are methyl ketones, so the product class does not decide it; the halide does.

q: Which reagent performs the hydrolysis and decarboxylation?
e: One step does both, because the beta-keto acid does not survive the temperature.

q: What does the alkoxide base need to match?
e: Using ethoxide with an ethyl ester avoids scrambling the ester by transesterification.

q: Which carbon of malonate is alkylated?
e: That is the only acidic position, and it is acidic because of the flanking carbonyls.

q: What does a Baeyer-Villiger oxidation do to a ketone?
e: The product is an ester, and almost nothing else in the course touches that bond.

q: What kind of step is the migration?
e: The same motion that rearranges a carbocation, running on a neutral intermediate.

q: What does the migrating group take with it?
e: Which is why it never exists as a free species and never loses its configuration.

q: What migrates in a methyl ketone?
e: Methyl is last in the series, which makes methyl ketones the predictable substrates.

q: What leaves in a Baeyer-Villiger?
e: The peroxyacid's other half, which is what makes the O-O bond a good place to break.

q: Why is this reaction usable on a chiral center?
e: One of very few reactions at this level where a stereocenter survives a bond change intact.

q: What class of compound is the product?
e: Which you already know how to hydrolyze, so the reaction slots into longer routes.

q: What kind of ring expansion is this?
e: One of the few reliable ring expansions at this level, and the only one adding oxygen.

q: Which retrosynthetic clue suggests a Baeyer-Villiger?
e: Esterifying a tertiary alcohol is hard; migrating a tertiary group is the easiest case.

q: Why will chlorobenzene not undergo SN1?
e: The positive charge would sit in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, with no way to delocalize.

q: What is the SNAr intermediate called?
e: Negatively charged and not aromatic, which is what the withdrawing groups pay for.

q: Why is fluorine best in SNAr?
e: The C-X bond is not breaking in the rate-determining step, so electronegativity decides.

q: What is benzyne's extra bond made from?
e: They point away from each other rather than overlapping properly, which is why it is strained.

q: What proved benzyne exists?
e: No direct displacement could put the nucleophile on a carbon that never bore the leaving group.

q: Why is the Meisenheimer complex stable enough to form?
e: Delocalization onto the substituents is what makes losing aromaticity affordable.

q: Which halide is worst for SNAr?
e: Iodine is the least electronegative of the four, so it activates the carbon least.

q: Why is a benzylic cation stabilized?
e: The charge spreads over the benzylic carbon plus both ortho and the para positions.

q: What does hot KMnO4 do to propylbenzene?
e: Chain length makes no difference; everything past the benzylic carbon is cut away.

q: What should a benzoic acid suggest retrosynthetically?
e: Oxidation converts any alkyl chain to a carboxyl, so the chain identity is free.

q: Which product comes from isopropylbenzene and hot KMnO4?
e: One benzylic hydrogen is enough, and both methyls go with the rest of the chain.

q: What is a phenol?
e: An OH on a carbon next to the ring is a benzylic alcohol, which behaves quite differently.

q: Which base deprotonates a phenol?
e: Bicarbonate is not strong enough, which is what makes it useful as a discriminator.

q: What is carbonic acid's pKa?
e: Between a phenol at 10 and a carboxylic acid at 4.8, which is the whole basis of the separation.

q: Is OH ortho/para or meta directing?
e: Donation reaches the ortho and para positions, which is where the substitution goes.

q: What does phenol plus bromine water give?
e: No Lewis acid catalyst is needed, and all three activated positions react at once.

q: What is 2,4-dinitrophenol's approximate pKa?
e: Two nitro groups in resonance-capable positions, and now as acidic as a carboxylic acid.

q: Which is more acidic, phenol or acetic acid?
e: 4.8 against 10, because a carboxylate spreads charge over two equivalent oxygens.

q: Why does a carboxylate beat a phenoxide at stabilizing charge?
e: A phenoxide spreads charge onto carbons, which hold it less well than oxygen does.

q: Why is the 1,4-diene formed rather than the 1,3?
e: Protonation happens where charge density is highest, not where stability is greatest.

q: With a withdrawing group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
e: A withdrawing group holds the charge on its own carbon, so that carbon is protonated.

q: Which reaction uses the same electron-then-proton pattern?
e: Both are dissolving-metal reductions running on solvated electrons, and both give the opposite outcome from catalytic hydrogenation on the same substrate.

q: Which starting material gives an enol ether on Birch reduction?
e: The methoxy stays on a double bond, and a C=C with an OR on it is an enol ether.

q: Why can an unconjugated diene be functionalized selectively?
e: A conjugated diene reacts as one system, which makes single-site chemistry harder.

q: Why does a withdrawing group put its carbon sp3?
e: The carbanion sits where the substituent lets it, and that carbon gets the proton.

q: Why does the Birch not over-reduce to cyclohexane?
e: Adding an electron to an isolated alkene is far harder than to an aromatic ring.

q: What does warm water give?
e: The standard way phenols are made, since no substitution works at that C-O bond.

q: What intermediate forms when a diazonium salt loses N2?
e: Badly unstable, which is why it grabs whatever nucleophile is present at once. In warm water that nucleophile is water, and the product is the phenol.

q: Which reaction sequence lets you place a group meta when it would go ortho/para?
e: Directing effects cannot be argued with, so you change what is doing the directing.

q: What is a monomer?
e: The repeating piece inside the chain is the repeat unit, which may differ from the monomer.

q: How do you tell addition from condensation quickly?
e: A lighter repeat unit means something was expelled; matching formulas mean nothing was, so for an alkene monomer, addition.

q: What is a thermoset?
e: Heating destroys it rather than softening it, because melting would mean breaking bonds.

q: What polymer comes from tetrafluoroethylene?
e: Teflon, and there is no head-to-tail question because both carbons are identical.

q: What does tacticity describe?
e: Each substituted backbone carbon has a fixed orientation, and tacticity names the pattern they make.

q: What tacticity does radical polymerization give?
e: A planar radical has no strong preference about which face the next monomer arrives on.

q: Why is ordinary polystyrene amorphous?
e: Syndiotactic polystyrene has the same phenyl group and is crystalline, melting near 270 C, so bulk is not the cause. Atacticity is.

q: What is nylon 6,6 made from?
e: First number the diamine's carbons, second the diacid's: hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid.

q: What is Kevlar made from?
e: Both aromatic and both para-substituted, which is what makes the chains straight.

q: Which resists hydrolysis better?
e: Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative, which carries over to the material.

q: Why does polyester fabric lose strength in hot alkali faster than nylon?
e: The acyl reactivity ladder applied to a material. It is not a blanket ranking: nylon is the one attacked by acid, chlorine and sunlight.

q: Is Kevlar a thermoset?
e: No cross-links, so not a network. It has no melt either, decomposing near 500 C and spun from solution.

q: What are the two monomers of a polyester, read backwards?
e: Cut the acyl C-O bond, leaving the oxygen on the alcohol side, and check each fragment has two reactive sites.

q: What happens to a stretched rubber band when heated?
e: The entropic restoring force scales with temperature, unlike almost every other material.

q: What do bulky side groups do?
e: They raise Tg and slow crystallization. In polystyrene the random placement is what actually prevents packing.

q: A polymer backbone contains esters. What were the monomers?
e: Cut the acyl C-O bond of each ester: OH to the acid side, H to the alcohol side.

q: A disconnection gives a fragment with one reactive group. What does that mean?
e: Every chain-forming monomer must have two, which is what let it join on both sides.

q: How do you check a polyester disconnection by atom count?
e: One water per ester bond, and a diacid-plus-diol repeat unit has two. PET: 166 + 62 - 192 = 36.

q: Why is polyethylene not chemically recyclable?
e: No bond hydrolysis can pick out from any other. Cracking it back to feedstock works, but that is pyrolysis, not selective cleavage.

q: What does an amorphous rigid polymer get its rigidity from?
e: PMMA through bulky side groups; polycarbonate through rigid bisphenol A units in the backbone.

q: Toward nucleophiles, the reactivity order is:
e: Sterics and electronics point the same way, and the hydration table measures it.

q: Why does fructose give a positive Benedict's test?
e: Through an enediol, which is why a free anomeric carbon rather than an aldehyde is the real test.

q: Why is sucrose not a reducing sugar?
e: The glycosidic bond ties up both anomeric carbons, and a free one is what a positive test needs.

q: RCN with aqueous H3O+ and heat gives:
e: Through the amide, and no oxidant is needed because it is a move along the rung.

q: Which conditions give clean monohalogenation?
e: The halogen makes the carbonyl harder to protonate, so the second enol forms more slowly.

q: Why does base halogenation run past one halogen?
e: Halogen stabilizes the next enolate's charge, so each step speeds up the one after.

q: Does LDA at room temperature give the thermodynamic enolate?
e: Its own deprotonation never reverses, though the amine it leaves behind will equilibrate the mixture if warmed.

q: What lets the two enolates interconvert?
e: Leftover ketone or the amine the base generated will do it; NaH is irreversible and still thermodynamic.

q: Why does an enamine stop after one alkylation?
e: No nucleophilic carbon is left and no base is present to restore one, so a second alkylation is impossible.

q: Why does ammonia plus RX give mixtures?
e: Each added alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so the product outruns the ammonia still in the flask.

q: Direct alkylation of ammonia delivers what?
e: Relative rates decide it, so adding less halide does not help; only a big excess of ammonia biases it.
